courses.title: The robotics workstation
courses.subtitle: Build a reproducible Linux environment and write programs that fail predictably.
courses.description: Begin with the tools that make every later robot experiment understandable: the operating system, terminal, network, source history, Python, and C++. You will record a complete environment manifest, distinguish host and container networking, validate numerical inputs, and reason about memory ownership. The examples operate on invented telemetry and local processes. This lets you make mistakes without moving a robot. Completion means you can reproduce a small program from a clean checkout and explain its inputs, outputs, failure behavior, and dependencies. It does not require prior programming experience, but it requires doing the exercises rather than watching demonstrations.
prerequisites: A computer capable of running an Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine or Linux installation
outcomes: Produce a versioned environment manifest
Diagnose process, path, permission, and network failures
Implement checked numeric functions in Python and C++

courses.title: ROS 2 applications from first principles
courses.subtitle: Design a graph, choose the correct interfaces, and build a working ROS package.
courses.description: Learn ROS 2 by inspecting the information a running application actually exchanges. Separate processes from nodes, names from types, and communication success from application correctness. Use topics for streams, services for bounded transactions, and actions for work that needs feedback or cancellation. Build a small telemetry package with an explicit interface contract and a repeatable build. You will measure the behavior of existing demo nodes before writing your own. Every exercise asks for evidence, including a deliberately introduced failure and its explanation, so successful completion demonstrates more than remembering command names.
outcomes: Draw and inspect a ROS graph
Justify topic, service, and action choices
Build and run an installable Python ROS package

courses.title: Time, frames, and distributed ROS
courses.subtitle: Find the failures hidden between machines, callbacks, clocks, and coordinate systems.
courses.description: A program can compile correctly and still interpret the wrong time, coordinate frame, or network endpoint. This course develops a systematic way to find those failures. You will distinguish discovery from message delivery, predict requested and offered QoS compatibility, measure callback delays, and compose transforms with explicit frame conventions. The final lesson separates network partitioning from authentication and authorization. These are the foundations for reading any vendor SDK critically: a transport connection is not proof that data is fresh, meaningful, or authorized. Exercises use local DDS participants and mathematical examples before any robot network is involved.
outcomes: Diagnose discovery and QoS mismatches
Calculate stale-data and scheduling budgets
Transform vectors between documented frames
Explain ROS network security boundaries

courses.title: Models, configuration, and evidence
courses.subtitle: Describe a robot and make its behavior reproducible, observable, and testable.
courses.description: Turn a collection of scripts into an inspectable robotics project. You will distinguish visual geometry from collision and inertial models, build repeatable launch configuration, record a narrowly scoped bag, and construct tests that catch the failure modes your application claims to handle. Configuration and logs become part of the experiment instead of afterthoughts. The exercises deliberately include misleading success signals: a model that looks correct but has implausible inertia, a launched process that is not ready, and a passing test that checks too little. Completion requires artifacts another learner can use to reproduce your results.
outcomes: Audit a minimal URDF and its frame tree
Launch a namespaced graph with validated parameters
Record and replay a reproducible dataset
Create tests and a diagnostic failure report

courses.title: Unitree G1: SDK2 and ROS 2
courses.subtitle: Build an auditable G1 integration from exact hardware identity to verified simulation.
courses.description: Learn the parts of a G1 integration that determine whether software communicates correctly: edition, joint configuration, pinned SDK versions, DDS discovery, wire types, coordinate conventions, control ownership, and timing. Work through vendor source rather than assuming every example is a safe diagnostic. The course builds a read-only state inspector and a simulation validation record, with concrete evidence for each compatibility decision. Hardware operation is an additional supervised stage for supported development editions; a successful simulator run does not certify a physical controller. The result is an integration package another engineer can reproduce and review.
outcomes: Distinguish hardware edition from software compatibility
Explain HG state and command schemas
Diagnose discovery and data validity separately
Validate an isolated G1 simulation

courses.title: Unitree Go1: the legacy SDK
courses.subtitle: Understand UDP control, firmware compatibility, and the real cost of a ROS 2 bridge port.
courses.description: Go1 uses a different development generation from G1 and Go2. This course keeps that difference visible while teaching version contracts, UDP packet structure, high-level versus joint control, and the limitations of the historical ROS 2 bridge. You will inspect actual source, design a transport-independent fixture, and test command freshness and conversion behavior without sending motor commands. The capstone is an evidence-backed migration plan with a tested offline adapter contract. The course does not imply that an old Eloquent project is already validated on Humble, or that every retail Go1 edition includes development access.
outcomes: Match legacy SDK and firmware versions
Trace bridge transport and callback behavior
Design a stale-command gate
Build a reproducible migration evidence package

courses.title: AGIBOT X2: AimDK engineering
courses.subtitle: Build an observable, version-matched X2 application from simulation to supervised deployment.
courses.description: Learn the actual X2 integration contract: hardware variants, Humble environments, motion modes, input ownership, sensor timing, model calibration, and failure behavior. Work from current official AimDK documentation and immutable robot-model references. Most labs run offline or in simulation; hardware labs begin with observation. The course treats locomotion, upper-body control, and low-level joint control as different interfaces with different guarantees. You will finish with a tested application design, an explicit evidence bundle, and a reviewable transition plan for your particular robot. A simulation pass demonstrates software behavior; it does not certify physical balance or task safety.
prerequisites: ROS 2 topics, services, QoS and transforms
outcomes: Select the correct model and SDK for an X2 nameplate
Diagnose mode and ownership failures separately
Measure sensor timing and application stop behavior
Produce an X2 integration acceptance report

courses.title: AGIBOT D1 Ultra: SDK and ROS 2 bridge
courses.subtitle: Understand the supplied native SDK and engineer a measured, bounded ROS 2 adapter.
courses.description: This course examines the official D1 EDU/Ultra SDK down to its native headers, architecture-specific libraries, network configuration and state transitions. It teaches how to resolve discrepancies between prose documentation and the shipped interface, measure telemetry, and design a ROS 2 bridge without claiming an undocumented vendor driver exists. Offline models make ownership, stale data, motion requests and stop behavior testable before hardware is involved. D1 Ultra is not an X2 variant and does not inherit Unitree Go1 networking or command layouts. Hardware work requires the exact supplied model, matching binary architecture and an operator-approved procedure.
outcomes: Audit native API names against the pinned header
Diagnose network and binary compatibility independently
Specify and test a ROS 2 bridge contract
Review low-level joint ordering without actuating hardware

courses.title: Unitree Dex3 and Dex5 hands
courses.subtitle: Model dexterity precisely, inspect real interfaces, and test retargeting before connecting hardware.
courses.description: A hand course must separate kinematics, actuators, communication, feedback, and contact. Work with Dex3 joint maps and verified SDK2 examples, then investigate Dex5-1 and Dex5-1P as distinct variants with their own protocol boundary. Build offline joint-limit and retargeting tests, analyze synthetic pressure signals, and define grasp success with measurable criteria. The course teaches why an attractive URDF or a supported teleoperation menu is not proof of an interchangeable hand driver. Device-specific live API steps remain gated on the correct vendor protocol package; original exercises remain useful and fully executable without a robot.
outcomes: Validate side-specific hand mappings
Separate active and coupled joint counts
Evaluate retargeting errors
Design measurable contact and grasp experiments

courses.title: BrainCo Revo: hands, control and integration
courses.subtitle: Develop a hand interface that respects generation, transport, timing and kinematics.
courses.description: Start by identifying the Revo generation and hardware variant, then trace commands and feedback through the SDK, transport and ROS 2 controller. Build a reproducible Revo2 FakeSystem planning environment, characterize read-only communication, and examine tactile control as a delayed feedback problem. The final module studies the official Revo2 integration with Unitree G1, including arm ownership and waist-motion hazards. Revo3 is documented as a separate SDK generation; this course never treats its independent joints as a drop-in Revo2 upgrade. Exercises distinguish software configuration, simulated movement and real contact so that each result supports a specific claim.
outcomes: Select a compatible Revo SDK and transport
Measure communication percentiles and failure rates
Explain commanded, coupled and simulated joints
Produce a G1/Revo integration readiness dossier

courses.title: Simulation, control, navigation, manipulation
courses.subtitle: Connect the major robotics stacks while preserving their distinct responsibilities.
courses.description: Use simulation as an experiment with assumptions, then connect sensing, planning, control, and execution without confusing their roles. Work through a numerical joint controller, a mobile navigation acceptance scenario, and a planar arm planning example. The ROS 2, Gazebo, Nav2, MoveIt, and ros2_control sources provide entry points to full implementations; the lessons explain what must be measured around them. The core labs remain runnable without a particular vendor robot. Optional stack extensions require the documented package versions and simulator setup. Passing this course demonstrates software integration reasoning, not qualification to commission an unsupported physical robot.
outcomes: Define and test simulation assumptions
Explain controller and hardware-interface boundaries
Design navigation and manipulation acceptance tests
Distinguish planning success from safe execution

courses.title: AGIBOT G1 and GO-1: robot learning
courses.subtitle: Audit demonstrations, adapt observation contracts and evaluate generalist policies.
courses.description: AGIBOT G1 is a data-collection robot platform; GO-1 is the Genie Operator-1 policy family. Neither is Unitree Go1. This research course follows the official AgiBot World release through dataset inspection, synchronization, normalization, action-space mapping, fine-tuning configuration and evaluation. You will work with small, authorized data samples and offline contracts before considering GPU training or hardware execution. The emphasis is experimental validity: disjoint episodes, reproducible configuration, meaningful baselines, latency budgets, and clearly bounded claims. A checkpoint that loads successfully is not a validated controller for a different robot, hand, camera arrangement or firmware.
outcomes: Distinguish platform, dataset and model identities
Audit episode integrity and action semantics
Design leakage-resistant evaluations
Build a deployment gate for embodiment transfer

courses.title: Estimation, robot learning, and the capstone
courses.subtitle: Measure uncertainty, curate demonstrations, evaluate policies, and defend an engineering result.
courses.description: Move from demonstrations that look convincing to experiments that support defensible conclusions. You will calculate a simple estimation update, design a calibration procedure, identify imitation-learning leakage, and evaluate a reinforcement-learning policy against a fixed baseline. The capstone combines interfaces, timing, fault handling, reproducibility, and task-level metrics in one evidence package. The rubric makes missing hardware validation visible rather than rewarding confidence. This course can prepare you for a supervised vendor-specific engineering assessment; it cannot replace physical commissioning, system-level risk assessment, or extended operational experience with the exact hardware and firmware you intend to use.
outcomes: Quantify an estimation and calibration error budget
Split and audit demonstration data
Evaluate learned control without overstating generalization
Submit and defend a reproducible capstone with fault injection

courses.title: Unitree research and deployment
courses.subtitle: Turn demonstrations and learned policies into reproducible, testable engineering work.
courses.description: Move beyond a working demonstration to the evidence needed for a research or deployment decision. Study the XR data path, timestamp alignment, episode acceptance, policy input contracts, sim-to-sim testing, fault injection, and release provenance. Each lesson produces concrete artifacts: a dataset manifest, a policy contract, a test matrix, or an operations runbook. The emphasis is on discovering mismatches before physical execution and preserving enough information to explain failures. This is advanced engineering practice rather than a promise of universal robot autonomy; passing the course documents completed assessments, not vendor certification or independent authorization to operate hardware.
outcomes: Audit demonstration timing and leakage
Specify policy observation/action contracts
Design perturbation and fault tests
Prepare reproducible releases and recovery plans

lessons.title: Choose and prove the development environment
lessons.summary: Set up a documented Jazzy learning environment and keep vendor environments separate. Verify the installation through evidence rather than a successful installer message.
objectives: Identify OS, architecture, ROS distribution, and middleware
Explain underlays and overlays
Create an environment manifest and run a talker/listener check
prerequisites: An Ubuntu 24.04 Linux machine or virtual machine; administrator access for initial installation

sections.heading: The environment is part of the experiment
sections.body:
A robotics program depends on more than its source file. The operating system supplies device interfaces and libraries; the CPU architecture determines which binaries can run; the ROS distribution selects a compatible set of packages; the middleware transports messages. Record these choices before debugging application code. If a colleague runs the same script with a different message definition or shared library, you have two different experiments.

The foundations in this program use ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04. Follow the official installation page for repository setup because package-signing instructions can change. A vendor repository that specifies Humble and Ubuntu 22.04 belongs in a separate VM, container, or machine matching that contract. Do not source Jazzy and Humble into one shell and interpret the resulting build as a supported combination. A container isolates many user-space dependencies, but its kernel, device access, clock, and network configuration still come from the host.

sections.heading: Understand the shell before changing it
sections.body:
An environment variable is a value inherited by child processes. Sourcing a setup file changes the current shell so that executable and library lookup can find ROS. Executing that file in a separate process would not modify the parent shell. An underlay provides an installed dependency set; an overlay adds your newly built packages on top. Overlay order matters when package names collide, so use a fresh shell for a clean build and source only the intended underlay.

The following inspection commands do not install software. Run them in the Ubuntu learning environment after completing the official installation. Save the output alongside the exercise. A blank ROS_DISTRO usually means the shell has not loaded its setup file; it does not by itself prove ROS is absent. Check the installation path before reinstalling anything.
sections.code:
cat /etc/os-release
uname -m
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
printenv ROS_DISTRO
command -v ros2
ros2 doctor --report

sections.heading: Prove one narrow claim at a time
sections.body:
Run the standard C++ talker and Python listener in separate terminals, each sourced identically. Receiving numbered messages establishes that two local processes can discover one another and exchange the demo interface through the current middleware. It does not establish camera access, real-time performance, cross-machine discovery, or compatibility with a vendor SDK. Write the verified claim with that scope.

Create a manifest containing the date, OS release, architecture, ROS distribution, installed package versions, middleware selection, and any workspace commit. Add a short transcript of the successful exchange and the exact command that produced it. Then repeat from two fresh terminals. Reproducibility starts when your result survives removal of accidental shell state. Keep credentials, Wi-Fi passwords, and private network details out of shared evidence; the purpose of the manifest is dependency traceability, not copying the entire environment.
sections.code:
# Terminal A
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker
# Terminal B, separately
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener

lab.title: Prove a clean ROS installation
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04 with official ROS 2 Jazzy desktop installation
lab.safety: Use a local VM or workstation disconnected from robot control networks. Demo messages are not motion commands.
steps: Install Jazzy using the linked official instructions and record the package source used.
Run the inspection commands; save their output to an environment manifest.
Start the talker and listener in independently sourced terminals and capture ten consecutive received messages.
Close both terminals, open fresh terminals, and reproduce the exchange.
Compare the two runs and list precisely which capabilities this test does and does not verify.
lab.expected: The listener prints the same numbered strings published by the talker. Both runs identify Jazzy and the same architecture.
acceptance: All environment fields are present without secrets
Two fresh-shell runs exchange at least ten messages
No mixed ROS distribution is present in the documented shell setup

troubleshooting.symptom: ros2: command not found
troubleshooting.cause: ROS setup is not sourced or installation is missing
troubleshooting.fix: Check /opt/ros/jazzy first, source its setup file, then repeat command lookup.

troubleshooting.symptom: Both processes run but no strings arrive
troubleshooting.cause: Different domains, discovery settings, or middleware configuration
troubleshooting.fix: Compare the environment manifests before reinstalling packages.

questions.prompt: A vendor example requires Ubuntu 22.04 and Humble. Your course VM uses 24.04 and Jazzy. What is the defensible next step?
choices: Use a separate environment matching the vendor requirement
Rename the Humble folder to Jazzy
Assume Python examples are distribution independent
Source both setup files
questions.explanation: A separate environment preserves the stated compatibility contract. Sourcing both distributions can select incompatible libraries and does not establish support.

questions.prompt: A local talker/listener exchange passes. Which claim is supported?
choices: The physical robot can safely execute commands
Two local processes exchanged the tested interface
Every DDS machine on the network is reachable
The system meets a 1 ms deadline
questions.explanation: The observation proves the narrow local communication path. Timing and physical behavior require different measurements.

questions.prompt: ROS_DISTRO is empty in a new terminal. What should you inspect first?
choices: The C++ optimizer
The motor firmware
Whether the intended ROS setup file was sourced
The simulator friction coefficient
questions.explanation: A fresh terminal has independent environment state. An empty variable alone is not evidence of a broken installation.

lessons.title: Linux, networking, and a traceable workspace
lessons.summary: Learn the process, filesystem, and network observations needed to debug a robot workstation. Put a small experiment under source control so its history can be reviewed.
objectives: Explain paths, permissions, exit status, and processes
Distinguish interfaces, routes, addresses, and listening sockets
Create a Git commit containing a reproducible experiment
prerequisites: Git and standard Ubuntu command-line tools

sections.heading: Read the failure at the right layer
sections.body:
A path identifies a filesystem object; a process is a running program; a socket is a communication endpoint. These are different objects with different diagnostics. A missing file is not fixed by opening a network port. A process that exited with an error is not fixed by increasing a topic queue. Begin by identifying the first observable failure and the layer that owns it.

Use an absolute path when recording a result, and a project-relative path in reproducible scripts. Check the current directory before creating or moving files. File permissions distinguish reading, writing, and executing; avoid granting broad permissions simply because an error mentions access. Capture standard output, standard error, and the exit status separately when they matter. A command returning zero supports the claim that its own operation succeeded, not that the entire robot task was completed.

sections.heading: Network facts before network guesses
sections.body:
An interface is a local connection such as Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or loopback. An IP address names an endpoint on a network; a route determines where packets go next. A listening socket indicates a process is ready at a particular transport and address. Ping tests a particular kind of reachability and can fail when a service works, or succeed when the application is broken. Use the observation that matches the claim.

The commands below inspect the Linux host without changing its network configuration. A VM with network-address translation can access the internet while being unreachable by inbound discovery traffic. Docker and VPN adapters can also change which interface middleware selects. Document the topology before touching addresses or firewall rules. Never substitute an assumed robot IP address for a value read from the correct vendor setup guide.
sections.code:
pwd
id
ip -brief address
ip route
ss -lntu
ps -eo pid,comm,etime --sort=comm

sections.heading: Git records intentional changes
sections.body:
Git is a database of snapshots, not an automatic backup of every file. The working tree contains your current files; the staging area selects the changes for the next commit; a commit binds a snapshot to its history. Inspect the diff before staging so generated logs, large recordings, and secrets do not enter the repository accidentally. A commit message should explain the change and the reason another engineer would care about it.

Create a small repository for an experiment with a README, a script, and a dependency note. Ignore build products and private credentials explicitly. Commit the initial working version, make one deliberate change, and inspect the difference. Record the commit identifier in each lab report. If an experiment depends on uncommitted changes, state that fact and save the patch. A revision label that points to different code than the code actually tested is worse than no label because it gives false confidence.
sections.code:
mkdir -p robotics-labs/linux-check
cd robotics-labs/linux-check
git init
printf 'Reproduce with: python3 experiment.py
' > README.txt
printf 'print("local experiment")
' > experiment.py
git status --short
git add README.txt experiment.py
git diff --cached
# After inspecting the staged changes:
git commit -m 'Add reproducible local experiment'
git rev-parse HEAD

lab.title: Create a diagnosable experiment
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04; Git configured with your chosen author identity
lab.safety: Only inspect network configuration. Do not scan other machines, change robot addresses, or publish private interface details.
steps: Run the read-only network and process commands and annotate one interface, one route, and one local listening socket if present.
Create the repository shown above and run its script.
Change the output string, inspect git diff, and commit the intentional change.
Run the script from the wrong directory and record the resulting failure; fix it using a documented path.
Write a reproduction note containing the tested commit and the exact command from a clean terminal.
lab.expected: The committed script produces a predictable line; the path failure can be explained and reproduced.
acceptance: A fresh checkout can reproduce the script result
No credentials or recordings are committed
The report distinguishes process, filesystem, and network evidence

troubleshooting.symptom: Git refuses to commit
troubleshooting.cause: Author identity is not configured
troubleshooting.fix: Configure user.name and user.email according to your own identity; do not invent an identity.

troubleshooting.symptom: A service is reachable inside a container but not outside
troubleshooting.cause: The socket binding or network mapping differs
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the binding address and container mapping; document the topology before changing it.

questions.prompt: Ping succeeds but the ROS subscriber receives nothing. What does ping prove?
choices: The topic type is correct
The robot accepts commands
ROS QoS compatibility
Some ICMP reachability, not ROS application delivery
questions.explanation: Ping tests one network mechanism. ROS discovery, type matching, QoS, and application behavior remain separate.

questions.prompt: A result was produced after editing a file but before committing. Which report is accurate?
choices: The commit identifier plus the uncommitted patch
A new invented version number
No version information
Only the previous commit identifier
questions.explanation: The patch identifies the actual tested state. The previous commit alone omits changes that affected the run.

questions.prompt: A script says it cannot open a relative data path. What should you check first?
choices: Clock synchronization
The current directory and expected file location
Motor current limits
DDS multicast
questions.explanation: Relative paths are resolved against the current working directory. This is a filesystem issue before it is a robotics issue.

lessons.title: Python for checked telemetry and numerical reasoning
lessons.summary: Write a small telemetry calculation with explicit units and rejected invalid inputs. Use tests to expose hidden assumptions before those assumptions reach a robot.
objectives: Implement functions with explicit input contracts
Calculate speed from position and elapsed time
Test finite values, invalid time intervals, and unit errors

sections.heading: A numeric value needs a contract
sections.body:
The float 90 has no physical meaning until you attach a quantity, unit, frame, and time. It could be an angle in degrees, a joint temperature in Celsius, or a timestamp. Variable names and function documentation should make those meanings visible. Use SI units internally when the interface permits it and convert at the boundary. A conversion scattered through several callbacks is difficult to audit and easy to apply twice.

Python functions let you isolate a calculation from message transport. Accept plain values, validate them, return a result, and test the function without ROS. This separation shortens the feedback loop: a unit error should fail in a millisecond-scale local test, not after you start a simulator. Validation should reject NaN and infinity as well as obvious negative values because non-finite numbers can propagate through arithmetic without raising an exception.

sections.heading: Derive the example before typing it
sections.body:
Average speed along one measured axis is displacement divided by elapsed time. A change from 0.20 m to 0.26 m over 0.10 s gives 0.60 m/s. This is an average over the interval, not an instantaneous sensor truth. Measurement noise in the two positions is amplified as the interval becomes small. A timestamp that goes backward is not an invitation to take the absolute value: it means the assumed ordering is broken.

The function below defines a deliberately narrow contract. It accepts two positions in meters and a strictly positive elapsed time in seconds. It returns signed velocity in meters per second. It raises an exception for invalid input instead of inventing a plausible value. A higher-level application can then decide whether to drop the sample, mark an estimate invalid, or enter a defined degraded state.

sections.heading: Test behavior, not implementation spelling
sections.body:
A useful test states an expected property of the problem. If both positions are equal, velocity should be zero. Exchanging positions should reverse the sign. Multiplying displacement by two at fixed time should double the result. These properties catch mistakes without duplicating the function line for line. Use approximate comparisons for floating-point arithmetic because many decimal fractions do not have exact binary representations.

Now consider an upstream source that reports centimeters. The function cannot detect that 26 means 26 cm rather than 26 m; both are finite numbers. This is why numeric validation and interface validation solve different problems. Add a named conversion function at the boundary and record the original unit in your dataset manifest. Type hints improve readability and tooling but do not automatically enforce physical units at runtime. The engineering task is to make assumptions reviewable and test the assumptions that can actually fail.

lab.title: Build a telemetry calculation with rejection tests
lab.environment: Any Python 3 environment; no ROS installation required
lab.safety: Use invented numbers only. This function is a teaching calculation, not a control loop.
steps: Save and run the complete example.
Add zero-displacement, doubled-displacement, infinity, and negative-position tests.
Write a centimeters-to-meters conversion and test a 20 cm to 26 cm sample over 0.1 s.
Repeat with a 1 mm perturbation at intervals of 0.1 s and 0.01 s; compare the velocity error.
Record the contract, test results, and the reason shorter intervals amplify position noise.
lab.expected: All valid examples match the derived values; invalid time or non-finite inputs are rejected.
acceptance: At least seven meaningful cases pass
Centimeter inputs are converted exactly once
The report distinguishes average velocity from instantaneous velocity

troubleshooting.symptom: 0.6 is displayed as a nearby decimal
troubleshooting.cause: Binary floating-point representation
troubleshooting.fix: Use math.isclose with a justified tolerance rather than comparing formatted strings.

troubleshooting.symptom: Results are exactly 100 times too large
troubleshooting.cause: Centimeters were interpreted as meters
troubleshooting.fix: Move the conversion into a clearly named input-boundary function.

questions.prompt: A position source reports centimeters. A finite-value check passes but velocity is 100 times too large. What is missing?
choices: A lower sampling rate
A larger queue
An explicit unit conversion at the input boundary
A faster executor
questions.explanation: Finite-value checks cannot infer units. A documented conversion is necessary; transport tuning would not correct the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Why reject a negative elapsed time instead of taking its absolute value?
choices: Negative velocity is impossible
All timestamps must start at zero
Python cannot divide by negative values
It reveals an ordering or clock assumption failure
questions.explanation: A backward interval violates this estimator contract. Taking the absolute value would hide the failure and can change the interpreted motion.

questions.prompt: Which test adds the most independent evidence?
choices: Check that reversing endpoints reverses velocity
Check that the function name contains velocity
Only print the result
Copy the implementation into another function
questions.explanation: The sign-reversal property follows from the problem definition and can catch implementation mistakes without repeating them.

lessons.title: C++ ownership, lifetimes, and bounded computation
lessons.summary: Understand the memory and timing concepts behind C++ SDK examples. Build a checked calculation without confusing fast code with a real-time guarantee.
objectives: Explain automatic storage, references, and ownership
Compile a warning-clean C++17 program
Identify operations that make timing unpredictable
prerequisites: A C++17 compiler such as GCC on Ubuntu; standard library headers

sections.heading: Ownership answers who must release a resource
sections.body:
A C++ value has a type and a lifetime. A local object normally lives until its scope ends; its destructor then releases resources it owns. This mechanism supports RAII: acquiring a resource into an object and releasing it when the object leaves scope. A reference observes an existing object and must not outlive it. An owning smart pointer has different responsibilities from a borrowed pointer, even when both provide access to the same data.

When reading an SDK callback, ask who owns the message, whether the callback receives a copy or a view, and whether it stores a pointer after the callback returns. A program can appear to work while reading expired memory. Copying a small required value into an owned structure is often easier to reason about than retaining a borrowed buffer. Do not infer a lifetime guarantee from the fact that a pointer is non-null.

sections.heading: Compile a small complete unit
sections.body:
Begin with a function that accepts fixed-size state and returns a checked result. The array in this example owns three values. The const reference permits observation without making another array and prevents mutation through this parameter. Returning the norm by value gives the caller an independent result. The finite-value checks are part of the function contract rather than comments the compiler cannot enforce.

Compile with warnings enabled and fix the warnings you understand. Warnings are diagnostic evidence, not a proof of correctness. Test the numeric result independently: the vector (3, 4, 0) has magnitude 5 by the Pythagorean theorem. Then change one input to a non-finite value and confirm rejection. Keep exception handling at a deliberate boundary; in a hard timing path, a prevalidated status-return design may be more appropriate than throwing.

sections.heading: Throughput is different from a deadline
sections.body:
A benchmark that reports a low average execution time does not prove that every invocation meets a deadline. Allocation, page faults, logging, locks, and operating-system scheduling can create rare long pauses. A 1 kHz loop has a nominal one-millisecond period; if computation, scheduling delay, and transport consume more than that budget, being written in C++ does not rescue the deadline.

Separate setup from repeated work. Allocate buffers during setup where practical, make ownership explicit, avoid unbounded operations in time-sensitive callbacks, and measure the distribution of execution and arrival intervals. Report worst observed latency together with sample count and conditions. It remains an observation, not a universal bound. Vendor low-level loops may depend on thread priority, kernel configuration, and a carefully controlled command interface. This lesson prepares you to inspect those requirements; it does not authorize copying an example loop into a running robot.

lab.title: Compile and inspect a numeric C++ unit
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ supporting C++17
lab.safety: Compile and run offline. Do not attach this teaching program to a motor or SDK callback.
steps: Save the code as norm.cpp and compile with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic norm.cpp -o norm.
Run ./norm and verify the output and exit status.
Add tests for the zero vector and a vector with a negative component.
Add a try/catch test for a NaN component and confirm invalid_argument is produced.
Annotate each value or reference with its owner and lifetime, and list three operations to keep outside a timing-critical callback.
lab.expected: The complete program prints 5 and returns success; added invalid-input testing proves rejection.
acceptance: Compilation completes without warnings
Valid and invalid numeric cases are checked
No borrowed reference is stored beyond its source lifetime

troubleshooting.symptom: Compiler reports no matching hypot overload
troubleshooting.cause: The selected language standard or compiler is too old
troubleshooting.fix: Check compiler version and explicitly enable C++17.

troubleshooting.symptom: A pointer works intermittently after a callback
troubleshooting.cause: The pointed-to object may have expired
troubleshooting.fix: Identify ownership; copy required data or use an explicit supported lifetime mechanism.

questions.prompt: A callback stores a pointer to a stack-local message for another thread. What is the main risk?
choices: The topic name changes
The pointer can outlive the message
The compiler always makes a deep copy
The network becomes reliable
questions.explanation: A pointer does not extend object lifetime. The delayed thread may access invalid storage even if the pointer is non-null.

questions.prompt: A loop averages 0.2 ms at a 1 ms period. What remains unproven?
choices: Whether C++ supports arrays
Whether the code contains a loop
Whether rare invocations exceed the deadline
Whether 0.2 is less than 1
questions.explanation: Average time hides tail latency, scheduling delays, and other contributors to missed deadlines.

questions.prompt: What does a const reference parameter communicate?
choices: It guarantees thread safety
It keeps the object alive forever
It owns a copy of the argument
It observes an existing object without modifying it through that reference
questions.explanation: Const restricts modification through that reference, while lifetime and concurrent access still require separate reasoning.

lessons.title: Inspect the ROS graph before writing code
lessons.summary: Use running demo nodes to discover names, types, and communication relationships. Build a graph from observation rather than assuming every executable is a single node.
objectives: Distinguish process, node, topic, and message type
Use ROS CLI inspection to reconstruct a graph
Predict the effect of namespacing and remapping

sections.heading: The graph is a set of relationships
sections.body:
ROS 2 organizes an application into nodes that exchange typed data. A process can contain one node or several nodes, and the same executable can be started more than once with different node names. Keep the operating-system process view and ROS graph view separate. A node is a logical participant; the process is the container in which its code runs.

A topic name identifies a stream within the graph. Its message type defines the structure of each sample. Namespaces group names, while remapping changes how a particular node resolves a name. Neither operation converts data into another type. Two endpoints that appear to share a name may still fail to exchange useful data because their types or QoS differ. Inspect these properties directly instead of concluding that an empty subscriber is a network failure.

sections.heading: Inspect a known small system
sections.body:
Start the standard demo talker and listener, then inspect the graph in a third terminal. Read node information to see what the node publishes, subscribes to, and exposes through services. Read topic information to count endpoints and inspect their quality-of-service policies. Finally inspect the message definition. These are different observations: endpoint count does not prove useful payloads are arriving, and a payload on one topic does not prove the downstream application accepts it.

The commands below operate on the default demo topic. Capture only a short sample when a topic is continuous. For a new project, create an interface table containing the resolved name, type, publisher, subscriber, unit or semantic meaning, expected rate, and freshness requirement. A graph diagram is valuable when its arrows correspond to a table that makes those assumptions explicit.
sections.code:
ros2 node list
ros2 node info /talker
ros2 topic list -t
ros2 topic info /chatter --verbose
ros2 interface show std_msgs/msg/String
ros2 topic echo /chatter --once

sections.heading: Use deliberate variation to test your model
sections.body:
Stop the original demos and restart them under a namespace such as /lab. Predict the resolved topic name before inspecting it. Then remap only the talker to a different topic and observe that the listener no longer receives its strings. Restore the connection by applying the matching remap to the listener. The important result is not a command you memorized; it is a causal explanation of why the connection changed.

Built-in topics and parameter services may appear even in a small demo. Do not mistake them for your application interface. Record application edges separately from supporting infrastructure. Duplicate node names make logs and introspection ambiguous, so give independently meaningful nodes unique names. In later vendor work, the same discipline prevents you from confusing an SDK bridge, a state estimator, and a motion-command owner simply because all three run on the robot computer.
sections.code:
# Run these in two separate terminals after stopping old demos.
ros2 run demo_nodes_cpp talker --ros-args -r __ns:=/lab
ros2 run demo_nodes_py listener --ros-args -r __ns:=/lab
# Inspect from a third terminal:
ros2 topic info /lab/chatter --verbose

lab.title: Reconstruct and perturb a two-node graph
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04; Jazzy desktop demos; local discovery only
lab.safety: Use string demos on a local learning environment. Do not introspect an unknown robot network.
steps: Run a demo talker and listener in separate terminals.
Execute the graph-inspection commands and create the interface table.
Restart both under /lab and compare the resolved names with your prediction.
Remap the talker chatter topic to /lab/alternate; record the loss of delivery.
Remap the listener consistently and capture restored delivery.
lab.expected: The table and graph match observed names and types, and delivery follows the deliberate remapping.
acceptance: Every application arrow has an observed name and type
The namespace prediction is checked against the CLI
The failure and recovery have a causal explanation

troubleshooting.symptom: Old and new topics both appear
troubleshooting.cause: An earlier demo process remains running or discovery cache is stale
troubleshooting.fix: Check running processes and stop old nodes; wait briefly and inspect again.

troubleshooting.symptom: The listener is visible but silent
troubleshooting.cause: The resolved topic names or types differ
troubleshooting.fix: Compare verbose topic information and remap arguments on both endpoints.

questions.prompt: One executable contains three nodes. How many processes must appear?
choices: Possibly one
None
One per topic
Exactly three
questions.explanation: Composition permits multiple logical nodes inside one process. A node count is not a process count.

questions.prompt: You rename a topic from /a to /b. Does its message type change?
choices: Yes, types come from topic spelling
No, remapping changes names, not schemas
Only for Python nodes
Only across machines
questions.explanation: Type information comes from the interface used by the endpoint. Remapping alone cannot convert a message.

questions.prompt: Topic inspection reports one publisher and one subscriber. What further evidence is needed?
choices: A second namespace
None; task success is proven
Observed payloads and application-level acceptance
A prettier graph
questions.explanation: Matched endpoints do not prove correct units, freshness, or downstream task behavior.

lessons.title: Design a telemetry topic and its contract
lessons.summary: Build a local publisher and distinguish a message schema from its meaning. Define freshness, units, and validity before connecting downstream consumers.
objectives: Create a complete rclpy publisher
Specify units, range, rate, and freshness for a topic
Explain why a transport schema alone is insufficient

sections.heading: A schema is necessary but incomplete
sections.body:
A message definition tells a receiver how fields are serialized. It does not automatically say which physical quantity a bare float represents, when it was measured, or which coordinate frame it belongs to. Production telemetry should use an appropriate standard message or a carefully documented custom interface with timestamps and frame information when those concepts apply. A generic Float64 is useful for a first exercise precisely because its missing semantics are easy to see.

Our teaching topic represents an invented temperature in degrees Celsius, generated once per second. It has no physical sensor and no relationship to motor thermal limits. Write that fact into the contract. Specify the source of timestamps, acceptable range, behavior on invalid data, and maximum tolerated age. A consumer that cannot distinguish a stale value from a current one cannot make a defensible decision from the stream.

sections.heading: Keep the node small enough to inspect
sections.body:
The program below creates one node, one publisher, and one timer. The publisher object remains alive as a member of the node. Each timer callback constructs a message, assigns its data, and publishes it. The executor runs callbacks while spin is active. The finally block gives the program a clear cleanup path after interruption.

Run the script directly in a sourced Jazzy shell for this exercise. Packaging it comes next. The queue-depth argument selects a shorthand QoS configuration; it does not guarantee a one-second update deadline. Measure reception separately. Do not add a while loop that publishes continuously, because that would replace an intentional sampling interval with an uncontrolled busy loop. The teaching goal is to connect a visible contract to a visible execution mechanism.
sections.code:
import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node
from std_msgs.msg import Float64

class TemperatureDemo(Node):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__("temperature_demo")
        self.publisher = self.create_publisher(Float64, "/lab/temperature_c", 10)
        self.timer = self.create_timer(1.0, self.publish_sample)
        self.sample = 20.0

    def publish_sample(self):
        message = Float64()
        message.data = self.sample
        self.publisher.publish(message)
        self.sample = 20.0 if self.sample >= 22.0 else self.sample + 0.5

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    node = TemperatureDemo()
    try:
        rclpy.spin(node)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.try_shutdown()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

sections.heading: Choose behavior for absent and invalid samples
sections.body:
A consumer should define what happens before its first valid sample, after a sample fails validation, and after samples stop arriving. Those are different states. Reusing the last number indefinitely can conceal a dead source. Clearing all state on a single malformed message can produce unnecessary instability. The policy must match the task and should be testable through deliberate source interruption.

For this exercise, design a display consumer with three states: waiting, current, and stale. It may show the last value while visibly labeling it stale after a chosen timeout. A future command-producing consumer would need a separate, reviewed fallback policy. The same distinction applies to message loss: missing one temperature sample may be acceptable for a dashboard, while an expired state estimate may invalidate a controller input. Record why the timeout matches your application rather than copying a number from a tutorial.

lab.title: Publish and document synthetic temperature
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04, sourced Jazzy shell; Python script with rclpy and std_msgs
lab.safety: The /lab topic contains invented temperature only. No commands or hardware interfaces are used.
steps: Save the program as temperature_demo.py and run python3 temperature_demo.py.
Inspect its type and observe at least six messages with ros2 topic echo.
Measure the approximate received rate with ros2 topic hz /lab/temperature_c.
Stop the source and specify how a display should distinguish waiting from stale state.
Write a contract table including meaning, unit, range, rate, freshness, and invalid-data behavior.
lab.expected: The generated values cycle from 20.0 through 22.0 at approximately one sample per second.
acceptance: Observed values match the documented generator
The rate is measured rather than claimed from the timer value
The contract explicitly identifies synthetic data and absence behavior

troubleshooting.symptom: ImportError for rclpy
troubleshooting.cause: The script is using an unrelated Python environment or unsourced ROS installation
troubleshooting.fix: Use the system Python associated with the Jazzy installation and source its setup.

troubleshooting.symptom: Rate measurement is briefly unstable
troubleshooting.cause: Too few samples or startup scheduling variation
troubleshooting.fix: Measure over a longer fixed interval and record duration instead of selecting a favorable instant.

questions.prompt: A Float64 arrives successfully. Which fact is still missing?
choices: Whether the field is numeric
Whether ROS can represent it
Whether bytes can be serialized
Its physical meaning and unit
questions.explanation: The schema describes representation, not the full semantic contract. A bare float could represent many quantities.

questions.prompt: The publisher timer is set to one second. What is the strongest rate claim?
choices: The node requests a nominal one-second callback period; reception must be measured
The loop is hard real time
The network cannot drop a sample
Every receiver always gets exactly 1 Hz
questions.explanation: Scheduling and transport affect observed behavior. Timer configuration alone is not a delivery guarantee.

questions.prompt: A dashboard has received a value before, but its source stopped five minutes ago. Which state is appropriate?
choices: Waiting for the first sample
Stale with the last value clearly identified
Silently pretend nothing changed
Current
questions.explanation: Stale differs from never initialized. Preserving a visibly labeled last observation may be useful; silently treating it as current is misleading.

lessons.title: Choose services and actions by lifecycle
lessons.summary: Compare a bounded request/response with a cancellable operation in turtlesim. Trace success, rejection, cancellation, and timeout as different outcomes.
objectives: Choose topics, services, or actions for a concrete requirement
Inspect a service and action interface
Explain why cancellation acknowledgment is not instantaneous physical stopping

sections.heading: Choose by interaction, not by convenience
sections.body:
Topics suit ongoing streams whose consumers can join and leave independently. A service models a request with a corresponding response and works well for a short bounded transaction. An action adds a goal lifecycle, intermediate feedback, a result, and cancellation support for work that may take time. The distinction is semantic: forcing a long operation into a service does not make its failure or cancellation requirements disappear.

Consider three requirements for a simulated robot: report pose continuously, reset the scene, and rotate toward a heading while reporting remaining angle. Pose is a topic, reset is a service, and rotation is an action. The same reasoning applies to vendor systems, but the existence of a ROS interface does not guarantee the vendor implements a particular feature. Inspect the actual interface and documented behavior before designing around it.

sections.heading: Observe a complete transaction
sections.body:
Turtlesim provides a contained environment for these experiments. Start its node, list the services and actions, and inspect the types before sending requests. An Empty service has no request fields; this does not mean the operation has no side effects. Reset changes simulator state. The RotateAbsolute action has a numeric goal and feedback that can be observed while execution proceeds.

Record four distinct moments: the goal is sent, the server accepts or rejects it, feedback arrives, and the result is returned. A transport timeout is a client-side observation, not proof that the server did nothing. If retrying can duplicate side effects, the application needs a request identity or a way to determine current state. For example, creating a second object after a delayed first response is different from asking for a current sensor value again.
sections.code:
# Start in a separate terminal:
ros2 run turtlesim turtlesim_node
# Inspect from another terminal:
ros2 service list -t
ros2 interface show std_srvs/srv/Empty
ros2 service call /reset std_srvs/srv/Empty '{}'
ros2 action list -t
ros2 interface show turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute
ros2 action send_goal /turtle1/rotate_absolute turtlesim/action/RotateAbsolute '{theta: 1.0}' --feedback

sections.heading: Cancellation is a protocol plus implementation
sections.body:
An action client can request cancellation, but the server determines whether to accept it and must implement a coherent transition. Cancellation can race with completion. A result should tell the client which terminal state actually occurred. On a real system, accepting a cancel request is not the same as an emergency stop, a verified zero velocity, or removal of actuator power. Those are separate mechanisms and measurements.

Write a state table for your own hypothetical inspection task: idle, accepting, executing, canceling, succeeded, canceled, and aborted. Define what data is valid in each state and which transitions are permitted. Decide how a client recovers after losing communication while execution continues. This exercise reveals requirements that a happy-path demonstration hides. An expert interface design is precise about uncertainty: if the client cannot determine whether the task completed, it reports an unknown outcome and reconciles state before retrying.

lab.title: Trace a simulated operation lifecycle
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04; Jazzy turtlesim; graphical desktop or VM display
lab.safety: All commands target turtlesim. Keep the exercise off physical robot domains.
steps: Start turtlesim and inspect the reset service and rotation action types.
Reset the scene and save the request/response transcript.
Send a one-radian rotation goal with feedback and record acceptance, feedback, and result.
Repeat from a different starting angle and compare elapsed duration and feedback.
Draw a lifecycle table for an inspection task, including cancellation and loss of communication.
lab.expected: The turtle rotates in simulation and returns a result; the learner can distinguish protocol stages and outcome uncertainty.
acceptance: Interface choices are justified by duration and interaction
The report separates acceptance from completion
Retry policy accounts for potentially completed side effects

troubleshooting.symptom: No action server is found
troubleshooting.cause: Turtlesim is not running in the same graph
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect nodes and domains before resending goals.

troubleshooting.symptom: An operation returns quickly with little feedback
troubleshooting.cause: The target is already close to the current heading
troubleshooting.fix: Start from a different simulated heading and compare the full lifecycle.

questions.prompt: A scan takes 30 seconds, provides progress, and must allow cancellation. Which interface best fits?
choices: A parameter
A topic with no task identity
An action
An Empty service that blocks indefinitely
questions.explanation: An action explicitly represents long-running work, feedback, and cancellation. A blocking service leaves those requirements to an ad hoc protocol.

questions.prompt: A request times out after the server changed state. What is a dangerous assumption?
choices: State reconciliation may be needed
The request may have completed
The result is currently uncertain
The server definitely did nothing, so retry blindly
questions.explanation: A timeout only describes the client observation. Blind retries can duplicate a completed side effect.

questions.prompt: A server accepts cancellation. What has that alone proven?
choices: The cancellation request was accepted by the action protocol
Physical velocity is zero
The emergency stop is healthy
Actuator power is removed
questions.explanation: Protocol acceptance must be followed by the server transition and, on hardware, independent measurements and safety mechanisms.

lessons.title: Package, build, and reproduce a ROS application
lessons.summary: Turn the telemetry script into an installable ament Python package. Learn why dependency declarations and clean-shell builds matter more than a successful local import.
objectives: Create an ament_python package with declared dependencies
Install and run a console entry point through ros2 run
Distinguish source, build, install, and log directories

sections.heading: A package is a distribution boundary
sections.body:
A ROS package groups code, metadata, dependencies, and installation rules. Its manifest describes what it needs to build, execute, and test. The package name is not necessarily the same as a Python module name or a node name, although tutorials often make them similar. Keeping these concepts distinct helps explain why a script can import successfully from its source directory yet fail after installation.

The workspace contains source packages under src. Colcon builds selected packages and writes generated files under build, runnable installed artifacts under install, and diagnostic records under log. Treat generated directories as disposable outputs, not the authoritative source. Do not repair an installed copy of a file and then assume the change lives in your repository. Rebuild from source and verify the installed behavior.

sections.heading: Make the entry point explicit
sections.body:
Create a package named lab_telemetry with dependencies on rclpy and std_msgs. Copy the earlier temperature program into its Python module directory. The console-script entry point maps a command name to the module's main function. The generated setup.py already contains an entry_points section; replace its console_scripts list with the item shown below rather than adding a second conflicting entry_points argument.

Build from the workspace root in a shell with the Jazzy underlay sourced. Open a new terminal for execution, source the underlay and workspace install setup, then run the package command. Keeping build and execution shells separate prevents a previously sourced overlay from silently supplying a missing dependency. If the clean-shell run fails while the source-directory run succeeds, investigate installation metadata before changing the node logic.
sections.code:
# From the parent directory where you want the workspace:
mkdir -p lab_ws/src
cd lab_ws/src
ros2 pkg create --build-type ament_python lab_telemetry --dependencies rclpy std_msgs
# Copy temperature_demo.py into:
# lab_ws/src/lab_telemetry/lab_telemetry/temperature_demo.py
# In generated setup.py, set console_scripts to:
# ['temperature = lab_telemetry.temperature_demo:main']
cd ..
colcon build --packages-select lab_telemetry --symlink-install
# In a fresh shell at lab_ws:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
source install/setup.bash
ros2 run lab_telemetry temperature

sections.heading: Reproducibility includes the dependency graph
sections.body:
A package that imports an undeclared library can pass on a developer machine because another project installed that library. A clean environment exposes the missing dependency. Use rosdep according to the official setup instructions to resolve declared system dependencies; record the package version set used for the exercise. A dependency declaration is not a version lock, so document the tested environment separately.

Save a build transcript, the package manifest, and the source commit. Then ask a second shell to locate the package prefix and run the entry point. This checks the installed artifact instead of relying on the current directory. For a release-quality handoff, reproduce from a clean checkout or clean image and include tests. The purpose is to turn a personal success into a result another engineer can verify without inheriting your shell history.

When using symlink installation, some source edits become visible without copying files, but metadata changes still require rebuilding. Record that build mode so another learner understands which artifacts were generated and which reference source files.

lab.title: Install the telemetry node as a package
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04; Jazzy with colcon and development tools
lab.safety: The package publishes only synthetic telemetry under /lab. No vendor SDK is connected.
steps: Create the package and copy the complete temperature program into its module directory.
Edit the generated console_scripts list to expose the temperature command.
Build the package from the workspace root and save the transcript.
Run it from a fresh sourced shell and verify the topic with the CLI.
Use ros2 pkg prefix lab_telemetry, record the source commit, and explain each workspace directory.
lab.expected: ros2 run locates the installed entry point and produces the same telemetry as the original script.
acceptance: The node runs without executing its source file directly
Dependencies are declared in package.xml
The documented path points to the intended workspace installation

troubleshooting.symptom: No executable found
troubleshooting.cause: The console entry point is absent or the package was not rebuilt
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect setup.py console_scripts, rebuild, and source the correct install setup.

troubleshooting.symptom: An older version runs
troubleshooting.cause: Another overlay shadows the intended package
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect ros2 pkg prefix and start a clean shell with only the desired underlay and overlay.

questions.prompt: Your node runs from its source folder but ros2 run cannot find it. Where should you look first?
choices: Motor firmware
Installation metadata and the console entry point
The joystick battery
Transform interpolation
questions.explanation: Source execution bypasses the package installation path. The entry point and sourced install prefix are the relevant evidence.

questions.prompt: Why build with a clean underlay rather than an old overlay already sourced?
choices: It guarantees real-time performance
It makes Python compiled
It exposes hidden dependency and package-shadowing problems
It deletes source history
questions.explanation: An old overlay can accidentally satisfy missing dependencies or resolve the wrong package. It does not affect real-time guarantees.

questions.prompt: Which directory should contain the authoritative edited node source?
choices: log
A temporary compiler directory
install only
src under version control
questions.explanation: Generated installed and build outputs should be reproducible from source; editing only an installed copy loses the change on rebuild.

lessons.title: Diagnose discovery and QoS compatibility
lessons.summary: Separate graph discovery from data delivery and deliberately create a QoS mismatch. Explain what reliability, durability, and queue depth do—and what they do not guarantee.
objectives: Identify domain and discovery configuration
Predict requested/offered reliability compatibility
Repair a local QoS mismatch with measured evidence
prerequisites: Default DDS-based rmw_fastrtps_cpp installed with Jazzy

sections.heading: Discovery finds peers; it does not validate meaning
sections.body:
The ROS middleware layer connects client libraries to a communication implementation. Many common ROS 2 deployments use DDS, whose participants discover endpoints and match compatible publishers and subscriptions. The ROS_DOMAIN_ID separates discovery domains, but it is a routing and organization mechanism rather than a security credential. All participants in a test must use the intended domain and compatible discovery configuration.

Jazzy exposes discovery-range controls, including localhost-only discovery for contained exercises. Set them before starting nodes. A command-line daemon started under older environment settings can make introspection confusing, so stop the daemon after changing domain or middleware settings and let it restart consistently. Diagnose in order: process alive, correct environment, endpoint visible, compatible type and QoS, actual payload, application acceptance. Skipping directly to firewall changes can conceal a simple configuration mismatch.

sections.heading: QoS is a contract between endpoints
sections.body:
Reliability asks whether lost samples should be retried; durability asks whether a late subscriber can receive retained data; history and depth constrain stored samples. A subscriber requesting reliable delivery cannot match a publisher offering only best effort. A best-effort subscriber can accept a reliable publisher. Compatibility must hold for all relevant policies, not just one.

Reliable delivery does not make a message timely, nor does it make an old command safe. A queue of 100 samples at 100 Hz can represent a second of backlog if the consumer falls behind. For a display, old samples may be useful for plotting; for a state-dependent decision, stale samples may be unusable. Choose policies from the application requirement and measure age and loss. Do not increase queue depth as a universal fix for a slow callback.
sections.code:
# In every terminal used for this isolated exercise:
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_fastrtps_cpp
unset ROS_STATIC_PEERS
export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=42
export ROS_AUTOMATIC_DISCOVERY_RANGE=LOCALHOST
ros2 daemon stop
# Publisher terminal:
ros2 topic pub /lab/qos std_msgs/msg/String '{data: "sample"}' --rate 2 --qos-reliability best_effort
# Subscriber terminal: deliberately incompatible request.
ros2 topic echo /lab/qos std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability reliable
# Stop echo, then use a compatible request:
ros2 topic echo /lab/qos std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort

sections.heading: Interpret observations without overclaiming
sections.body:
The incompatible subscriber should receive no messages and may report an incompatible-policy warning. The compatible subscriber should receive strings. Save verbose topic information in each condition so the result is tied to observed endpoint settings. If behavior differs, inspect the running processes and middleware version instead of editing the report to match the expected result.

Now write a QoS proposal for a camera stream, a static calibration value, and a short configuration service. Explain the desired behavior when a subscriber starts late, when packets are lost, and when the consumer pauses. Sensor data often values recent samples over complete delivery; retained configuration may need late-joiner behavior. These are design choices, not rules that every vendor must follow. When interfacing with an existing SDK, inspect its actual offered policy and verify compatibility before introducing a bridge.

These discovery controls assume a DDS-based middleware; rmw_zenoh uses its own configuration path. Keep the middleware implementation in the test manifest.

lab.title: Create and repair a QoS mismatch
lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04; Jazzy; localhost-only discovery on domain 42
lab.safety: String messages only. Domain selection reduces accidental mixing but does not provide access control.
steps: Set the domain and localhost discovery environment consistently in fresh terminals.
Start the best-effort publisher and the reliable subscriber shown above.
Save verbose endpoint QoS and note whether any samples arrive.
Restart the subscriber with best-effort reliability and capture five samples.
Create a three-row QoS proposal for camera data, calibration, and a configuration service.
lab.expected: No data is delivered for the incompatible reliability pair; the compatible pair receives strings.
acceptance: The mismatch is explained using requested versus offered policy
All test processes use the documented domain
The design table discusses freshness as well as delivery

troubleshooting.symptom: No endpoints appear even for the compatible case
troubleshooting.cause: The processes have different domains or discovery settings
troubleshooting.fix: Compare their launch environments and restart the CLI daemon under the same settings.

troubleshooting.symptom: Messages arrive despite the intended mismatch
troubleshooting.cause: An old compatible publisher remains active
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect publisher count and stop extra test processes before repeating.

questions.prompt: A best-effort publisher and reliable subscriber share a topic and type. What is expected?
choices: No match for that reliability requirement
Automatic upgrade of the publisher
The subscriber changes itself to best effort
Reliable delivery
questions.explanation: A subscriber cannot demand a guarantee the publisher does not offer. Matching the name and type is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A 100 Hz stream accumulates 100 queued samples. What can that imply?
choices: The newest data is always current
Approximately one second of historical backlog
A faster physical robot
Guaranteed lossless task execution
questions.explanation: Queue depth translates to time at a given rate. Processing every old sample may increase latency rather than solve it.

questions.prompt: Why is ROS_DOMAIN_ID not a security control?
choices: It exists only in ROS 1
It is always ignored
Other participants can choose the same domain; it is not authentication
It encrypts only images
questions.explanation: Domain separation organizes discovery. Authentication and authorization require separate mechanisms.

lessons.title: Clocks, callbacks, and stale-data budgets
lessons.summary: Calculate an end-to-end age budget and distinguish wall, steady, and ROS time. Explain how callback scheduling can make fresh-looking data arrive too late.
objectives: Choose clock semantics for timestamps and timeouts
Calculate data age from a staged pipeline
Explain callback blocking and executor starvation

sections.heading: Time has several jobs
sections.body:
A sensor timestamp describes when a measurement was acquired. A reception timestamp describes when software received it. A timeout measures how long the application has waited. These jobs do not always belong to the same clock. System time relates to calendar time and can be adjusted. A steady clock is intended for elapsed intervals without wall-clock jumps. ROS time can follow a simulation clock and may pause or jump when a simulator or recording is paused, reset, or replayed.

Subtracting timestamps only makes sense when their clock domains and synchronization assumptions are known. Two machines can each have precise clocks with an unknown offset between them. A negative apparent message age may indicate clock disagreement rather than data traveling backward. Record the acquisition clock, synchronization method, and use_sim_time configuration alongside the data. Do not use ROS simulation time for a host watchdog that must keep expiring while simulation is paused.

sections.heading: Callbacks compete for execution
sections.body:
A timer becoming ready does not mean its callback runs immediately. The executor dispatches callbacks according to its available threads and callback-group constraints. A single-threaded executor cannot run a subscriber while another callback blocks for a long operation. A multithreaded executor allows concurrency, but it also introduces shared-state and ordering questions. Changing executor type is not a substitute for understanding the work performed by callbacks.

Separate fast state capture from expensive processing. A callback can validate and copy a bounded amount of data into owned state, while another component performs heavier analysis with an explicit freshness policy. Avoid synchronous waiting inside a callback for work that requires that same blocked execution path to complete. Describe the dependency graph before adding threads; otherwise a deadlock may become an intermittent race instead of being resolved.

sections.heading: Budget the full path, then measure it
sections.body:
Suppose acquisition and encoding take 8 ms, transport takes 12 ms, queueing takes 20 ms, and inference takes 35 ms. The decision uses a measurement at least 75 ms old before command transport or actuator response is considered. Comparing only inference time with the deadline would miss most of the path. Each stage also has variation, so measure percentile and worst-observed values under representative load rather than adding favorable averages.

The complete offline example below computes a simple budget and flags measurements older than a chosen teaching threshold. Its threshold is an exercise value, not a vendor safety limit. Extend the table with clock uncertainty and actuator delay, keeping measurement and assumption columns separate. A robust report says which stages were observed and which remain estimates. An unmeasured stage is not zero merely because no timestamp was collected there.
sections.code:
stages_ms = {
    "acquisition_encoding": 8.0,
    "transport": 12.0,
    "queue": 20.0,
    "inference": 35.0,
}
budget_ms = sum(stages_ms.values())
threshold_ms = 60.0
assert budget_ms == 75.0
print({"age_ms": budget_ms, "accepted": budget_ms <= threshold_ms})

samples_ms = [44.0, 47.0, 59.0, 82.0, 48.0]
accepted = [age <= threshold_ms for age in samples_ms]
assert accepted == [True, True, True, False, True]
print("worst observed age:", max(samples_ms))

lab.title: Write a timing contract
lab.environment: Python 3 offline; optional observation of the earlier Jazzy telemetry node
lab.safety: Analyze synthetic timings only. No timeout in this exercise is a physical robot stop guarantee.
steps: Run the age-budget example and derive its result manually.
Add 6 ms command transport and 15 ms actuator response as explicitly assumed stages.
Create a table assigning acquisition stamps, host timeouts, and simulator playback to clock types.
Draw a single-threaded callback timeline with a 100 ms blocking callback and a 20 ms subscription period.
Write a stale-data policy and identify which elapsed-time checks must continue during simulator pause.
lab.expected: The initial data age is 75 ms; the extended path is 96 ms, with measured and assumed values clearly separated.
acceptance: Clock domains are stated before timestamp subtraction
The full path includes queueing
No average timing is presented as a worst-case guarantee

troubleshooting.symptom: Apparent message age is negative
troubleshooting.cause: Clock domains or machine offsets differ
troubleshooting.fix: Verify timestamp origin and synchronization before changing subtraction order.

troubleshooting.symptom: A subscriber misses updates during a long callback
troubleshooting.cause: The executor cannot dispatch it in time
troubleshooting.fix: Measure callback duration and remove blocking work or redesign concurrency with owned state.

questions.prompt: A simulator pauses and ROS time stops advancing. Which clock should a host elapsed-time watchdog normally use?
choices: The message sequence number as seconds
A random offset
The paused ROS clock
A steady elapsed-time clock
questions.explanation: A watchdog that must expire during simulation pause needs an independently advancing elapsed clock.

questions.prompt: Inference takes 35 ms but the data is already 40 ms old on arrival. What age does the decision have before command transport?
choices: 75 ms
5 ms
35 ms
40 ms
questions.explanation: The decision includes the prior age plus processing time. Measuring only inference understates the end-to-end delay.

questions.prompt: Why can a synchronous wait inside a callback deadlock?
choices: All waits always deadlock
The awaited completion may need the same executor path that is blocked
DDS cannot use threads
Python prohibits callbacks
questions.explanation: The dependency cycle is the problem. Additional threads may help only when callback groups and shared state are also designed correctly.

lessons.title: Coordinate frames, rotations, and tf2
lessons.summary: Calculate a transform by hand before inspecting it with tf2. Track frame direction, timestamp, and quaternion ordering so numerically plausible data is not interpreted in the wrong geometry.
objectives: Transform a point through a planar rotation and translation
Explain parent/child direction and transform composition
Diagnose missing versus mistimed transforms

sections.heading: Coordinates belong to frames
sections.body:
A position vector is incomplete without the coordinate frame in which its components are expressed. A point one meter in front of a camera is not automatically one meter in front of the robot base. A rigid transform consists of rotation and translation. When mapping a point from a source frame to a target frame, rotate its coordinates according to the stated convention and then apply the source origin expressed in the target frame.

ROS conventions generally use meters and radians, right-handed frames, and a robot body convention of x forward, y left, z up. Camera optical frames use a different documented axis convention. Verify the actual sensor documentation and frame names rather than assigning a familiar convention by guess. A mesh that looks correctly oriented in a viewer does not prove its frame axes match the message contract.

sections.heading: Work a transform before building a tree
sections.body:
