lessons.summary: Trace the official bridge’s callback-coupled transport. Design a port that separates receive timing, command age, and state publication.
objectives: Explain the existing callback flow
Identify failure propagation and missing argument checks
Specify a testable modern adapter architecture
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: Read the callback as a sequence of obligations
sections.body: The pinned Go1 bridge converts a ROS command inside its callback, sets the UDP send buffer, sends, receives, converts state back to ROS, and publishes it. That sequence means state publication is coupled to command callbacks in the examined code. A learner who subscribes to the state topic and sees no updates might wrongly conclude the robot or network has failed. The source shows another possible explanation: no command callback has run. Do not fix that uncertainty by publishing a live motion command. Reproduce the callback behavior with a fake transport and document the coupling before choosing a new architecture.
sections.code:
# Source inspection; does not start the bridge or open UDP sockets.
rg -n 'Callback|SetSend|Send\(|Recv\(|publish|argv\[1\]' \
  unitree_ros2_to_real/src/ros2_udp.cpp
# Trace the matched lines in function order, not search-result order.
sections.callout: Course-authored offline exercise. It does not publish robot commands or establish hardware acceptance.

sections.heading: Blocking work can stall unrelated progress
sections.body: When send or receive work occurs inside a subscription callback, its timing becomes part of callback execution. Depending on the executor and transport behavior, delays can affect command handling or other callbacks. The source alone may not reveal every runtime timeout behavior, so inspect the SDK contract and measure a fake transport with controlled delays. Also examine startup argument handling: the historical main function reads argv[1], making validation of missing arguments an immediate porting concern. These are concrete engineering issues rather than reasons to discard the project. The code is useful as a reference, but a new deployment should make lifecycle and failure behavior explicit.

sections.heading: Define independent components with clear contracts
sections.body: A modernized design can separate ROS input validation, command selection, transport scheduling, state reception, and state publication. This is an application architecture proposal, not a claim that the vendor bridge already implements it. Each component should have bounded queues or latest-value semantics appropriate to its role. A command gate checks freshness and mode before transport, while a receive path reports state even when no new motion request is accepted, if the documented protocol permits that behavior. Do not assume a passive receive path works on hardware without verifying the protocol. The distinction is between designing the architecture and proving the device-specific exchange requirements.

sections.heading: Make migration acceptance observable
sections.body: A successful build on Humble is only the first migration milestone. Add tests for missing arguments, malformed command messages, stale requests, delayed receives, repeated samples, transport failure, and shutdown during an in-flight callback. The fake transport should expose intended sends so tests can prove none occur for rejected input. Track state publication independently in the fixture and explain any deliberate polling behavior. Retain a comparison between the historical implementation and the proposed adapter so reviewers can see changed semantics. The outcome is not a claim of a finished physical driver; it is a port specification with meaningful offline evidence and a clearly bounded list of remaining hardware checks.

troubleshooting.cause: The historical bridge publishes state inside command callbacks
troubleshooting.fix: Verify with the fake transport; do not send a physical motion command merely to probe telemetry

questions.prompt: Why can the historical bridge’s state topic be silent even if ROS discovery works?
choices: ROS discovery itself polls the vendor transport for new state
ROS high-level and low-level messages share one interchangeable state type
The transport receives state only when a ROS subscriber requests it
State publication occurs inside command callbacks in the examined source
questions.explanation: The callback structure couples publication to incoming commands. That is a source-backed hypothesis to test offline.

choices: Changing middleware defaults before checking startup arguments
Running a motion demo before validating startup failure behavior
Missing command-line argument handling
Checking steady-state throughput while ignoring invalid launch arguments

choices: Conversion, timing, failure and shutdown behavior
Only a topic-list snapshot, without conversion or failure tests
Only successful linking against the selected SDK library
Only the build exit code, because runtime compatibility follows from it

lessons.title: Capstone: release a Go1 adapter evidence package
lessons.summary: Combine compatibility, conversion, freshness, and fault tests into a reviewable release candidate. State exactly what offline evidence does and does not establish.
objectives: Produce a reproducible release manifest
Define migration acceptance criteria
Separate offline approval from physical acceptance
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: A release is a set of linked artifacts
sections.body: The adapter source is only one part of the release. Include the pinned SDK, build environment, message definitions, conversion rules, configuration schema, test fixtures, logs, and known limitations. Link each test result to the exact revision and configuration that produced it. A file named latest-results is weak evidence if it can refer to several code versions. Use a stable release identifier and content hashes for the artifacts that matter. This is particularly important in a legacy migration where the bridge, SDK, compiler and ROS distribution may all differ from the original reference stack. The package should let a reviewer recreate the offline evidence without guessing which instructions were used.

sections.heading: Acceptance criteria must be falsifiable
sections.body: Replace vague statements such as handles errors with specific expected outcomes. For example, a missing mode argument must exit before transport initialization; a stale semantic request must produce a named rejection and no intended send; a malformed joint vector must not be silently truncated. Choose numerical timing criteria only for the declared test environment and label them as project criteria rather than vendor specifications. Keep a test matrix with input, expected result, observed result and evidence location. Failed criteria remain visible. A release candidate with a documented failing gate can still be useful for review, but it is not a passed release.

sections.heading: Use fault injection to reveal hidden assumptions
sections.body: Normal-path tests often leave the most important assumptions untouched. Add delayed state, duplicate records, dropped input, unexpected mode, wrong configuration ID and cancellation while work is pending. A fake transport lets you make these cases repeatable. Check that recovery does not replay an old command simply because the connection returns. Recovery should re-establish required state and ownership through the supported process. Record whether a fault is detected, whether output is inhibited, and what evidence is required to leave the faulted state. This three-part analysis is more informative than a binary test passed label because it exposes both detection and recovery behavior.

sections.heading: Write the remaining physical test boundary
sections.body: The offline package does not prove the physical Go1 edition’s development access, firmware compatibility, supported control-state transitions, or operating performance. List these as remaining acceptance items with the appropriate vendor manual and local supervisor role. Do not include an automatic live-motion script that runs as part of a normal software test suite. The handoff should allow a reviewer to approve the offline engineering work while independently deciding whether a supervised hardware session is ready. This distinction is a strength: it prevents a clean CI result from being misread as operational authorization. The capstone succeeds when the evidence is complete, reproducible, and candid about what has not been observed.

The bridge is robust

Always

Vendor certification

All physical safety requirements

lessons.title: Identify the X2 you actually have
lessons.summary: Resolve X2 generation and configuration before installing software. Build a machine-readable capability record that prevents unsupported exercises.
objectives: Map a nameplate to the correct model
Separate mechanical and sensor capabilities
Record reproducible SDK evidence
prerequisites: Access to the robot nameplate or an instructor-supplied variant scenario

sections.heading: A product name is not a configuration
sections.body: The name X2 covers materially different machines. Current official specifications distinguish the original Ultra, Ultra new version, and EDU. The documented actuated counts are 30, 31, and 29 respectively. These numbers describe the body configuration; they are not a reliable shortcut for a hand's independent actuators. A program that allocates an array based only on the word X2 can be wrong before its first command. Establish an inventory with manufacturer, full model, nameplate suffix, serial number held privately, firmware, SDK archive identifier, end effector, compute units, and active sensor options. Treat unknown fields as unknown rather than filling them with the most capable configuration.

sections.heading: Build a capability contract
sections.body: The X2 EDU documentation limits secondary development to motion control and lists no Ultra perception or interaction package. Consequently, a camera lesson should not fail mysteriously on EDU: it should be classified as unavailable for that configuration. Represent each capability with three states: documented, observed, or unavailable. A documented camera still needs a live topic and valid frames before perception work begins. An observed topic without a matching model description is not enough to assign its optical frame. Capability records let the LMS select appropriate labs while retaining conceptual material for learners without that hardware. This is also how a mixed classroom avoids assuming everybody purchased the same robot.

sections.heading: Match model files deliberately
sections.body: The SDK download guidance maps original Ultra to the 1.3.0 model family and newer Ultra/EDU to 1.4.0. New Ultra also has hand-specific model files. Preserve that mapping alongside the exact repository commit, selected filename and file digest. A moving Git branch is useful for discovery but unsuitable as the only experimental identifier. A model update can alter limits, collision geometry or joint names, so rerunning yesterday's planner against today's model can change behavior. Compare the movable joint set and end-effector attachment against the real configuration before judging a planner. A visually plausible mesh is insufficient evidence that the kinematic chain is correct.

sections.heading: Turn differences into tests
sections.body: Consider an EDU scenario and a new Ultra scenario. Your loader should accept both inventory records but select different exercises and joint capabilities. A request for head pitch on EDU must be rejected before a publisher is created. A new Ultra model carrying the original model filename must produce a mismatch explanation that names the conflicting fields. Keep identifiers and facts separate from test results: passing an inventory validator proves internal consistency, not that the physical machine was inspected correctly. Have a second person compare the record to the nameplate before supervised operation. This small review is cheaper than debugging an entire integration around the wrong embodiment.

lessons.title: Reproduce the AimDK environment without altering motion control
lessons.summary: Choose external-host or container development according to your variant and firmware. Separate dependency errors from network discovery failures.
objectives: Specify a compatible development environment
Explain why motion control compute is not a build host
Design a reproducible environment manifest
prerequisites: Basic Linux shell and ROS 2 overlays

sections.heading: The computer is part of the experiment
sections.body: An SDK installation is a relationship among the operating system, ROS distribution, compiler, Python, middleware, messages and vendor binaries. AimDK's external-host requirements specify Ubuntu 22.04 and ROS 2 Humble. That combination is the baseline for this course even if a newer ROS release exists. Upgrading one layer without matching the vendor support matrix introduces an experiment whose outcome must be measured. Record CPU architecture, package versions, downloaded SDK identity and firmware pairing. Keep a fresh terminal procedure that sources the intended ROS installation and one workspace overlay. A terminal inherited from another project can resolve the wrong message package while appearing perfectly healthy.

sections.heading: Place work on the correct machine
sections.body: X2 Ultra includes a development computing unit; EDU requires an external development host. The documentation explicitly prohibits building or running secondary development on the motion-control computing unit. This is an architectural boundary: a compiler, package installer or memory-heavy application can compete with timing-sensitive control work. The supported development location is not interchangeable with every computer that answers SSH. Draw the network with each machine's role before entering it. The distinction matters more than memorizing an address, because addresses may be reconfigured while the separation of responsibilities remains necessary. Credentials are supplied through the owner's support channel, not invented by a course.

sections.heading: Containers preserve a known runtime
sections.body: AimDK 1.1.0 supports a transition to container development and announces a requirement for containers on the development unit from 1.2.0. Record this as a version rule, not a claim that the installed robot already runs 1.2.0. Containers package dependencies, but they still share host resources and may use host networking. They do not turn unbounded CPU work into safe work automatically. Review the vendor runtime mounts, devices and networking before launching. Preserve user code outside system-managed SDK directories and retain a copy outside the robot. A container rebuild should not require retrieving yesterday's only source code from a robot awaiting service.

sections.heading: Diagnose in dependency order
sections.body: First prove that the intended message packages can be located locally. Next prove a trivial local publisher/subscriber pair works. Only then test the wired path and vendor discovery configuration. A successful ping proves IP reachability, not ROS service health or matching type definitions. Conversely, a missing package does not become available by changing the robot's address. Capture each layer's result separately so a later technician can reproduce the failure. The exercise produces a deployment plan and a local environment fingerprint; it does not claim a completed hardware installation. If the required SDK archive or credential is unavailable, mark that gate pending and complete the offline dependency review.

lessons.title: Treat motion modes as a state machine
lessons.summary: Separate request delivery, request acceptance and observed state. Build a transition supervisor that explains rejected actions.
objectives: Interpret mode-switch result codes
Distinguish transport success from action success
Prevent repeated unsafe transitions

sections.heading: Three different meanings of success
sections.body: A service request reaching a server is not the same as an accepted transition, and an accepted transition is not the same as the robot completing that transition. Model these as separate observations. The request has a client-side deadline; the response has a vendor result; the measured state has a timestamp. If a UI collapses all three into a green button, it hides the distinction most useful during a fault. Build an application state machine with requested, accepted, transitioning, confirmed and failed states. Preserve the original result code and descriptive text rather than reducing every failure to false. This makes recovery a reasoned decision instead of a repeated button press.

sections.heading: Follow the actual mode contract
sections.body: The official interface names modes such as STAND_DEFAULT and JOINT_DEFAULT. Their similar English descriptions do not make their control semantics equivalent. Since the documented 0.8 transition, stable stand and locomotion are internally coordinated, so old examples may describe boundaries differently. Current SetMcAction responses include a switch result code. A rejection for invalid posture is different from one for an unknown action name or startup still in progress. Your software should classify each outcome and show an operator what evidence is missing. A generic retry loop can turn an ordinary transition delay into a stream of contradictory requests.

sections.heading: Authority and protection are distinct
sections.body: Input-source priority governs continuous control streams; it does not confer unlimited authority to switch modes. Safety protection and posture constraints remain separate. This is an important example of layered control: a source may own locomotion commands while a requested discrete transition remains invalid. Write state-machine guards in terms of observed prerequisites, not just the existence of an SDK connection. A stale mode sample should prevent a new movement sequence from starting. Where documentation is version-dependent, preserve the supported transition information for the exact firmware and test the interpretation in simulation before reviewing it for hardware.

sections.heading: Reconstruct an incident from a trace
sections.body: Imagine a client requests stand, receives a rejection during startup, retries immediately, and then publishes velocity. The first bad assumption is that submitting the stand request established the precondition for velocity. A better trace stops at the rejection, keeps motion disabled, and records the startup state until an operator or documented sequence resumes progress. In the lab, inject this failure into a mock service and verify the UI never reports ready. Also inject delayed success and dropped responses: an uncertain outcome calls for observation, not blindly resending a non-idempotent action. The result is a supervisor whose behavior is inspectable even when the underlying control service is temporarily unavailable.

lab.title: Build a mode-transition trace
lab.environment: Offline mock service or official X2 simulation
lab.safety: Only the simulator or a mock may receive transition requests in this lab.
steps: Create a table of five documented modes and their intended control level.
Model requested, accepted, transitioning, confirmed and failed application states.
Feed the model a startup rejection, unknown-action rejection, delayed success and lost response.
Require fresh observed state before permitting the next simulated movement step.
Export a timestamped trace with request ID, result and observation.
lab.expected: Rejected or uncertain requests cannot silently enable a movement stage.
acceptance: Response and observed state are separate
A startup rejection leaves movement disabled
A dropped response triggers observation or explicit timeout

troubleshooting.symptom: The UI says ready after any response
troubleshooting.cause: Transport completion is being treated as mode completion
troubleshooting.fix: Require a successful vendor result and a fresh expected-state observation

questions.prompt: A mode request returns a posture rejection. What is the correct next step?
choices: Publish velocity to force the state
Inspect the current posture and allowed transition
Ignore the response if the network is stable
Raise SDK priority
questions.explanation: Posture constraints are independent of continuous-input priority. A higher source priority does not repair an invalid transition.

questions.prompt: A response is lost after sending an action. What is unsafe to assume?
choices: Current state must be queried
The deadline should be logged
The result is uncertain
The action definitely did not happen
questions.explanation: A lost response may follow an accepted command. Resending without observing can duplicate a discrete action.

questions.prompt: Which evidence establishes readiness for a sequence?
choices: A fresh expected-state observation following an accepted transition
An open socket
A successful process exit
A successful response without a fresh state observation
questions.explanation: Readiness depends on current state, not just delivery or a past appearance.

lessons.title: Control ownership, zero commands and deadmen
lessons.summary: Analyze why a valid velocity command may be ignored. Test ownership handover and stale-command behavior using the documented arbitration rules.
objectives: Model source priority and timeout
Explain zero-command behavior
Separate velocity intent from position accuracy

sections.heading: Ownership is a separate variable
sections.body: A velocity message can be correctly typed, correctly timed and still not own the robot. AimDK arbitrates registered continuous-command sources. Keep desired source, currently selected source and observed motion as separate fields in your application. If the remote controller is active, an SDK request may be discarded as expected. Reporting that as a communications outage leads users to change the wrong subsystem. Give application sources unique sdk_ names and record registration outcomes. Do not impersonate built-in sources or modify them to make a demo work. A well-behaved application must explain why it is waiting for authority instead of silently competing for it.

sections.heading: Zero does not renew ownership
sections.body: The documented arbitration timer tracks nonzero commands. Zero commands are accepted but do not refresh that timer. Therefore, publishing zeros is not a general-purpose heartbeat proving continued ownership. Consider source A last moving at time zero and then repeatedly sending zero; source B may become eligible after A's configured timeout. The current-source label can also remain present after its command data expires. This means a label alone cannot answer whether the command is active. Design your monitor around the selected source, command age, registration state and motion observation. In a classroom simulator, these variables can be plotted together to make otherwise surprising handovers visible.

sections.heading: Distinguish the two timeout layers
sections.body: The locomotion interface documents command zeroing after 200 milliseconds without a new command and a return toward stable standing after 2000 milliseconds without locomotion commands. Source arbitration has its own timeout. These are related but different clocks: one manages stale velocity intent, another manages who can provide intent. Record the timing requirements from the exact installed version and measure observed behavior rather than treating a nominal period as a guarantee. A 50 Hz publishing loop has a nominal 20 millisecond interval, but scheduling pauses can be much longer. Monitor maximum gaps and percentiles, not only the average message rate.

sections.heading: Velocity is not a destination
sections.body: A forward command sustained for a calculated duration does not promise an exact endpoint. Gait, terrain and payload affect tracking, and the official interface explicitly describes velocity-level open-loop control. An application that needs a location must close the loop using localization and an appropriate navigation interface. For an illustrative simulator test, compare integrating commanded velocity with integrating measured velocity; their divergence is a tracking-error estimate, not automatically a localization error. A safe control design also handles authority loss: discard stale accumulated intent, reobserve the state, and require a deliberate resume policy. Otherwise a returning controller can replay motion that was appropriate seconds ago but is now wrong.

lab.title: Simulate command arbitration on a timeline
lab.environment: Offline event table or X2 simulator with no hardware network
lab.safety: Keep all injected nonzero commands inside the mock or simulator.
steps: Create two custom sources with different priorities and finite timeouts.
Simulate a nonzero command, repeated zeros, source timeout and another source requesting control.
Add independent 200ms and 2000ms missing-locomotion events to the trace.
Introduce a delayed publishing interval despite an acceptable average rate.
Write an application policy for losing and regaining ownership without replaying old intent.
lab.expected: The trace distinguishes selected source, active intent and motion timeout.
acceptance: Zero commands do not renew the nonzero timer
Command age and ownership are independent fields
Regaining control drops stale intent

troubleshooting.symptom: Commands publish but simulated motion stays zero
troubleshooting.cause: The source lacks authority or a prerequisite mode
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect registration, selected source and mode before changing QoS

questions.prompt: Source A sends zero continuously after its last nonzero command. Does that renew its source timer?
choices: Only if it is an SDK source
Always
No, under the documented arbitration rule
Only at 50Hz
questions.explanation: The timer is based on nonzero commands; zero acceptance does not imply ownership renewal.

choices: A higher velocity fixes the pause
The message gap exceeds the documented locomotion zeroing interval
Only its average rate
Its name
questions.explanation: Averages hide deadline misses. A 300ms gap exceeds the documented 200ms command timeout.

choices: Time cannot be measured
The command has no notion of forward direction
The message cannot represent yaw motion
The velocity interface does not guarantee precise tracking or endpoints
questions.explanation: The motion controller tracks a target subject to physical variation; destination control needs observed position feedback.

lessons.title: Time, calibration and sensor evidence
lessons.summary: Inspect sensor streams without commanding motion. Establish whether geometry and timing support the perception claim you want to make.
objectives: Distinguish nominal and measured transforms
Validate image synchronization assumptions
Document usable observation quality
prerequisites: ROS 2 transforms and image message concepts
Ultra hardware or authorized recorded data

sections.heading: An image needs a geometric contract
sections.body: An RGB image is an array of pixel values, not a set of metric points. To turn a pixel and a depth measurement into a spatial observation, you need the correct camera model, intrinsics, distortion handling, depth units and transform. A plausible visualization can conceal a systematically wrong frame. AimDK separates nominal URDF geometry from per-unit factory calibration. The former describes the designed kinematic chain; the latter captures measured sensor placement and camera parameters. Preserve both versions and their roles. Do not overwrite factory calibration to make a visual overlay look better. First determine whether the selected transform is being interpreted in the correct direction.

sections.heading: RGB and depth are not interchangeable grids
sections.body: Current X2 documentation states that RGB and depth pixels are not directly aligned and that the streams are published independently. Consequently, sampling depth at an RGB detector's raw pixel index is not a valid general recipe for object position. Reproject using the correct camera models and transform, and match observations in time. A stationary scene may hide timing errors; a moving object exposes them as inconsistent depth association. In an offline exercise, shift one stream by several frames and inspect how the estimated point changes. Label that shift as an injected defect so nobody mistakes it for a measured sensor characteristic.

sections.heading: Test freshness and completeness separately
sections.body: A stream can be active while delivering stale frames, mismatched timestamps or an unexpected encoding. Record receive time and sensor timestamp where available, plus sequence continuity, frame identifier, dimensions and encoding. Separate transport dropouts from processing backlog: a subscriber processing every old frame may show no apparent packet loss while its output age grows continuously. Bounded queues and an explicit newest-frame policy can be appropriate for live perception, but archival recording has different requirements. Define the acceptable age and synchronization window for the task before tuning the queue. There is no universal window that makes every manipulation or mapping application correct.

sections.heading: Use evidence appropriate to the claim
sections.body: A colored point cloud is a useful diagnostic, not a complete calibration certificate. Evaluate multiple scene depths, static landmarks and known orientations. A rotated axis or inverse transform may look reasonable near one plane and fail elsewhere. For read-only hardware work, keep the robot in the vendor-approved stationary configuration and avoid adding large numbers of nodes at once. A recorded-data lab can validate the pipeline's handling of missing frames and invalid calibration without touching the robot. The final sensor report should state exactly what was tested: stream availability, time alignment, geometric consistency and processing delay. It should also state which properties remain unmeasured, especially absolute accuracy without a reference target.

lab.title: Produce a sensor contract report
lab.environment: Recorded X2 Ultra bag or stationary Ultra under approved observation procedure
lab.safety: Subscribe only; do not publish robot commands or modify protected calibration files.
steps: Select one RGB/depth pair and record topic types, encodings, frame IDs and rates.
Read a copy of the matching calibration and model; note direction, units and timestamp.
Plot timestamp differences and end-to-end observation age over a short authorized recording.
Inject missing and delayed frames into offline replay and verify the pipeline rejects invalid pairs.
Explain whether the collected evidence supports visualization, metric localization or neither.
lab.expected: Invalid pairs are rejected and every metric point has an explicit transform and timestamp basis.
acceptance: No one-to-one RGB/depth alignment is assumed
Calibration is read without modification
Missing frames produce an explicit invalid observation

troubleshooting.symptom: A point cloud looks displaced despite valid images
troubleshooting.cause: Transform direction, calibration identity or synchronization is wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Test a known static landmark and inspect each transform/time assumption separately

questions.prompt: A detector returns RGB pixel (u,v). May you read the depth array at that index?
choices: Only after proving registration or performing reprojection
Yes on every RGB-D camera
Yes if both images are rectangular
Only if both streams have the same image dimensions
questions.explanation: Current X2 streams are not one-to-one aligned. Array indexing alone does not establish correspondence.

questions.prompt: Which source captures per-robot sensor placement?
choices: The matching factory calibration
Only the nominal mesh
The camera topic namespace alone
The nominal URDF shared by the product family
questions.explanation: Factory calibration records measured sensor parameters. URDF serves a different nominal kinematic role.

questions.prompt: A subscriber processes all frames but its output gets older. What is likely?
choices: Perfect real-time behavior
A processing backlog
Correctly synchronized capture and processing clocks
A policy that always processes only the newest frame
questions.explanation: Queue accumulation increases age even if every frame is eventually processed.

lessons.title: Run a complete X2 simulation stack
lessons.summary: Trace AimDK commands through motion control into MuJoCo. Prove which components are actually participating before evaluating a behavior.
objectives: Separate physics, motion control and SDK responsibilities
Diagnose missing state versus missing commands
Create a reproducible simulation trace
prerequisites: Matching simulation and MC packages from the official download channel

sections.heading: A model viewer is not the control stack
sections.body: Loading an X2 mesh or URDF proves that an asset can be interpreted. It does not prove the vendor motion controller is present, the SDK topics match, or a gait exists. The official simulation workflow has three roles: MuJoCo represents the physical body, the motion-control process produces joint commands, and AimDK provides application requests. Draw the complete feedback loop. Joint and IMU state flows back to motion control; high-level intent flows in from the application. When the robot stands still on screen, determine whether it is being actively controlled, frozen by the simulator, or merely displayed. These states can look deceptively similar in a screenshot.

sections.heading: Match delivered components
sections.body: The SDK archive and simulation or reinforcement-learning extras are separate downloads. Keep a manifest for every component and its expected relative directory. The official simulation setup targets an x86_64 Ubuntu 22.04 desktop and offers local and container routes. Do not substitute an unrelated X1 reinforcement-learning example and call it X2 simulation. A copied launch script can refer to an old model path or incompatible binary, so record the exact launch entry and working directory used. A process that starts is only the first acceptance gate. The next gate is coherent bidirectional data at the intended interfaces.

sections.heading: Trace the loop at its boundaries
sections.body: Inspect the state topics before sending application commands. Then observe whether a documented mode request reaches the motion controller and whether joint commands emerge. If state exists but commands do not, the failure lies above the physics boundary or in controller prerequisites. If commands exist but the body never changes, inspect simulator subscriptions, paused state and model joint mapping. This boundary-by-boundary method is more useful than reinstalling every dependency at once. Keep logging overhead bounded; tracing every high-rate sample to a terminal can itself change scheduling. Use short targeted captures and summarize rates, gaps and values after the run.

sections.heading: Fault injection gives the simulation purpose
sections.body: A successful nominal motion is the beginning of verification. Pause the application, delay state updates, remove a required process and restart components in the wrong order. Record how the application identifies the failure and whether it preserves a clear non-ready state. These tests validate your supervisory logic, not the physical robot's balance or contact model. Friction, latency and actuator characteristics in simulation are assumptions; document them before making a transfer claim. The final artifact is a reproducible experiment: component versions, launch sequence, initial conditions, commands, observations and outcomes. Another learner should be able to rerun the same failure and get the same application decision without relying on your memory.

lab.title: Trace one mode through three components
lab.environment: Official X2 MuJoCo/MC/AimDK package on Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64
lab.safety: Disconnect or isolate hardware discovery; commands are intended only for simulation.
steps: Inventory aimdk, sim_mujoco and mc artifacts and their versions.
Follow the official local or Docker launch sequence and verify each process is alive.
Record state topic activity, then perform one documented simulated mode transition.
Identify joint command output and correlate it with changing simulated state.
Stop the application, then stop MC in a separate trial; record the distinct fault observations.
lab.expected: The trace establishes which boundary fails in each injected fault.
acceptance: All three components are identified
A model render alone is not marked complete
Missing MC and missing SDK produce distinguishable reports

troubleshooting.symptom: The model displays but never responds
troubleshooting.cause: Only physics/viewer is running or the controller interface mismatches
troubleshooting.fix: Check MC presence and joint-command boundary before changing physics parameters

questions.prompt: What does a rendered X2 model establish?
choices: Complete AimDK compatibility
Successful physical deployment
That the model/viewer path works
That locomotion is stable
questions.explanation: Rendering validates an asset path, not the closed control loop.

questions.prompt: State topics are live but no joint commands appear after a request. Where should you inspect first?
choices: Camera calibration
The color of the model in the viewer
The visual mesh material definition
MC readiness and request handling
questions.explanation: The missing output is above the physics-state boundary; controller prerequisites and request handling are the next relevant checks.

questions.prompt: What can fault-injection simulation validate directly?
choices: The supervisor response to missing components
Real floor friction
Physical payload limits
The delivered robot certification
questions.explanation: The application decision can be tested directly; physical contact parameters need independent evidence.

lessons.title: Upper-body arrays and low-level control boundaries
lessons.summary: Audit joint order, units and message freshness before any movement. Compare the guarantees of upper-body and raw joint interfaces.
objectives: Validate array dimensions and ordering
Explain message freshness rejection
Design low-level failure containment
prerequisites: Joint-space position, velocity and torque concepts

sections.heading: A joint array is an ordered contract
sections.body: Fourteen arm values mean seven left-arm joints followed by seven right-arm joints in the documented upper-body interface. The array is not a bag of angles that the receiver sorts by intention. If a shoulder value lands in a wrist slot, every number can be individually finite while the command is semantically wrong. Construct a named internal representation and generate arrays from an explicit mapping. Validate missing names, duplicates, unexpected names, dimensions and units before serialization. Use a deliberately asymmetric offline test vector so swapping left and right cannot accidentally pass. Uniform all-zero tests are poor at detecting mapping mistakes.

sections.heading: Mode and freshness determine interpretation
sections.body: The upper-body interface uses /mc/upper_body_command, with hand content selected by submode. Different hand submodes have different array lengths and meanings. Head control also has a distinct supported mode and depends on the X2 variant. Do not assume that supplying head values in a combined upper-body request makes them active. The documented freshness rule rejects nonzero timestamps more than 200 milliseconds from receive time. Clock errors can therefore resemble a broken controller. Track clock synchronization and intended timestamp semantics in the environment manifest. A zero timestamp has a documented receive-time behavior, but using it should be a deliberate choice, not an accidental uninitialized header.

sections.heading: Lower level means fewer inherited protections
sections.body: Raw joint commands expose position, velocity, effort, stiffness and damping. Those fields correspond to different physical dimensions; a value copied between them is not meaningful because its numerical magnitude happens to look reasonable. Crucially, the current X2 documentation says low-level joint command topics have no automatic timeout or fail-safe protection when publishing stops. The locomotion watchdog cannot be assumed to protect this interface. A process crash can leave the last command relevant. This changes the architecture required for hardware execution: independent supervision, a validated stop strategy and a control owner become prerequisites, not optional polish after the demo works.

sections.heading: Design a gate before designing a trajectory
sections.body: The offline validator should reject nonfinite numbers, an incorrect model identity, missing measured initial state, stale observations, out-of-contract joint names and invalid array sizes. Limits must come from the correct model and validated device procedure; do not invent a universal safe pose or gain. Then inject a stopped publisher into a control-system model and describe which independent component detects it and which verified mechanism handles the robot. A Python finally block is useful cleanup but cannot run after every crash, power loss or host freeze. The lab ends at this design review. It deliberately does not supply a generic torque-control program that would pretend every X2 configuration and support setup behaves identically.

lab.title: Audit a joint-command serializer
lab.environment: Offline Python or spreadsheet; no robot or control publisher
lab.safety: This lesson does not actuate joints. Do not run generic low-level examples on an unsupported robot.
steps: Build named mappings for fourteen arm slots and each documented hand submode.
Generate an asymmetric synthetic pose with labels rather than hardware angles.
Test swapped sides, omitted values, wrong hand lengths, nonfinite values and stale timestamps.
Compare the upper-body freshness contract with the raw joint no-timeout warning.
Write a failure-containment review for a crashed publisher, including a genuinely independent observer.
lab.expected: All structural faults are rejected before a command could reach hardware.
acceptance: Joint order is explicit
Wrong hand submode lengths fail
No locomotion timeout is assumed for raw joints

troubleshooting.symptom: All-zero tests pass after a left/right swap
troubleshooting.cause: The fixture is symmetric and cannot detect permutation
troubleshooting.fix: Use distinct labeled values at every slot and compare the generated ordering

questions.prompt: Why is an all-zero joint fixture weak?
choices: Zero is always illegal
It cannot verify the number of array elements
It automatically verifies left-versus-right semantics
It cannot expose a permutation of identical values
questions.explanation: Equal values survive reordering, so swapped slots remain invisible.

questions.prompt: What happens when raw X2 joint publishing stops according to the documented interface?
choices: The locomotion 200ms watchdog always takes over
No automatic joint timeout/fail-safe is promised
All command fields automatically reset to zero
The current joint command is guaranteed to expire
questions.explanation: The low-level interface explicitly lacks the locomotion timeout guarantee; a separate containment design is needed.

questions.prompt: Why is a finally block insufficient as the sole stop mechanism?
choices: It cannot execute after every host crash or power loss
Cleanup code cannot access an SDK client
Cleanup code always changes the joint ordering
ROS automatically executes cleanup on a powered-off host
questions.explanation: Software cleanup covers orderly exits and some exceptions, not all process and host failures.

lessons.title: X2 capstone: a bounded observation-and-navigation task
lessons.summary: Assemble a task supervisor with observable preconditions and measured failures. Deliver a reviewable evidence bundle for a specific X2 configuration.
objectives: Define measurable task acceptance
Separate localization, navigation and motion authority
Produce a deployment readiness decision

sections.heading: Define the task so failure is measurable
sections.body: A useful capstone has a concrete starting condition, target, permitted area and termination rule. Use a simulated inspection waypoint: begin in a known location, reach a designated pose, obtain a fresh observation and finish in a documented nonmoving condition. Choose tolerances as experimental requirements, not as claimed vendor accuracy. Specify the position frame, orientation convention and how arrival is observed. If the only measurement is an integrated velocity command, you have not established arrival. Separate task success from motion success: a robot can reach the waypoint yet fail the inspection because the camera frame is stale or the target is occluded.

sections.heading: Build a supervisor above the components
sections.body: The supervisor coordinates readiness, authority, localization, navigation, observation and completion. It should not embed assumptions that a running process means every prerequisite is valid. Give each state an entry condition, deadline, expected observation and failure outcome. If localization becomes invalid while navigating, pause task advancement and report the relevant evidence. If control ownership changes, discard obsolete movement intent. Diagnostics should preserve first failure and subsequent consequences separately; otherwise a lost sensor followed by a navigation timeout may be misreported simply as slow navigation. Keep vendor result codes alongside application categories to support later investigation.

sections.heading: Choose an experiment matrix
sections.body: Run a nominal case, stale camera case, lost localization case, navigation rejection and ownership loss. Use fixed initial conditions for repeatability, then vary one condition at a time. Measure completion rate, time-to-detect failure and stop or hold behavior as observed in the simulator. Document the number of trials and all exclusions. Ten successes out of ten attempts is an observed result under defined conditions, not evidence of perfect reliability. The hardware readiness decision needs additional evidence about the real environment, operator procedure and independent stop mechanism. Keep that gate visibly separate from simulation results so a learner cannot earn physical readiness by clicking through text.

sections.heading: Package evidence for another engineer
sections.body: The handoff includes the capability manifest, component versions, diagram, state table, parameters, test fixtures, logs and acceptance decisions. For each claim, point to the artifact that supports it. A polished video is useful context but should not replace timestamps, rejected-request logs or configuration hashes. State what has not been tested: a different firmware, a different hand, outdoor terrain or a disconnected sensor can invalidate an assumption. The final review asks whether the system fails transparently, not merely whether it can complete the easiest demonstration. This is the difference between an application someone can maintain and a one-off choreography that only its author understands.

lab.title: Deliver an X2 task acceptance dossier
lab.environment: Official X2 simulator; hardware execution is a separate operator-reviewed stage
lab.safety: Keep waypoint trials in simulation. Physical approval requires the actual robot procedure and environment.
steps: Specify one inspection waypoint, observation requirement, frame and termination rule.
Implement or table-model the supervisor with deadlines and explicit readiness gates.
Run a nominal trial and four independently injected failures.
Record trial count, detection delay and final supervisor state for every case.
Write a release decision listing passed software evidence and unresolved physical gates.
lab.expected: Every scenario produces a deterministic task outcome and a traceable reason.
acceptance: Arrival is based on observation rather than command integration
All injected faults block false task completion
Simulation and physical evidence are reported separately

troubleshooting.symptom: Navigation succeeds but the capstone output is invalid
troubleshooting.cause: Task completion ignored observation freshness or content
troubleshooting.fix: Add an explicit observation acceptance stage after arrival

questions.prompt: The waypoint is reached but the image is stale. Is the task complete?
choices: Only the motor count matters
No, the inspection requirement failed
Yes, movement is the task
Yes if the video looks smooth
questions.explanation: The task includes a valid observation, so navigation success alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: What should a readiness report call ten successful simulator trials?
choices: Guaranteed field reliability
Vendor certification
Proof for all X2 variants
Observed simulation success under the recorded conditions
questions.explanation: The result supports its tested conditions; broader transfer requires evidence.

questions.prompt: Which artifact is most useful for diagnosing a false-ready state?
choices: An aggregate task-success percentage without event traces
A trace linking prerequisites, requests and observed states
A graph of average CPU usage without event timestamps
A controller configuration file without runtime observations
questions.explanation: A trace reveals which transition incorrectly accepted missing evidence.

lessons.title: Audit the D1 SDK before trusting an example
lessons.summary: Inspect headers, binaries and examples for the supplied D1 model. Resolve real discrepancies instead of copying plausible API names.
objectives: Locate the native public contract
Distinguish Python ABI from CPU architecture
Resolve documentation/header conflicts
prerequisites: C++ declarations and Python import basics

sections.heading: Start with the delivered interface
sections.body: The official D1 repository contains model-specific public headers, precompiled libraries and examples. It does not expose every controller implementation. That is enough to develop against a defined interface, but not enough to claim that you can inspect or modify the complete motion controller. Keep the public API contract separate from assumptions about internal behavior. Inventory the exact model directory, architecture, library file, header and sample that will be used together. A repository title containing EDU and Ultra does not prove that every class supports every shipping D1 variant. If the seller's model name and SDK model directory do not match clearly, obtain that mapping before any actuation.

sections.heading: Resolve a real naming conflict
sections.body: At the pinned revision, the ZSL-1 high-level header declares checkConnect() and standUp(). The prose API page instead shows checkConnection() and standUP(). These differences matter because identifiers are case-sensitive. The course therefore treats the actual pinned header as the C++ compilation contract and records the prose discrepancy. It does not silently invent an alias. The same principle applies to a Python extension: inspect the delivered binding and sample instead of assuming every C++ spelling was exported unchanged. A documentation audit is not pedantry; it prevents learners from diagnosing a nonexistent networking problem when their application cannot even call the intended method.

sections.heading: Binary compatibility has several dimensions
sections.body: A shared library for aarch64 will not become an x86_64 library because both machines run Ubuntu. A Python extension tagged for CPython 3.10 may not import into another interpreter ABI. Separately, the library may require compatible system dependencies and loader paths. Record architecture and Python ABI explicitly, then inspect the file before importing it. Distinguish a missing-file error from an incompatible binary or unresolved symbol. Reinstalling ROS does not repair all three. Keep the environment reproducible with an isolated dependency set and the original vendor artifacts; a locally renamed binary is not evidence that compatibility was established.

sections.heading: Turn the audit into a compile-only gate
sections.body: Create a small compile-only translation unit that includes the intended header and references a declared member type without constructing the robot object. This checks headers and compiler syntax without starting communication. Then inspect the example's startup path for initialization, network setup and motion side effects. An example named high-level can still issue real commands. Classify every executable as read-only, potentially motion-capable or unknown before deciding what the lab may run. The audit deliverable is a compatibility table with observed evidence and remaining questions. Passing it establishes that development can proceed coherently; it does not establish that the physical robot is ready to move.

lab.title: Produce a D1 SDK compatibility audit
lab.environment: Offline SDK checkout, compiler and binary-inspection tools
lab.safety: Do not instantiate SDK clients or execute motion examples during this audit.
steps: Pin the official repository and identify the supplied model folder.
Compare the high-level header, API prose and example names for connection and stand methods.
Record CPU architecture, Python extension ABI and library dependencies.
Compile a header-only inspection unit without linking or constructing a client.
Label example entry points by possible hardware side effects.
lab.expected: The audit identifies the genuine spelling conflict and a compatible artifact set.
acceptance: checkConnect and standUp are distinguished from prose spellings
CPU and Python ABI are separate fields
No hardware example is run

troubleshooting.symptom: An import fails although the file exists
troubleshooting.cause: The extension architecture or interpreter ABI may mismatch
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the binary and interpreter tags before changing network settings

questions.prompt: Which spelling does the pinned C++ header declare?
choices: connectCheck()
checkConnect()
check_connection()
checkConnection()
questions.explanation: The actual header declares checkConnect(); the prose discrepancy must be recorded instead of copied.

questions.prompt: A cp310 extension fails under another Python version. What should you inspect?
choices: The controller mode on a device never contacted
Interpreter ABI compatibility
The robot target address before inspecting the local binary
The network discovery domain before the extension imports
questions.explanation: The failure occurs at the binary/interpreter boundary before robot communication.

questions.prompt: Does a successful compile-only check prove hardware readiness?
choices: Yes if the repository is official
Only if root is used
No; it proves a limited software-interface property
Yes
questions.explanation: Compilation says nothing about live firmware, transport, mode or physical readiness.

lessons.title: Establish two-way D1 communication
lessons.summary: Model the complete host-to-robot and robot-to-host path. Diagnose connection failure without changing unrelated network services.
objectives: Explain local and target addressing
Distinguish connectivity from live telemetry
Create a reversible network runbook

sections.heading: The reply path matters
sections.body: A robot SDK often needs more than a target IP. The D1 high-level initialization declares a local IP, local port and robot IP; deployment guidance also configures where the robot sends data. The local address is the address the robot can reach, not whichever address happens to appear first on a laptop. A laptop may have Wi-Fi, Ethernet, VPN and virtual interfaces simultaneously. Draw both directions explicitly: outgoing client traffic and incoming robot telemetry. A one-way ping result does not establish that the robot is sending state to the intended host. Capture interface selection and routing evidence before adjusting timeouts.

sections.heading: Defaults are discovery aids, not authority
sections.body: The official README documents separate Wi-Fi and Ethernet defaults. Treat them as starting references and compare them with the delivered device configuration. Do not change every network address to fit an old example. On an authorized isolated setup, identify the intended physical port and host interface, then confirm addressing with the owner-approved procedure. Keep a before-and-after record for any necessary configuration change. The course does not supply credentials or suggest weakening access controls. Credentials and robot-side changes belong to the legitimate owner support process. An offline learner can complete the network diagram and failure analysis using supplied scenarios.

sections.heading: Connection and state freshness differ
sections.body: A connection indicator can remain true while feedback becomes old or incomplete. Record the last successful state update separately from a connection status. Distinguish host receive time from a robot timestamp where one is available; without a device timestamp, report that end-to-end freshness cannot be measured directly. A polling loop can repeatedly return cached data and appear active. Use changing counters or known benign state signals only when documented to verify updates, and label inference honestly. A read-only session should not issue stand or movement commands merely to prove that the network works. Communication validation is a prerequisite to motion validation, not a reason to bypass it.

sections.heading: Diagnose the narrowest failed layer
sections.body: If the library does not load, stop at binary compatibility. If local binding fails, inspect the chosen host interface and port. If local binding succeeds but connection times out, inspect the configured destination and return route. If telemetry arrives intermittently, measure packet gaps and host scheduling before increasing command rates. The D1 FAQ warns that particular robot interface configuration can prevent startup when an expected interface lacks an address. That makes speculative network-service edits especially poor troubleshooting. The runbook should offer observations, reversible changes and a known restore path. Conclude with the strongest claim supported: address reachability, SDK connection or fresh telemetry, rather than a single vague connected label.

lab.title: Map and verify the D1 telemetry path
lab.environment: Owner-authorized D1 wired observation setup or offline topology fixtures
lab.safety: Use only approved read-only SDK operations; do not alter startup services or issue stance commands.
steps: Draw all host interfaces, the selected cable, local bind address and robot target.
Record current addressing and the documented robot telemetry destination.
Check local SDK loading before testing network connectivity.
Observe connection state and telemetry age independently for a bounded capture.
Test an incorrect return address in an offline fixture and document the resulting diagnosis.
lab.expected: The report distinguishes local setup, forward reachability and return telemetry.
deliverables: Restore plan for any approved changes
acceptance: Local and target IP roles are distinct
Fresh telemetry is not inferred from ping alone
No unsupported service edits are used

troubleshooting.symptom: Local bind succeeds but the SDK times out
troubleshooting.cause: Target or return-path configuration may be wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Compare selected interface and robot destination with the recorded topology

questions.prompt: Which host IP belongs in a local bind field?
choices: Any public IP
The reachable address on the intended robot-facing interface
Always localhost
The address of the default internet gateway
questions.explanation: The local endpoint must exist on the host and support the intended return route.

questions.prompt: Why is ping insufficient?
choices: It verifies only the outgoing route and never a return path
It verifies every application port on the device
It tests reachability but not the SDK telemetry contract
It validates the Python extension ABI
questions.explanation: A reachable device can still send telemetry elsewhere or use incompatible SDK settings.

questions.prompt: What should happen before changing robot startup networking?
choices: Select a different robot interface before recording the original configuration
Increase connection timeouts before recording current configuration
Record the narrow fault and owner-approved restore path
Disable network services until the timeout disappears
questions.explanation: Startup networking has documented failure consequences; changes should follow evidence and a reversible procedure.

lessons.title: Build a telemetry contract with units and frames
lessons.summary: Normalize D1 observations without hiding their original semantics. Use synthetic telemetry to detect frame, ordering and freshness defects.
objectives: Map telemetry to explicit units and frames
Validate quaternion and vector shape
Represent unknown or stale observations honestly

sections.heading: A getter name is not a complete schema
sections.body: The D1 SDK exposes orientation, body acceleration, gyroscope data, position, body velocity, world velocity and joint observations. Each value needs a type, dimension, unit, frame, freshness definition and availability rule before it can feed another subsystem. Write these down rather than exposing an unlabelled vector to the rest of your application. The API documentation describes quaternion order as w, x, y, z and distinguishes world from body velocity. That order differs from some message conventions. Preserve the source representation at the boundary and convert deliberately to the chosen application representation. Never let a display widget quietly determine the convention used by the controller.

sections.heading: Coordinate frames change meaning
sections.body: Suppose a robot faces ninety degrees relative to a world axis. A forward body velocity is no longer the same vector as forward world velocity. Both can be correct measurements expressed differently. A bridge that relabels one as the other will produce an error that grows with heading, which can look like an odometry calibration problem. Use an explicit rotation and known synthetic cases to verify your conversion. Units deserve the same attention: radians and degrees are both ordinary-looking floating-point numbers. A stationary orientation fixture, quarter-turn fixture and known angular-rate fixture are more informative than testing only zeros.

sections.heading: Freshness is part of every observation
sections.body: A getter returning a value does not, by itself, prove when the hardware produced it. Preserve receive time, device time if supplied, validity and source identity. If the SDK provides no reliable device timestamp for a particular observation, state that limitation instead of fabricating nanosecond precision. An application can enforce a host-age policy, but must distinguish it from guaranteed sensor age. Do not replace missing data with zeros: zero velocity is a valid physical observation, while missing velocity is unknown. Downstream consumers should be able to reject stale or invalid state explicitly. This prevents a disconnected device from appearing perfectly still and healthy.

sections.heading: Validate structure before interpreting physics
sections.body: Check vector lengths, finite values, expected joint ordering and plausible quaternion normalization. A quaternion with small numerical norm error can be normalized for a clearly documented visualization path; a near-zero quaternion is invalid and should not be silently repaired. Preserve the original sample for diagnosis. For joint arrays, the SDK architecture specifies a leg order; bind it to named joints rather than relying on an undocumented position in a list. The lab uses synthetic records to test these boundaries. Its outcome is a trustworthy data contract and conversion tests, not a claim that the real D1's inertial sensors or odometry have been calibrated.

lab.title: Implement an offline telemetry validator
lab.environment: Python standard library or another offline test environment
lab.safety: Use synthetic records only; no motor commands are needed.
steps: Create a telemetry schema with units, frame, timestamp and validity for each selected getter.
Add identity and quarter-turn quaternion fixtures using the documented source ordering.
Transform a body-forward synthetic velocity into the chosen world frame.
Inject NaN, wrong-length vectors, stale timestamps and a zero-norm quaternion.
Verify invalid observations remain invalid rather than becoming zeros.
lab.expected: The validator catches structural defects and preserves distinctions between frames and missing data.
acceptance: Quaternion ordering is explicit
Body and world frames cannot be silently relabelled
Stale and missing values stay distinct from physical zeros

troubleshooting.symptom: Velocity errors vary with heading
troubleshooting.cause: A body-frame vector may have been labelled as world-frame data
troubleshooting.fix: Use a quarter-turn synthetic fixture and inspect the rotation direction

questions.prompt: Why is replacing missing velocity with zero dangerous?
choices: Zero increases transport latency
It converts a body-frame vector into world coordinates
It converts unknown state into a false claim of stillness
It changes a quaternion from wxyz to xyzw
questions.explanation: A numerical zero has a physical meaning; missing data requires an explicit validity state.

questions.prompt: What makes a quarter-turn fixture useful?
choices: It hides axis swaps
It establishes the accuracy of real odometry
It validates the message arrival timestamp independently
It reveals frame and rotation-direction mistakes
questions.explanation: Known asymmetric geometry exposes transformations that all-zero fixtures cannot.

questions.prompt: What should a near-zero quaternion produce?
choices: An arbitrary identity orientation
An invalid observation
A normalized but otherwise unreviewed quaternion
A successful calibration
questions.explanation: A near-zero quaternion cannot encode a valid rotation; silently substituting identity hides corruption.

lessons.title: Design a ROS 2 bridge with explicit command ownership
lessons.summary: Specify a custom bridge around the native SDK without claiming an official ROS driver. Test intent validation, acknowledgements and failure transitions.
objectives: Separate transport adapter from supervisory policy
Define mode-aware ROS command semantics
Prove stale intent cannot replay after recovery
prerequisites: ROS 2 services, topics and lifecycle concepts

sections.heading: The bridge is an application you own
sections.body: The inspected D1 SDK provides native C++ and Python interfaces. This course does not infer a supported ROS 2 driver merely because the system can be wrapped in a ROS node. A custom bridge must document what it adds: message conversion, lifecycle, timestamps, ownership, limits and error handling. Keep the native adapter small and testable. It should translate a request and preserve the vendor result rather than decide the entire task policy. A separate supervisor decides whether a request is allowed in the current state. This separation lets you test most failure behavior offline without creating a hardware connection.

sections.heading: Continuous intent and discrete actions differ
sections.body: Velocity intent is a stream whose old values lose relevance quickly. Standing, lying down and other discrete operations are state transitions with prerequisites and completion semantics. Do not multiplex both into an undocumented string command topic. Define a bounded velocity contract with timestamp, owner and validity window; define a transition request with an acknowledged result and an observed-state follow-up. The D1 documentation lists nonzero error codes for state and motor faults. Preserve those distinctions. A ROS service returning successfully only proves your bridge handled the request; it does not prove the underlying robot accepted or completed the requested behavior.

sections.heading: Ownership must survive failure coherently
sections.body: The D1 FAQ says SDK control takes priority over the handheld controller while the SDK program is running. That is a significant operational property, so a bridge must not assume that a remote controller will always override it. Establish the approved independent stop procedure before hardware tests. In the offline model, only one logical owner may submit movement intent. When feedback becomes stale or ownership is revoked, reject new movement and clear pending intent. After reconnection, reobserve the robot state and require a deliberate resume condition. Replaying the final pre-disconnection velocity because it remains in a queue is an avoidable integration fault.

sections.heading: Test the contract without a robot
sections.body: Implement a fake native adapter that returns scripted statuses and observations. Feed it a valid request, rejected transition, stale state, lost connection and recovered connection. Assert that the bridge does not claim successful movement when it only published a message. Test a command arriving from a second owner and a command whose timestamp is too old. Keep limits and deadlines configurable but tied to a reviewed configuration, rather than allowing a user interface to alter them casually mid-run. The deliverable is a bridge specification and fault-tested state model. Hardware execution remains a separate stage requiring the actual SDK model mapping, operator procedure and measured stop behavior.

lab.title: Fault-test a custom bridge contract

lessons.title: Low-level D1 review: joint indexing, gains and timing
lessons.summary: Examine raw joint command structure and physical units. Produce a low-level readiness review without executing unvalidated motor code.
objectives: Audit leg and joint ordering
Explain proportional and damping contributions
Identify the evidence needed for low-level execution

sections.heading: Ordering is a mechanical assumption
sections.body: The D1 architecture documents leg ordering as front right, front left, rear right, rear left. It groups abduction, hip and knee quantities into separate arrays. That layout differs from common flat interleaved layouts used by other robots. A twelve-element vector can therefore be the right size and still address every motor incorrectly. Create a named joint table that includes leg, joint type, sign, unit and source position. Verify both serialization and deserialization against this table. Importing a Unitree command vector because both robots are quadrupeds is not a valid compatibility argument. Similar morphology does not establish identical indexing or mechanics.

sections.heading: Gains have units and consequences
sections.body: A simplified impedance relation combines position error multiplied by stiffness, velocity error multiplied by damping, and a feedforward term. This equation explains why a small position error with a large gain can produce a substantial torque request. It is a teaching model, not a promise about undocumented internal saturation or motor control. Keep the physical dimensions visible when reviewing code. Position, speed, torque and gains are different quantities even when the API stores all of them as float. Never copy gains from another robot, simulation or tutorial without a validated identification and test procedure for this exact system.

sections.heading: Timing belongs in the stability argument
sections.body: A loop's average rate is insufficient to describe its behavior. Delayed state makes feedback refer to an older physical configuration; bursts of queued commands can be equally problematic. Measure command spacing, state age and scheduling jitter in an offline or hardware-in-the-loop setup approved for the device. A desktop process can miss deadlines while reporting a healthy average frequency. Decide what detects a missed deadline and what verified independent mechanism contains the failure. Do not assume a high-level stand command is always reachable from an arbitrary low-level state. Transitions themselves have mechanical prerequisites and must follow the device-specific procedure.

sections.heading: Review the complete failure envelope
sections.body: A low-level readiness dossier should include model identity, supported interface, joint mapping, mechanical support, initial state, gain rationale, limits, timing results, ownership, power state and stop mechanism. The D1 FAQ specifically warns that SDK use lacks a particular low-battery protection behavior and may lead to abrupt power loss. Treat power as a monitored precondition rather than assuming the SDK silently handles it. For this course, the lab stops at an offline audit and a simulated command validator. A learner can demonstrate advanced understanding by identifying missing evidence and refusing to label an untested motor controller ready. Expertise includes knowing exactly what a calculation proves and what still requires supervised physical validation.

lessons.summary: Build a seven-joint hand map from the official sources. Audit the example’s startup behavior and keep left and right semantics distinct.
objectives: Create a side-specific joint map
Identify active command paths in the sample
Validate feedback array lengths and channel names
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: A three-finger hand still needs a precise joint contract
sections.body: Dex3-1 has seven active joints per hand in the documented arrangement: three thumb joints and two each for the index and middle fingers. The useful software artifact is not just the number seven. Name each joint, its index, units, sign convention, limits, and relation to the hand frame. The vendor joint-order reference gives thumb indices first, followed by index and middle joints. Left and right mechanisms use side-specific ranges in the SDK example, so copying one limit vector to both hands can change the meaning of opening and closing. Preserve side as a typed configuration value and reject an unrecognized side before constructing any command object.

sections.heading: Read actual startup control flow
sections.body: The official Dex3 example is command-capable and transitions from INIT to ROTATE. It is not a passive hand diagnostic simply because it also contains a print-state option. Its main function selects a left or right command namespace and a low-frequency state namespace, overriding an earlier global default. This is a good source-reading exercise: the final assigned value matters more than the first string found by search. Trace initialization, topic selection and state transitions in order. For the course lab, inspect the source and work from synthetic data. A later read-only utility should omit command publisher creation entirely rather than depend on the user avoiding a keyboard shortcut.

sections.heading: Hand feedback has variable-length arrays
sections.body: The HG HandState schema contains motor state and pressure-sensor arrays rather than the body’s fixed motor capacity. A consumer must validate available lengths before indexing and must not assume the tactile option is installed just because the field exists. Preserve error and supply information as separate health indicators. If an expected array is absent, classify the cause: unsupported option, missing data, startup state, or configuration mismatch. Do not fill missing sensor values with zeros and interpret them as no contact. A missing measurement and a measured zero carry different information, especially when contact detection or grasp control depends on the distinction.

sections.heading: Worked left-right mapping review
sections.body: Create a synthetic left-hand pose with distinct values for all seven joints and convert it to a normalized display only using the left-hand bounds. Then repeat using the right-hand mapping and explain any differences. This exercise is about semantics, not mirroring a physical motion. A naive sign flip may be insufficient because joint axes, offsets and ranges can differ. Store mapping provenance with the data so a replay tool knows which convention was used. The completed artifact should let a reviewer trace a named finger joint through index, raw angle, normalized display value and side. That trace is the foundation for later retargeting and contact experiments.
