lessons.title: Retarget hand motion with limits and continuity
lessons.summary: Translate human or abstract hand targets into a constrained robot configuration. Evaluate geometric error and temporal behavior separately.
objectives: Define a retargeting objective
Explain redundancy and limit constraints
Test discontinuities with synthetic target sequences
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: Retargeting is an optimization problem
sections.body: Human and robot hands have different geometry, degrees of freedom and reachable motions. Retargeting chooses robot joint values that approximate a task-relevant feature of the source motion. That feature might be fingertip positions, vectors between fingertips, or a grasp aperture. It should not be assumed that matching every human joint angle is meaningful. Define the objective explicitly: for example, minimize weighted fingertip-vector error plus a continuity penalty relative to the previous robot pose. This is an illustrative mathematical design, not a claim about one exact vendor implementation. Inspect the official teleoperation adapter to see how its selected retargeting library and configuration connect to the hand command path.

sections.heading: Constraints are part of the solution
sections.body: Joint bounds restrict the feasible set, while self-collision, contact, rate limits and hardware conventions may impose additional constraints. A target outside the reachable set has no exact solution. The solver should report residual error and constraint activity rather than conceal the mismatch. Simply clipping a solution after optimization can change the fingertip geometry substantially. For an offline course exercise, use a simplified two-link finger or the verified hand model and compare constrained results with naive clipping. Keep the distinction visible between a numerical solution and a physically validated grasp. A pose that looks close in a viewer may still involve poor contacts or an infeasible approach path.

sections.heading: Temporal consistency matters as much as pose error
sections.body: Independent per-frame optimization can jump between equivalent solutions. The resulting sequence may have low geometric error but large joint velocities. Add continuity reasoning: compare each solution with the previous accepted pose, measure per-joint increments, and detect source tracking dropouts. A smoothing filter can reduce jitter but introduces delay, which can worsen interaction with moving objects. Report that tradeoff instead of claiming filtering is universally beneficial. When tracking disappears, the correct application response must be defined separately from ordinary retargeting. In the offline lab, output an unavailable or inhibited record rather than manufacturing hand motion from the last valid frame indefinitely.

sections.heading: Build a diagnostic sequence rather than one perfect pose
sections.body: Use a synthetic sequence that opens a grasp, approaches a pinch, moves beyond reach, and includes a dropped frame. Give every target a timestamp and known reference frame. Plot or tabulate geometric residual, active constraints, joint increments and validity state. A useful worked comparison is a solver that achieves slightly higher pose error but avoids a sudden branch switch; the better choice depends on the task and stated criteria. Do not select by visual smoothness alone. The final report should explain where the mapping fails, how uncertainty is represented, and which parts were tested only in a simplified model. That is stronger evidence than a single attractive hand screenshot.

lessons.title: Distinguish Dex5-1, Dex5-1P, and a verified device API
lessons.summary: Reconcile the product table with model files and missing protocol evidence. Build an adapter contract that never assumes Dex3 compatibility.
objectives: Separate active and coupled DOF
Identify the tactile variant accurately
Audit a URDF without mistaking it for a driver
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: Resolve the exact variant before writing a driver
sections.body: The reviewed Unitree product table distinguishes Dex5-1 from Dex5-1P. It describes sixteen active degrees of freedom plus four coupled joints, and lists pressure sensing for the P variant. The table’s communication interface is USB2.0. These facts prevent several plausible but wrong assumptions: twenty independently commandable motors, pressure arrays on every base hand, or automatic DDS parity with Dex3. Use the exact shipped model and documentation revision in the manifest. A headline that celebrates tactile capability is weaker evidence for an individual configuration than a variant-specific table and the supplied device documentation. Resolve the discrepancy explicitly rather than choosing the more impressive description.

sections.heading: Kinematic models and actuator interfaces answer different questions
sections.body: The official Unitree ROS repository includes Dex5-1 URDF files. A URDF can describe links, joint axes, transforms, bounds, inertial properties and coupling conventions represented in that model. It does not by itself specify the USB packet layout, command acknowledgement behavior, device enumeration, calibration procedure, or firmware watchdog. Count non-fixed joints and inspect relationships, but do not equate every modeled joint with an independent motor command. Build a table with modeled joint, independent actuator, coupling relation, and evidence source. If a relation is not specified, mark it unresolved. This separates geometry work that can proceed offline from device integration work that requires the correct protocol package.
sections.code:
# Usage: python audit_urdf.py /path/to/official-hand.urdf
import json, sys
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
root = ET.parse(sys.argv[1]).getroot()
joints = []
for joint in root.findall("joint"):
    if joint.get("type") == "fixed":
        continue
    limit, mimic = joint.find("limit"), joint.find("mimic")
    joints.append({"name": joint.get("name"), "type": joint.get("type"),
                   "limit": None if limit is None else dict(limit.attrib),
                   "mimic": None if mimic is None else dict(mimic.attrib)})
print(json.dumps(joints, indent=2))
# Missing mimic metadata is an unresolved modeling question,
# not proof that every listed joint has an independent motor.

sections.heading: Define a driver boundary before implementing transport
sections.body: A useful hand adapter exposes a semantic command with named actuators, units, configuration identity and timestamp. Its feedback contract distinguishes measured position, estimated torque, pressure data, device health and unavailable fields. Beneath that boundary, a device-specific implementation handles transport and protocol. This lesson deliberately does not invent Dex5 topic names or packet fields: the public developer portal indexed an SDK guide, but its detailed command protocol was not retrieved during the audit. The absence of verified protocol is a specific research gap, not a reason to fill it with generic code. You can still test the semantic adapter with a fake device and document exactly what evidence is needed next.

sections.heading: Work through a coupled-joint example
sections.body: Consider an illustrative finger whose distal joint follows an intermediate joint through a known coupling function. A planner may reason about both angles, but the device command may expose only the independent input. Sending two conflicting targets would be meaningless unless the hardware supports that independence. In your offline model audit, derive or record the coupling from the actual model or documentation; do not invent a ratio. Then verify that the adapter accepts only the independent actuator set and computes dependent visualization state through the documented relation. If the relation is unavailable, the correct output is an unresolved coupling entry. The lesson’s completion artifact is a precise integration contract, not a claim of working USB control.

lessons.title: Analyze tactile signals without inventing contact certainty
lessons.summary: Build a pressure-data validity and contact-detection pipeline using synthetic fixtures. Separate missing sensors, baseline drift, noise, saturation, and slip hypotheses.
objectives: Compute baseline-corrected features
Distinguish contact inference from sensor validity
Test thresholds and hysteresis on labeled fixtures
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: Begin with the measurement contract
sections.body: A tactile value has meaning only with a channel identity, location, unit, calibration, timestamp and validity status. Do not infer physical force units from a field named pressure. The exact sensor conversion belongs to the selected hand’s documentation. Optional tactile hardware also means that a schema can exist without populated measurements. Represent unavailable arrays explicitly rather than padding them with zeros. For a course fixture, use clearly labeled arbitrary units and a known synthetic baseline. This lets you learn signal processing without implying that the values are calibrated physical forces. Preserve raw data alongside derived features so a later calibration correction does not require collecting every experiment again.

sections.heading: Correct baseline and characterize noise
sections.body: A contact detector often starts by subtracting a no-contact baseline from each channel. Estimate baseline and noise over a recorded interval, not from a single convenient sample. A robust median can reduce the influence of occasional spikes, while a spread estimate helps define a threshold appropriate to the fixture. Baseline drift can arise in many sensors, so evaluate behavior when the baseline changes slowly. Do not automatically adapt the baseline during sustained contact, because the algorithm may learn the contact away. Keep baseline update conditions explicit and test them. Distinguish per-channel saturation from strong contact: a saturated reading loses information about further increases even if its numeric value looks stable.

sections.heading: Use hysteresis and confidence carefully
sections.body: A single threshold can flicker when noise crosses the boundary repeatedly. Hysteresis uses a higher threshold to enter contact and a lower threshold to leave it, often with a minimum duration. This reduces chatter but introduces delay. Report the detection latency and false-positive rate on labeled fixtures. A changing pressure distribution may be evidence relevant to slip, but pressure variation alone is not universal proof of object motion. Treat slip detection as a hypothesis that needs an independently labeled experiment or another sensor. Keep sensor-validity logic upstream: a stale or missing array should not be classified as confident no-contact simply because the detector received default zeros.

sections.heading: Worked synthetic evaluation
sections.body: Construct four channels with a baseline near ten arbitrary units, small noise, a step contact, a short spike, and a missing-data segment. Subtract the baseline, then compare a single threshold with a hysteretic detector. Count false transitions and measure the delay from the labeled contact onset. Next, inject a stuck-at maximum value and a slow drift. The goal is not to find one perfect threshold but to explain which assumptions fail. Save labels separately from observations so the evaluation can be repeated. A completed report states the data are synthetic, records all thresholds and units, and shows how invalid data propagates. That is a useful foundation for later calibrated physical experiments without pretending the fixture proves real grasp reliability.
sections.code:
# Synthetic arbitrary units; not a calibration for any physical hand.
values = [10, 10, 11, 10, 18, 19, 17, None, 11, 10]
baseline, enter, leave = 10, 6, 2
contact = False
result = []
for value in values:
    if value is None:
        result.append("unavailable")
        contact = False  # Explicit reset policy for this fixture.
        continue
    corrected = value - baseline
    contact = corrected > leave if contact else corrected >= enter
    result.append("contact" if contact else "no_contact")
assert result[4:7] == ["contact"] * 3
assert result[7] == "unavailable"
print(result)

lessons.title: Capstone: define and evaluate a grasp experiment
lessons.summary: Combine kinematics, retargeting, sensing, and task metrics into a reproducible experiment. Make failure categories and evidence as explicit as success.
objectives: Define a task-specific grasp benchmark
Separate completion from stability and damage
Create an auditable trial record
prerequisites: The preceding lesson in this course, where present
An isolated Linux development environment; no robot connection required

sections.heading: A grasp is a task outcome, not a closed hand
sections.body: Closing fingers does not prove an object was acquired, retained, oriented correctly, or released safely. Define the task in observable stages: approach, contact establishment, lift or transfer in simulation, hold, placement and release. Specify the object geometry, mass model, friction assumptions, initial pose and allowed variation. For an offline or simulated course benchmark, these values are experiment settings rather than claims about real materials. Define what counts as success before looking at results. A grasp that completes one stage but fails another should produce partial progress and a failure category, not a single flattering success flag.

sections.heading: Use multiple metrics because objectives conflict
sections.body: Success rate is important but incomplete. Also track pose error, retention time, object slip, peak modeled contact force, joint-limit activity, cycle duration and invalid-sensor events where the model supports them. Be careful with simulator contact forces: they depend on model and solver assumptions and are not calibrated measurements of a physical hand. Compare approaches under the same conditions and report trial count. A controller that succeeds by applying excessive force may be unacceptable for a delicate object. A slower strategy may improve retention. The benchmark should expose these tradeoffs so the chosen policy follows the task requirements instead of optimizing whichever number is easiest to increase.

sections.heading: Separate training, tuning and evaluation cases
sections.body: If every test object and initial pose is used to tune the controller, a high reported success rate may reflect memorization of the benchmark. Hold out some initial conditions and, where appropriate, object shapes or friction settings. Record random seeds and perturbation ranges. Do not hide failed trials or restart them without retaining the original result. Categorize failure causes such as unreachable approach, joint-limit saturation, contact loss, invalid input, collision in the model or release error. These categories guide improvements much better than a single average. When ground truth is available in simulation, label it as ground truth and distinguish it from observations the deployed controller would actually receive.

sections.heading: Write a result another engineer can challenge
sections.body: A useful capstone report contains the task definition, model and adapter revisions, parameter values, trial manifest, per-trial outcomes and representative failure traces. Include at least one ablation: remove continuity smoothing, change a contact threshold, or disable a feature and show what changes under the same evaluation conditions. An ablation helps distinguish a useful design choice from an attractive explanation added afterward. State what remains untested on hardware, including calibration, friction, compliance, transport and firmware behavior. The course completion claim is that the learner designed and evaluated the stated experiment. It is not that the hand can grasp arbitrary objects or that the result transfers unchanged to a different end effector.

lessons.title: Choose the correct Revo generation and transport
lessons.summary: Distinguish Revo1, Revo2 and Revo3 before selecting software. Build a capability matrix that keeps transport, tactile hardware and command semantics separate.
objectives: Identify generation-specific SDKs
Separate connector presence from protocol support
Select an appropriate simulation asset
prerequisites: Basic serial, CAN and Ethernet concepts

sections.heading: Revo is a family name
sections.body: The BrainCo ecosystem contains more than one generation. The Revo1/2 SDK and the Revo3 SDK are separate projects with distinct examples and development contracts. A course that says install the Revo SDK without identifying the hand can lead learners to an apparently successful but incompatible environment. Record generation, left or right side, hardware variant, firmware, supported transport, adapter and power arrangement. Keep the physical hand identity private where appropriate while retaining reproducible software identifiers. Do not infer compatibility from appearance or connector shape. A replacement hand may fit mechanically yet require a different transport, model or command interpretation.

sections.heading: Protocol, adapter and driver are different layers
sections.body: RS-485 describes an electrical communication layer; application protocols define the messages carried over it. CAN, CAN FD and EtherCAT have distinct host and device requirements. The SDK capability matrix is useful, but firmware variants and chosen adapters still matter. A host with a CAN-capable socket is not necessarily configured for the device's CAN FD timing. Similarly, a ROS package compiled without an optional driver cannot gain that capability from a launch argument. Build the matrix from physical device through adapter, host driver, SDK backend and application. Each boundary should have a specific observation that proves it works before introducing the next layer.

sections.heading: Count controlled variables carefully
sections.body: A dexterous hand can have multiple visible joint axes coupled to fewer independent actuators. A model's joint count is not automatically the command vector dimension. Distinguish independently commanded joints, passive or mimic joints and any virtual joints added for modeling. Revo2 control and model configuration must be read together; Revo3's independent-actuator architecture belongs to its own course extension. An old URDF may remain useful for legacy compatibility, while the current BrainCo description repository supplies newer simulation assets. Record which asset and SDK generation you selected and why. A realistic mesh alone does not establish the command mapping.

sections.heading: Capability checks should shape the lesson
sections.body: Tactile examples require the corresponding sensor-equipped variant; motor-only hardware cannot provide a missing tactile array through software. Let learners complete the data-processing portion with clearly labeled synthetic signals when that hardware is absent. For real equipment, distinguish documented capability from observed availability and measured performance. An example that supports multiple variants may choose a different backend after discovery; capture that choice in the experiment record. The finished matrix should make unsupported combinations obvious before a learner installs dependencies or opens a serial port. This is how a serious curriculum remains useful across actual purchased configurations instead of quietly assuming the most expensive bundle.

lessons.title: Measure hand communication before closing a loop
lessons.summary: Use the official read-only benchmark to separate requested rate from achieved throughput. Interpret latency distributions and serialized request behavior.
objectives: Measure achieved read rate and failures
Explain why target frequency is not throughput
Define a timing budget for feedback
prerequisites: Matched SDK environment and authorized powered hand

sections.heading: A requested rate is a hypothesis
sections.body: A program can request motor state one hundred times per second while receiving fewer valid responses. Measure attempted requests, successful responses, error categories and the time occupied by each request. The official unified BrainCo benchmark reports these quantities and latency percentiles. Use its read-only test before considering write or mixed tests, which move the fingers. Preserve connection backend, SDK version, firmware, adapter and host load so the result can be compared later. A screenshot showing 100Hz in a command line describes the requested setting; it is not evidence that the full measurement path achieved it.

sections.heading: Serialized requests impose a ceiling
sections.body: The SDK guide explains that motor-status request/response calls on a single DeviceContext are serialized. If a request takes twelve milliseconds, that path cannot sustain one hundred sequential successful reads per second even before scheduling overhead. Raising a target-frequency parameter does not create hidden parallel transactions. A naive application may respond by adding threads that merely queue behind the same context, increasing delay without improving throughput. First determine whether the API and transport support concurrency at all. For multi-hand systems, distinguish separate communication contexts and buses from multiple tasks sharing one physical bottleneck.

sections.heading: Percentiles reveal deadline risk
sections.body: The mean gives a useful overall summary but can hide occasional long delays. Compare P50, P95, P99 and maximum latency with the application's observation-age budget. Count failures in the denominator instead of computing a flattering mean only over a few fast successes. Run enough samples to interpret percentiles sensibly and report sample count and duration. A short classroom benchmark cannot establish a rare-event guarantee. Repeat under the relevant host workload, then compare like for like. If you change firmware, adapter, bus timing and software simultaneously, an improvement cannot be attributed to any one change with confidence.

sections.heading: Feedback design uses the measured budget
sections.body: A tactile or position controller includes acquisition, processing, command transmission and actuator response. Communication latency is only one part. A fast motor read cannot compensate for a slow tactile stream or a vision pipeline several frames behind. Write the budget in milliseconds and identify which stages are measured and which remain unknown. The official tools support different monitoring modes for motor and sensor variants; do not assume they all produce equally fresh observations. The focused lab produces a read-only communication characterization, not a grasping controller. Its practical engineering value is a defensible, measured constraint for later design: the application should operate within measured timing and expose missed deadlines instead of hiding them behind an optimistic nominal rate.
sections.code: python comm_frequency_test.py 1 --duration 10 --target-hz 100 --output report.json

No, its ideal limit is already below 100/s
questions.explanation: One hundred reads would require at most ten milliseconds each; serialized twelve-millisecond transactions cannot meet that.

choices: All tests

choices: To prove a universal worst case

To establish a guaranteed maximum latency
To expose tail delays the mean can conceal
questions.explanation: P99 summarizes the observed tail; it still is not a guaranteed worst case.

lessons.title: Revo2 ros2_control, FakeSystem and planning
lessons.summary: Trace a trajectory through planning and controller interfaces. Distinguish a software-only FakeSystem result from simulated contact and real hand behavior.
objectives: Inspect controller claims and joint names
Run the official FakeSystem planning entry point
Explain the limits of simulated execution

sections.heading: Three environments answer different questions
sections.body: A FakeSystem allows planning and controller integration without physical hardware. A physics simulator adds contact and dynamic assumptions. A real hand adds actual transport, actuators, sensing and mechanical variation. Passing one environment does not imply passing the next. The official BrainCo ROS 2 collection provides paths for hardware, Gazebo and MoveIt FakeSystem. Choose the route explicitly, then inspect the resulting hardware component before executing trajectories. An accidental hardware launch is not an acceptable shortcut for a missing simulation package. Preserve the chosen launch file and parameters in the report so another learner can tell what kind of result was obtained.

sections.heading: Controllers claim interfaces
sections.body: The robot description identifies joints; the hardware interface exports state and command interfaces; controllers claim the command interfaces they need. A visible model does not prove a trajectory controller is active or that its joint list matches the intended planning group. Inspect controller state, exported interfaces and joint names. Trace a request from MoveIt through the trajectory action to the selected controller and back to observed joint state. A planning success means a path was found under the model's constraints. Execution acceptance and execution completion are separate events. Keep those stages distinct in both the UI and the test log.

sections.heading: Coupling changes command interpretation
sections.body: A hand model may include mimic joints that follow a controlled joint. Do not send independent target values to every visible link simply because RViz displays them. Compare the controller's actuated joint list with the kinematic model and planning group. A trajectory must use the required joint names and compatible dimensions, with meaningful timing. The right and left hands are not interchangeable strings if the model encodes different signs or geometry. Use a known configuration from the pinned package for initial software verification, then deliberately remove or rename a joint in a local test fixture to prove that the integration detects a mismatch.

sections.heading: Planning validity is conditional
sections.body: A collision-free plan is collision-free within the modeled environment, resolution and assumptions used by the planner. Missing a table, cable or attached hand changes that claim. FakeSystem cannot validate grasp friction or motor tracking because it does not provide real contact evidence. Gazebo contact behavior also depends on configured materials and dynamics. The lab therefore asks for a precise statement: a particular software configuration planned and executed through a particular interface. It also asks for a negative result: an invalid joint contract must fail visibly. This pairing develops the habit of proving both expected operation and a meaningful rejection before proceeding toward hardware.
sections.code:
ros2 launch brainco_moveit_config revo2_right_moveit.launch.py
ros2 control list_controllers
ros2 control list_hardware_components

lessons.title: Tactile grasping as a delayed feedback system
lessons.summary: Analyze contact detection, filtering and grasp-state logic using synthetic tactile traces. Separate sensed contact from inferred grip stability.
objectives: Design a contact detector with hysteresis
Account for sensing and command delay
Evaluate false contacts and missed releases

sections.heading: Contact is an inference from a signal
sections.body: A tactile reading is not automatically a stable grasp. Sensor baseline, noise, drift, placement and object material influence the signal. Start by defining what each channel measures and how its values are calibrated. A capacitive touch channel is not the same measurement as a force or pressure array; do not relabel it in newtons without a valid calibration model. The official Revo2 tactile example separates acquisition, tactile processing and grasp control. That separation is a useful engineering pattern because you can inspect the signal-processing decision independently from the motor command it might eventually influence.

sections.heading: Hysteresis reduces chatter
sections.body: A single threshold can repeatedly alternate between contact and no-contact when a signal hovers near the boundary. Use different enter and exit thresholds, or a persistence rule, and explain the resulting detection delay. Filtering also trades noise reduction for lag. For a simple moving window, a longer window smooths spikes but can delay release detection and mask a rapid change. Select thresholds from a recorded or synthetic baseline experiment and label which is used. Do not copy a threshold from another hand or object and assume the units and noise distribution match. Evaluate both false positives and missed contacts.

sections.heading: The controller sees yesterday's world
sections.body: The feedback loop includes sensor sampling, buffering, transport, processing, command delivery and mechanical response. An aggressive current adjustment based on old contact data can overshoot before the next observation arrives. Set a bounded state machine: approach, contact candidate, hold, release and fault are conceptually distinct stages. The course uses these as an original control design, not as claimed vendor mode names. A missing or stale tactile observation must produce an explicit policy rather than silently retaining a confident grasp label. Any real force or current limit requires the correct hand variant and manufacturer procedure; synthetic experiments do not establish safe physical limits.

sections.heading: Evaluate the decision before adding movement
sections.body: Create traces for a clean contact, isolated noise spike, slow drift, intermittent contact, saturated sensor and delayed release. Annotate ground truth because the signals are deliberately constructed. Measure detection latency, false-contact duration and whether the state machine exits contact after a valid release. Then replay the same traces at different sampling rates to reveal hidden assumptions about time versus sample count. A detector that waits ten samples behaves differently at ten hertz and one hundred hertz. The lab's output is a tested interpretation pipeline. Physical grasping remains explicitly unvalidated until real sensor calibration, actuator behavior, object interaction and an approved release procedure are measured together.

lab.title: Test a tactile contact state machine
lab.environment: Offline synthetic time series in Python or a spreadsheet
lab.safety: Use synthetic signals; no finger current or position commands are issued.
steps: Generate six labeled traces: contact, spike, drift, intermittent contact, saturation and delayed release.
Implement baseline subtraction and a contact detector with separate enter/exit rules.
Add freshness and saturation handling to a grasp-state model.
Measure false-contact time and detection/release delay for every trace.
Repeat at two sampling rates while preserving the same physical event times.
lab.expected: The detector handles noise and missing data without claiming unsupported force measurements.
acceptance: Touch is not mislabeled as calibrated force
Threshold persistence is expressed in time
Stale and saturated signals reach explicit fault handling

troubleshooting.symptom: Contact chatters around a threshold
troubleshooting.cause: Noise crosses a single decision boundary repeatedly
troubleshooting.fix: Add measured hysteresis or persistence and report the added delay

questions.prompt: Can a capacitive touch value be called force in newtons automatically?
choices: No, a valid calibration and sensor model are required
Only after low-pass filtering the touch channel
Yes
Only after normalizing the channel into a zero-to-one range
questions.explanation: The physical quantity and calibration determine units; a touch signal alone does not establish force.

questions.prompt: What is the main cost of stronger smoothing?
choices: Guaranteed better control
No effect on timing
More immediate release
Additional lag and possible masking of rapid changes
questions.explanation: Noise reduction often delays changes; the control loop must account for that tradeoff.

questions.prompt: Why test at two sample rates?
choices: To prove the physical sensor is correctly calibrated
To establish the real transport latency without a device
To expose sample-count rules that accidentally change physical timing
To select a threshold from the largest observed value
questions.explanation: Ten samples represent different durations at different rates; timing rules should be intentional.

lessons.title: Integrate Revo2 with Unitree G1 without conflicting controllers
lessons.summary: Review the official dual-hand G1 integration as a complete system. Identify mode, waist, mounting and controller-ownership dependencies before combined motion.
objectives: Separate arm and hand control paths
Explain conflicting arm ownership
Build a staged integration acceptance plan
prerequisites: Unitree G1 variant and control fundamentals

sections.heading: Treat the combination as a new system
sections.body: The official BrainCo integration targets Revo2 hands on Unitree G1, with support differences between 23-DoF and 29-DoF configurations. This is a specific integration, not evidence that any Revo hand works on any humanoid. Record the G1 variant, arm model, hand side, mounting, mass assumptions, serial adapters and software revisions. A hand replacement changes geometry and payload at the wrist; even when the arm API stays the same, collision models and motion assumptions may no longer be valid. Inspect the combined model rather than appending a decorative mesh to an unchanged planner.

sections.heading: There are two communication paths
sections.body: The reference architecture uses Unitree arm control and dual RS-485 paths for the Revo2 hands. The two hands communicate through separate serial devices. Serial enumeration can change across boots, so a robust installation needs an explicit device-to-side mapping and a verification procedure. Do not assume that whichever device becomes ttyUSB0 is always the left hand. Trace observations and commands independently for each side. A successful right-hand response does not prove the left-hand channel is healthy. Integration logs should name the physical role alongside the transport endpoint so crossed wiring or mapping is visible before a combined action.

sections.heading: Controller conflicts are a concrete risk
sections.body: The reference project's update notes describe disabling the built-in Unitree arm service before using its developed arm path to avoid conflicting arm control. They also note that certain upper-limb motions do not lock waist roll and pitch. These are not details to omit from a polished tutorial: two writers to the same joints or a moving waist can invalidate an otherwise correct end-effector target. The lesson does not instruct learners to disable services blindly. It asks them to map which component owns each joint group, how ownership is established, and what state is observed before combined control. The exact procedure must match the reference version and purchased robot.

sections.heading: Stage the integration by evidence
sections.body: Start with offline model and mapping checks, then separately reviewed arm and hand subsystems, then combined motion in a cleared controlled environment using the vendor procedure. Vision, replay and lower-body motion add further dependencies and should be introduced only after simpler stages pass. A camera transform calibrated for one waist posture may be wrong when that posture changes. Your acceptance plan should therefore include state assumptions and failure criteria for every stage. The final artifact is a readiness dossier, not an automatic permission to run. It can be complete as an engineering review while still reporting physical tests pending; that honesty is more useful than a fabricated successful grasp video.

lab.title: Prepare a G1/Revo2 integration dossier

lab.safety: Do not run launch scripts, disable services or move the robot during this design review.

Draw arm-control and two hand-transport paths with device-to-side mapping.
Inspect the reference ownership behavior and note waist-lock limitations.
Compare the combined model and camera transforms with the intended mounting.
Write staged acceptance gates for individual subsystems, combined upper body, vision and lower-body motion.
lab.expected: The dossier identifies every ownership and calibration assumption before execution.
acceptance: G1 23 and 29 DoF are not conflated
Two serial ports have explicit physical identities
Arm-service and waist constraints are documented

troubleshooting.symptom: An end-effector target shifts while arm joints appear correct
troubleshooting.cause: Waist motion or an incorrect mounting transform changes the world pose
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect the full chain and current waist state, not only the arm solution

questions.prompt: What proves the correct hand is attached to a serial endpoint?
choices: The order returned by a file listing after one boot
An explicit verified device-to-side mapping
The endpoint number alone

questions.explanation: Enumeration is not a durable physical identity; mapping must be verified.

choices: They can issue competing commands to the same joints
Two nodes cannot discover the same joint-state topic
The transport always serializes the writers safely

questions.explanation: Independent valid controllers still need exclusive ownership of commanded joints.

choices: It only affects appearance

lessons.title: Gazebo, ROS bridges, and simulation validity
lessons.summary: Run a small Gazebo world and bridge simulation time into ROS. Build an assumption ledger so a successful simulation is interpreted with the right limits.
objectives: Use the Jazzy/Harmonic pairing and verify bridge direction
Observe clock pause and playback behavior
Define a simulation validity and sensitivity test
prerequisites: Ubuntu 24.04 graphical environment; Jazzy and ros-jazzy-ros-gz

sections.heading: A simulator is an executable model
sections.body:
Simulation combines a dynamics model, contact model, sensor model, numerical integration, and software interfaces. Each piece is an approximation with an intended range of use. A visually realistic world can still have inaccurate friction, latency, motor behavior, or camera noise. Decide which phenomena matter for the question you are testing before increasing rendering quality.

The foundation environment pairs Jazzy with Gazebo Harmonic using the documented ros_gz packages. Gazebo Classic and modern Gazebo have different packages and integration paths; mixing instructions across them is a common source of failure. Record the simulator and ROS package versions. A vendor model or simulator may require a different supported stack, which should remain a separate environment. Successful execution of a generic world is evidence about that installation, not compatibility with a particular humanoid or dexterous hand.

sections.heading: A bridge maps specific message contracts
sections.body:
Gazebo Transport and ROS are distinct communication systems. A bridge connects selected topic names and message types in a chosen direction. An active bridge process does not prove the mapping is correct or the source is publishing. Inspect each side, then inspect the translated payload. Avoid bridging every topic by default, especially when a graph could contain command channels.

This exercise bridges only the simulation clock from Gazebo into ROS. The square bracket in the bridge specification requests Gazebo-to-ROS direction. Quote the entire argument so the shell does not interpret its punctuation. Start the world, unpause it, and watch the clock. When the simulator pauses, simulation time should stop advancing even while wall time continues. This directly tests the clock distinction introduced earlier.
sections.code:
# Install the documented Jazzy integration package if it is absent:
# sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz
# Terminal A:
gz sim shapes.sdf
# Terminal B, with Jazzy sourced:
ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge '/clock@rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock[gz.msgs.Clock'
# Terminal C:
ros2 topic echo /clock --once

sections.heading: Use sensitivity instead of a single attractive run
sections.body:
Write an assumption ledger with nominal values, plausible ranges, source, and expected effect. Examples include contact friction, payload mass, sensor delay, and control period. Change one parameter at a time initially so you can explain the effect, then test combinations that could occur together. Keep the random seed and initial state fixed when isolating a cause, and vary them when evaluating robustness.

A simulation-to-hardware gap is not repaired by declaring more randomization. The randomized distribution must cover physically meaningful uncertainty, and the observation and action interfaces must match deployment. Measure both task outcome and constraint violations. A controller that reaches the goal after crossing an unacceptable contact or joint limit should fail the test. Report which conditions were exercised and which remain unmodeled. Simulation is valuable precisely because it makes assumptions testable, not because it removes the need to identify them.

An assumption ledger should also name the observation that would falsify each assumption. This makes model refinement a specific engineering action rather than an open-ended tuning exercise.

troubleshooting.cause: The world is paused, the source clock topic differs, or the bridge type is wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect Gazebo topics with gz topic -l, unpause, and compare the exact source topic and bridge specification.

choices: None of the physical-model accuracy claims follow from appearance alone
Motor delay matches hardware
The policy is deployment ready
Contact friction is accurate
questions.explanation: Rendering fidelity and dynamics fidelity are different. The relevant physical assumptions need measurements.
