choices: Only the window theme
Whether the source topic publishes and the direction/types match
The course title
A physical motor encoder
questions.explanation: A process can run with no valid source or an incorrect mapping. Inspect both sides of the bridge.

questions.prompt: Why keep initial state fixed while changing one simulation parameter?
choices: Because all randomness is invalid
To prove universal robustness
To isolate the causal effect of that parameter
To avoid collecting evidence
questions.explanation: Controlled comparisons help attribute changes. Broader robustness testing should subsequently vary initial states and seeds.

lessons.title: Joint control and the ros2_control boundary
lessons.summary: Simulate a bounded single-joint controller and inspect the read-update-write architecture. Separate numerical stability, interface ownership, and physical commissioning.
objectives: Derive a proportional-derivative control law
Measure tracking error and saturation in a toy plant
Explain controller-manager and hardware-interface responsibilities
prerequisites: Basic derivatives and Newtonian mechanics; Python 3

sections.heading: A controller closes a loop around a model
sections.body:
A feedback controller compares a desired state with an observed state and calculates an input intended to reduce the error. For a joint-angle target, a simple proportional-derivative law can use torque = kp(target − angle) − kd(angular velocity). The proportional term reacts to position error; the derivative term damps motion. These gains have physical units, and their useful values depend on inertia, friction, sampling, and actuator behavior.

A controller is not a universal formula that becomes safe after clipping its output. Saturation changes the system dynamics, observation delay changes the effective feedback, and a sign error can turn damping into excitation. Start with a known mathematical plant and measure its response. Vendor joint interfaces may expose position, velocity, torque, impedance, or another contract, and the meanings cannot be inferred from a field name alone.

sections.heading: A complete toy experiment
sections.body:
The example models one rotational degree of freedom with inertia 1 kg·m² and viscous damping 0.2 N·m·s/rad. It integrates angular velocity and angle with a fixed step. The controller uses invented gains and a ±1 N·m torque cap. These values are educational and are not parameters for any physical robot.

Record final error, peak angle, and the number of saturated steps. Increasing kp may improve initial response while increasing overshoot or saturation. Changing the timestep can also change the simulated result even though the continuous equation is unchanged. A credible experiment reports those sensitivities. The torque cap in this model is an arithmetic bound; it is not a verified hardware interlock, collision limit, or emergency stop.

sections.heading: Framework boundaries do not erase hardware details
sections.body:
In ros2_control, a controller manager coordinates controller lifecycles and resource use. Hardware components expose state and command interfaces, and the control cycle reads state, updates active controllers, and writes commands. This separation makes components reusable, but the hardware adapter must still implement the exact device contract, error handling, timing, and lifecycle behavior.

Before integrating a vendor SDK, identify the command owner, supported mode, required update rate, units, joint ordering, stale-state behavior, and response to communication loss. Two controllers must not accidentally claim incompatible authority over the same command interface. Validate the adapter with a mock or simulator before supervised physical commissioning. A successful toy controller or framework demo proves neither that a particular vendor driver exists nor that the same gains transfer to the real mechanism.

For a fair gain comparison, preserve the same target, initial condition, duration, and plant parameters. Changing the plant and gains together prevents you from attributing the observed improvement to the controller change.

lab.title: Measure a toy joint response
lab.environment: Python 3; entirely numerical simulation; no ROS hardware component loaded
lab.safety: Never send these gains, torques, or target values to physical hardware. The model omits many real actuator and contact effects.
steps: Run the complete simulation for the three gain pairs.
Record final error, peak angle, and saturation count in a comparison table.
Repeat the baseline with dt values 0.02, 0.01, and 0.005 seconds and compare convergence.
Add a fixed observation delay using a history buffer, label the change, and compare the response.
Draw a read-update-write boundary diagram and list the missing requirements for a real vendor adapter.
lab.expected: The different damping, gain, timestep, and delay choices produce measurable differences in the toy response.
acceptance: All model quantities and units are stated
Saturation and tracking are measured separately
No toy result is labeled a validated hardware controller

troubleshooting.symptom: The angle grows without bound
troubleshooting.cause: Feedback sign, timestep, or delayed-state assumptions may destabilize the model
troubleshooting.fix: Check the zero-error case, damping sign, and timestep sensitivity independently.

troubleshooting.symptom: Higher gain fails to improve the result
troubleshooting.cause: The actuator model may spend more time saturated or overshoot
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect peak angle and saturation count rather than final error alone.

questions.prompt: In the stated PD law, what does the negative kd times velocity term do?
choices: Guarantees collision avoidance
Removes all delay
Changes the desired angle
Adds damping when signs and units are correct
questions.explanation: The term opposes velocity in this model. It is not a safety or latency guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why measure saturation count?
choices: It reveals when the requested input exceeds the modeled actuator bound
It replaces tracking error
It identifies a ROS namespace
It proves torque calibration
questions.explanation: Saturation changes the realized controller response. A final error alone can hide how the system reached the target.

questions.prompt: A ros2_control demo works with mock hardware. What remains to validate for a vendor robot?
choices: Nothing
The exact hardware contract, timing, lifecycle, ownership, and failure behavior
Only the README font
Only the compiler name
questions.explanation: Framework integration with a mock does not validate a physical adapter or commissioning procedure.

lessons.title: Navigation as localization, planning, and execution
lessons.summary: Run the official Jazzy Nav2 simulation and evaluate navigation with a predefined acceptance table. Diagnose the difference between a path, a localization estimate, and a completed task.
objectives: Explain localization, global planning, local control, and costmaps
Run the documented Nav2 simulator and establish initial pose
Evaluate goals using tolerance, timeout, and failure criteria
prerequisites: Ubuntu 24.04/Jazzy graphical simulation; nav2_bringup and Navigation2 packages

sections.heading: A path is only one part of navigation
sections.body:
Navigation requires an estimate of where the robot is, a representation of traversable space, a path or route toward the goal, and a controller that executes feasible motion while reacting to local conditions. A planner can return a mathematically valid path through a map that is stale or misregistered. A controller can track that path accurately while the localization estimate is wrong. Inspect each subsystem before treating the whole task as one opaque failure.

The map, odom, and base_link frames serve different purposes. Odometry is useful for locally continuous motion but can drift; a global localization estimate can correct drift and may jump. The transform tree must connect them consistently. Robot footprint and obstacle inflation affect which spaces are considered traversable. A point-sized path checker can accept a corridor that the actual robot body cannot enter.

sections.heading: Use a documented generic robot first
sections.body:
The official Nav2 quickstart provides a simulated TurtleBot environment for Jazzy. That environment is a foundation exercise, not a Unitree or AGIBOT integration. After installing the documented packages, launch the simulation with the command below. Inspect the world and initialize the robot pose in RViz using the 2D Pose Estimate tool. Check localization and the transform tree before issuing a goal.

Select three goal poses in free space and record them before running trials. A pose includes heading as well as position. Use the RViz navigation goal tool to send a goal, then observe action status, planned path, robot motion, and final pose. If the task aborts, preserve the failure and inspect the first relevant diagnostic. Repeatedly clicking the same goal without understanding state can obscure whether a new goal replaced an old one.
sections.code:
# After following the pinned Nav2 Jazzy installation source:
source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash
ros2 launch nav2_bringup tb3_simulation_launch.py headless:=False
# Inspect from another sourced terminal:
ros2 action list -t
ros2 topic list -t
ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map base_link

sections.heading: Measure the task you actually promised
sections.body:
Define success before collecting results: the action succeeds, final position and heading are within stated tolerances, no forbidden contact occurs, and elapsed time is below a declared limit. The tolerances in your exercise must be labeled course choices rather than manufacturer claims. Run the same goal set from documented initial conditions. Include an intentionally unreachable goal or blocked route and check for a bounded, explainable failure.

Recovery behavior is part of the application contract. A behavior such as rotating or backing up may be acceptable in an open simulator and unacceptable near an obstacle or person on hardware. Do not equate a configured recovery plugin with permission to execute it everywhere. When moving toward a vendor platform, verify its locomotion interface, footprint, sensor coverage, localization, timing, and supported command semantics independently. Nav2 availability does not establish that any named humanoid has a ready-to-use navigation driver.

lab.title: Evaluate three navigation goals and one failure
lab.environment: Official Jazzy Nav2 quickstart simulator with Gazebo; RViz; local simulation domain
lab.safety: Only the generic simulated robot may move. Do not bridge its velocity commands to a physical platform.
steps: Install and launch the exact Jazzy quickstart configuration linked in sources.
Set the initial pose and verify the map-to-base transform and visible localization state.
Record three free-space goal poses, tolerances, and a timeout before testing.
Execute the goals, collecting outcome, duration, final pose error, and any recovery behavior.
Try one deliberately unreachable goal and document how the system terminates or times out.
lab.expected: The report contains successes and failures with predefined criteria, not just a screenshot of a planned path.
acceptance: Initial pose and goal heading are documented
A planned path is never counted as completed navigation
The failed scenario has a bounded observation window and recorded outcome

troubleshooting.symptom: No map-to-base transform exists
troubleshooting.cause: Localization or initial pose is not established
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect frame connectivity and initialize the pose according to the quickstart.

troubleshooting.symptom: The path crosses space the body cannot fit through
troubleshooting.cause: Footprint or obstacle representation may be wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Review footprint, inflation, and map alignment before changing planner weights.

questions.prompt: A global path is returned. Which outcome is still unproven?
choices: A planning request was processed
A planner produced a path
The robot actually reached the goal under the acceptance constraints
The path data exists
questions.explanation: Planning is an intermediate result. Execution and final task criteria must be checked independently.

questions.prompt: Why can a point-robot plan fail for a real body?
choices: ROS requires circular robots
All planners ignore geometry
Maps cannot contain walls
The footprint and clearance requirements may exclude that path
questions.explanation: Robot geometry and clearance turn point reachability into a different problem.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest way to evaluate a navigation change?
choices: Use a fixed documented scenario set and predefined success criteria
Show only the best video
Count every recovery as success
Choose tolerances after seeing the result
questions.explanation: Predefined scenarios and criteria reduce selective reporting and permit meaningful comparison.

lessons.title: Kinematics, collision checking, and manipulation execution
lessons.summary: Solve a planar arm example and connect the result to MoveIt concepts. Distinguish reachable poses from collision-free trajectories and verified grasp outcomes.
objectives: Compute forward kinematics for a two-link arm
Identify unreachable targets and multiple inverse solutions
Explain planning-scene and trajectory-execution responsibilities
prerequisites: Trigonometry; Python 3; optional MoveIt tutorial environment

sections.heading: Kinematics describes geometry, not task success
sections.body:
Forward kinematics maps joint positions to an end-effector pose. Inverse kinematics seeks joint positions that realize a desired pose. A target may be unreachable, admit multiple solutions, or lie near a singularity where small Cartesian changes require large joint changes. A valid inverse solution also needs joint limits and collision checks. None of these geometric calculations establishes that an object will remain grasped.

For a planar arm with link lengths L1 and L2, x = L1 cos(q1) + L2 cos(q1 + q2), and y = L1 sin(q1) + L2 sin(q1 + q2). The reachable radial distance lies between |L1 − L2| and L1 + L2, before considering joint limits or obstacles. This simple model lets you test reasoning that later appears inside much more capable planning systems.

sections.heading: Work both inverse-kinematics branches
sections.body:
The law of cosines gives cos(q2) = (x² + y² − L1² − L2²)/(2 L1 L2). A value outside [-1, 1] indicates an unreachable target under this model, apart from tiny floating-point tolerance. Choosing positive or negative q2 yields elbow-up and elbow-down branches. q1 then accounts for the direction to the target and the triangle formed by the two links.

The complete example computes both branches and checks them through forward kinematics. That round trip verifies the geometry for the chosen target. It does not include joint limits, self-collision, payload, contact, or actuator dynamics. These omissions are explicit so the result cannot be mistaken for a ready-to-execute trajectory on a dexterous hand or humanoid arm.

sections.heading: Planning and execution use additional contracts
sections.body:
MoveIt combines robot and semantic descriptions, a planning scene, kinematics, planning algorithms, and execution interfaces. A planning scene must include relevant collision objects and attached bodies. If an object is grasped, its geometry and attachment affect subsequent collision checks. A plan computed from an old joint state or incomplete scene can be invalid by the time execution begins.

A trajectory adds time and joint motion constraints to a geometric path. Its controller interface must agree on joint names, order, units, and supported tolerances. Execution success should be checked against observed state, not assumed because a planner returned a result. For manipulation tasks, define object-level success: stable grasp, acceptable pose error, no forbidden contact, and correct release. A video of a hand closing is not evidence that the commanded grasp force, object retention, or tactile feedback works as intended.

Near full extension, compare small target displacements with the resulting joint-angle changes. This makes sensitivity visible and motivates avoiding configurations where limited sensing or actuator resolution causes large task errors.

lab.title: Solve and challenge a two-link arm
lab.environment: Python 3 offline; optional MoveIt tutorial setup for a separate planning-only extension
lab.safety: The toy joint solutions must never be sent to physical arms or hands. They have no vendor joint mapping or collision model.
steps: Run the complete inverse/forward-kinematics example.
Test targets inside, outside, and at the edge of the ideal reachable annulus.
Add invented joint limits and determine which of the two branches remain admissible.
Sketch an obstacle that invalidates one branch, explaining why endpoint reachability is insufficient.
Write a MoveIt integration checklist covering model, planning scene, state freshness, controller contract, and object-level success.
lab.expected: Both branches reach the sample target; additional constraints can reject a geometrically valid branch.
acceptance: Forward checks validate every returned inverse solution
Unreachable targets produce explicit failure
Planning success and object-level success are separate criteria

troubleshooting.symptom: acos reports a domain error
troubleshooting.cause: The target is unreachable or roundoff lies just outside the valid interval
troubleshooting.fix: Check reachability first; use a small justified tolerance only for numerical boundary error.

troubleshooting.symptom: A solved pose collides with an obstacle
troubleshooting.cause: Inverse kinematics did not include collision constraints
troubleshooting.fix: Evaluate the full configuration and path against the scene before considering execution.

questions.prompt: An inverse-kinematics solution reaches the target. What remains to check?
choices: Nothing
Joint limits, collision, trajectory feasibility, and task constraints
Only the target filename
Only whether both angles are positive
questions.explanation: IK establishes a geometric relationship. It does not include every physical or task constraint.

questions.prompt: For links 0.4 m and 0.3 m, is an ideal target 0.9 m from the base reachable?
choices: Yes, if the quaternion is normalized
Yes, by choosing the other elbow branch
No, maximum radial reach is 0.7 m
Only with a different topic name
questions.explanation: The maximum extension is the sum of link lengths. Changing branches does not increase it.

questions.prompt: A hand closes around an object in a video. Which claim is unsupported without more evidence?
choices: The scene was rendered or recorded
A closing motion occurred
The fingers visibly moved
The object meets a quantified stable-grasp acceptance test
questions.explanation: Stable retention and force/contact behavior require explicit measurements and tests beyond visible closure.

lessons.title: Separate AGIBOT G1, GO-1 and the dataset
lessons.summary: Map the research platform, recorded demonstrations and learned policy as different artifacts. Establish what each source actually supports.
objectives: Distinguish hardware, dataset and policy identities
Build an artifact provenance manifest
Limit transfer claims to verified evidence

sections.heading: Similar names conceal different objects
sections.body: AGIBOT G1 is the robotic collection platform described in the AgiBot World project. GO-1 means Genie Operator-1, the project's learned policy family. Unitree G1 is a different manufacturer's humanoid, while Unitree Go1 is a quadruped. These are four different identities. A search result containing G1 or go1 is therefore insufficient evidence for an SDK choice. In your project manifest, use explicit manufacturer, artifact type and full name. This eliminates ambiguous imports, folder names and course prerequisites. A policy repository may contain robot deployment examples, but that does not turn the policy itself into a robot model or a universal hardware driver.

sections.heading: A research stack contains separate releases
sections.body: The project combines collected demonstrations, task descriptions, model checkpoints, preprocessing tools, training code and evaluation environments. Each artifact can have its own revision and conditions of use. A model checkpoint trained on one observation convention can be incompatible with a converter that changes camera ordering or action normalization. Preserve the dataset snapshot, converter commit, checkpoint revision, configuration and environment together. A Git repository SHA does not identify a separately downloaded checkpoint unless you record that too. Think of the experiment as a set of linked artifacts rather than one folder named latest. Reproducibility depends on the relationships between them.

sections.heading: Public availability is not unrestricted reuse
sections.body: The current GO-1 model card states CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and the Alpha dataset access page states the same license with an access agreement. Keep links to the original source and require learners to obtain their own authorized access. This LMS supplies original instruction and synthetic exercises; it does not mirror datasets or model weights. Do not assume that a code license automatically covers data or checkpoints, or that the ability to download establishes permission for every commercial deployment. Record the applicable terms at the artifact boundary and route unresolved use questions to the rights holder or appropriate review. This preserves the course's usefulness without inventing permissions.

sections.heading: Demonstrated research is not universal deployment
sections.body: A reported benchmark evaluates a defined configuration and distribution. It does not establish that a purchased robot with different grippers, camera placements or control interfaces can execute the same checkpoint directly. Build an evidence ladder: source establishes identity, code establishes an interface, offline inference establishes a numerical output, simulation establishes behavior under a model, and supervised hardware tests establish behavior in the tested physical conditions. Each step answers a different question. The lab asks you to classify claims using this ladder, including several deliberately overbroad claims. That skill prevents marketing language or a working import from becoming an unsupported statement about physical autonomy.

lab.title: Create an artifact and claim register
lab.environment: Offline browser, official sources and a text editor
lab.safety: No data agreement is accepted and no checkpoint is downloaded by this exercise.
steps: List AGIBOT G1, Unitree G1, Unitree Go1 and GO-1 with manufacturer and artifact type.
Create separate manifest entries for dataset, converter, checkpoint, code and evaluation environment.
Record the stated dataset/model access and license conditions with source links.
Classify five claims by the evidence needed: import, inference, benchmark, simulation and real deployment.
Reject an unsupported claim that the released policy controls every robot named G1.
lab.expected: Every artifact and deployment claim has an unambiguous identity and evidence requirement.
acceptance: All four names remain distinct
Checkpoint and code revisions are separate
No unsupported cross-robot compatibility is asserted

troubleshooting.symptom: Search results appear to contradict one another
troubleshooting.cause: The query may mix hardware and policy names
troubleshooting.fix: Add manufacturer, artifact type and exact repository to the lookup

questions.prompt: What is AGIBOT GO-1?
choices: A Unitree quadruped
An AGIBOT hardware transport protocol
A motion-control firmware release for X2
The Genie Operator-1 policy family
questions.explanation: GO-1 is a learned policy; Unitree Go1 is a separate physical robot.

questions.prompt: Does a code commit identify the downloaded model weights automatically?
choices: No, checkpoint revision must be recorded separately
Yes
Only if both artifacts were downloaded on the same day
Only if the checkpoint is stored beside the code
questions.explanation: The checkpoint is a separately versioned artifact and can change independently.

questions.prompt: A model returns an action array offline. What does that prove?
choices: Commercial license clearance
Numerical inference under that input contract
Universal hardware compatibility
Safe grasping on the learner robot
questions.explanation: Inference establishes an output, not physical validity or usage rights.

lessons.title: Audit a demonstration before training on it
lessons.summary: Inspect episode integrity, timestamps and state/action semantics on a small authorized sample. Detect leakage and mislabeled command data before expensive training.
objectives: Validate episode boundaries and temporal integrity
Distinguish commanded action from measured state
Construct a leakage-resistant split
prerequisites: Authorized sample access or synthetic fixture

sections.heading: The episode is the unit of reasoning
sections.body: A demonstration is a temporal record of a robot attempting a task. Inspect an entire short episode before treating individual frames as independent training examples. Record task identity, episode identity, camera streams, state, action, timestamps and annotation intervals. Check that required files exist and that their lengths and time coverage agree. A video can play correctly while proprioceptive data ends early or action labels use a different time base. An apparently large dataset can contain many correlated views of the same attempts, so count usable episodes and task coverage in addition to frames. Storage size is not a measure of learning value.

sections.heading: State and action are different signals
sections.body: Measured state describes what the robot observed or achieved. Action records describe what the controller was instructed to do. They need not be equal, especially during acceleration, contact, saturation or a failed attempt. Training against measured next state instead of the intended action can change the learning problem without an obvious shape error. The official dataset describes distinct action and state structures and uses different conventions for some effector observations and commands. Build a field dictionary with units, dimensions, indexing and meaning. Do not concatenate everything named position into one vector before understanding whether it refers to joint angle, Cartesian location or gripper opening.

sections.heading: Time integrity determines causal meaning
sections.body: For each stream, inspect monotonicity, duplicates, gaps and alignment with the action clock. A camera image from after a motion paired with an earlier state can leak information that will not exist at deployment time. Decide how to handle missing observations: reject the episode, mask the sample or resample with a documented rule. Blindly forward-filling across a long gap can create an artificial stationary period. Preserve an exclusion log with reasons. Data cleaning should produce an auditable new artifact, not silently mutate the original demonstration. Keep the raw sample immutable so another person can inspect the decision.

sections.heading: Split by what you want to generalize
sections.body: Randomly dividing adjacent frames between training and validation produces an easy test of near-duplicates. Start with episode-disjoint splits, then consider scene, object, operator or task separation depending on the research question. A within-task held-out episode asks a different question from an unseen object or task. Write the intended generalization claim before choosing the split. Use a small synthetic fixture containing duplicates and deliberately misordered timestamps to test your audit code. On authorized real data, report how many episodes were inspected, excluded and retained. A good audit can reveal that a planned experiment is underpowered or invalid before any GPU time is consumed.

lab.title: Build a demonstration audit report
lab.environment: Synthetic episode fixture or a small authorized AgiBot World sample
lab.safety: Do not download the full corpus automatically or redistribute licensed samples.
steps: Create an inventory of required streams and a field dictionary.
Check timestamps, sequence lengths, missing values and annotation boundaries.
Compare action and state semantics instead of assuming identical scales.
Identify duplicate episodes and build episode-disjoint train/validation lists.
Export an exclusion log with one reason per rejected episode.
lab.expected: The audit produces reproducible usable-episode lists and explicit data-quality findings.
acceptance: No episode appears in both splits
Nonmonotonic time is detected
State and action fields remain semantically distinct

troubleshooting.symptom: Validation looks excellent after a random frame split
troubleshooting.cause: Adjacent frames or duplicate episodes may leak across splits
troubleshooting.fix: Rebuild disjoint episode or scene splits according to the intended claim

questions.prompt: Why is a random frame split often misleading?
choices: Nearby frames can appear in both training and validation
It guarantees an object-disjoint evaluation
It necessarily changes the number of episodes available
The optimizer requires adjacent frames to stay together
questions.explanation: Near-duplicate observations make validation easier than genuine generalization.

questions.prompt: Should commanded action equal measured state in every sample?
choices: Only when actions are stored as floating-point values
Only when both arrays share the same shape
Yes
No, dynamics and tracking create meaningful differences
questions.explanation: Actions express intent while state records response; treating them as identical changes the learning problem.

questions.prompt: What is the right handling of an excluded episode?
choices: Keep an immutable original and a reasoned exclusion record
Add it to both splits
Delete it silently
Replace its data with zeros
questions.explanation: An exclusion log makes preprocessing decisions reviewable and reproducible.

lessons.title: Map observations and actions without changing their meaning
lessons.summary: Follow the actual GO-1 preprocessing and inference contract. Validate dimensions, camera roles, normalization and action timing with synthetic round-trip tests.
objectives: Audit observation-to-model key mapping
Verify normalization statistics and ordering
Explain action chunks in physical time

sections.heading: Shapes are necessary but not sufficient
sections.body: A model can accept an array of the expected size while receiving the wrong meaning in every slot. A left-arm state placed in the right-arm position remains a valid tensor. A wrist image substituted for a head image can also have the same dimensions. Read the pinned deployment code and configuration together to map external payload keys into the model's internal camera, language and state fields. Write a semantic contract that includes physical role, order, unit, coordinate frame and preprocessing. Test that contract with labeled synthetic values before loading a large model. Shape validation alone is a weak defense against embodiment mismatch.

sections.heading: Normalize with the matching experiment
sections.body: The GO-1 inference implementation uses saved state and action statistics when normalization is enabled. Those statistics belong to a particular training pipeline and variable ordering. Applying statistics from another dataset can yield finite but nonsensical commands. For a simple z-score transform, subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation; inversion restores the original scale. The implementation includes a small numerical stabilization in normalization. Preserve the exact behavior used by the checkpoint rather than casually rewriting it. Check that statistics have the expected length and finite values, then perform a round-trip test with asymmetric synthetic vectors. Record the statistics file digest alongside the checkpoint revision.

sections.heading: Action chunks occupy time
sections.body: A chunk is a sequence of future actions, not an unordered batch. Its duration depends on the control frequency. Thirty actions at thirty hertz represent about one second of command horizon; thirty actions at ten hertz represent about three seconds. The official LIBERO configuration changes both action chunk size and control frequency for its environment. This is an example-specific choice, not a universal recommendation for the learner's robot. Changing frequency without reconsidering action semantics, interpolation and observation timing can alter the behavior dramatically. State whether actions represent absolute targets, increments or another defined quantity before resampling them.

sections.heading: Validate the adapter independently
sections.body: Build an offline adapter that reads a small fixture, selects cameras by named role, reorders state according to a declared mapping, normalizes with a matching statistics object and checks the output schema. Reject missing images, unknown fields, nonfinite data, mismatched statistics and unsupported action dimensions. Generate one intentionally swapped camera-role fixture and ensure the manifest catches it even though the pixels have the correct dimensions. This lab does not run a policy or issue commands. It establishes that your software can preserve a known observation/action meaning across the interface, which is a prerequisite for interpreting any later inference result.

lab.title: Test the GO-1 data adapter
lab.environment: Offline Python arrays and synthetic images; no checkpoint needed
lab.safety: All generated values are synthetic and must not be sent to a robot.
steps: Extract the observation mapping from the pinned deployment and selected configuration.
Create distinct synthetic values for each state/action slot and named camera role.
Implement normalization and inverse conversion using a synthetic statistics file.
Test missing cameras, swapped roles, wrong dimensions and nonfinite statistics.
Calculate chunk horizon for two frequency/chunk combinations and document interpretation.
lab.expected: The adapter passes semantic round-trip tests and rejects incompatible records.
acceptance: Camera roles are explicit
Statistics identity is tied to the experiment
Chunk horizon changes are calculated correctly

troubleshooting.symptom: The output shape is correct but actions are implausible
troubleshooting.cause: Variable order, units or normalization may be wrong
troubleshooting.fix: Use labeled asymmetric fixtures and compare the exact statistics ordering

questions.prompt: Why can a correct tensor shape still be wrong?
choices: The slots can contain different physical meanings
Model loading automatically corrects variable order
Numerical ranges alone determine physical meaning
Camera roles can always be inferred from image dimensions
questions.explanation: Dimensions do not encode joint identity, unit or camera placement.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate horizon of 30 actions at 10Hz?
choices: 3 seconds
0.3 seconds
30 seconds
1 second
questions.explanation: Thirty sequential actions divided by ten actions per second yields three seconds.

questions.prompt: Which statistics should inverse-normalize an output?
choices: The matching training experiment statistics and variable order
Any dataset with the same length
The latest file on disk
A constant mean of zero always
questions.explanation: Statistics are part of the checkpoint's semantic contract, not an interchangeable convenience.

lessons.title: Design a fine-tuning experiment you can afford and interpret
lessons.summary: Turn the official LIBERO configuration into a reproducible experiment plan. Separate compute feasibility, trainable parameters and valid evaluation.
objectives: Explain full versus action-expert fine-tuning
Lock data, model and environment revisions
Define a small smoke test before a full run

sections.heading: Start from a question, not a GPU
sections.body: A fine-tuning run should answer a specific question: whether a policy improves on a defined held-out task distribution after a particular adaptation. State the baseline, training data, evaluation split, budget and success measure first. Otherwise a lower training loss may become the only result you can report, even though it does not demonstrate useful behavior. The official repository provides a LIBERO fine-tuning configuration with dataset, model, training and space arguments. Treat it as a worked example. Its state/action dimensions and ten-hertz setup belong to that environment and must not be copied into an unrelated robot configuration because the code runs.

sections.heading: Freezing changes the experiment
sections.body: Full fine-tuning adjusts a larger portion of the model; partial fine-tuning leaves selected components fixed and trains a subset such as the action expert. These approaches have different memory and optimization requirements and answer different adaptation questions. Record exactly which parameters are trainable, not just the phrase lightweight training. The vendor repository publishes approximate memory guidance, but your actual usage depends on batch size, sequence length, precision, optimizer state and implementation. Measure a small initialization and forward/backward smoke test on the intended machine before reserving a long job. An out-of-memory failure during setup is a feasibility finding, not a failed robot policy.

sections.heading: Preserve the entire run specification
sections.body: Save code commit, environment lock, checkpoint revision, dataset revision, split files, normalization statistics, configuration, random seeds and trainable-parameter summary. Record the effective batch size, including accumulation and device count. A run name alone is not enough. Keep training and evaluation data transformations separate where appropriate; augmentation or normalization leakage can change what validation measures. The official configuration includes fields that alter behavior in debug mode, so capture the resolved configuration rather than only the source file. Two runs launched from the same file can differ because environment variables or command-line overrides changed their effective settings.

sections.heading: Use small gates before large expense
sections.body: First validate the data loader on a handful of records and inspect decoded observations. Next run a tiny training smoke test to confirm finite loss, parameter updates and checkpoint save/reload. Then deliberately overfit a very small training subset as a diagnostic, while clearly labeling that it is not a generalization result. Finally evaluate on the frozen held-out split using a specified protocol. Monitor failure cases and retain unsuccessful runs rather than selecting only attractive curves. The lab asks for this plan and resolved configuration; it does not claim to have trained a checkpoint. Learners with authorized data and compute can execute the plan as an additional evidence stage.

lab.title: Create a costed reproducible fine-tuning plan
lab.environment: Offline configuration review; optional authorized GPU smoke test
lab.safety: Do not launch expensive training or download gated data as part of the default exercise.
steps: Inspect the official LIBERO configuration and list all embodiment-specific settings.
Define one baseline and one adaptation hypothesis with a fixed held-out split.
Create a resolved run manifest including trainable components and effective batch size.
Specify data-loader, finite-loss, checkpoint-reload and tiny-overfit smoke gates.
Estimate memory and time as provisional values and state how they will be measured.
lab.expected: The plan can be executed and interpreted without changing its success criteria afterward.
acceptance: LIBERO dimensions are not reused as universal dimensions
Trainable components are explicit
No unrun training result is claimed

troubleshooting.symptom: Two nominally identical runs diverge in setup
troubleshooting.cause: Environment overrides or unresolved debug settings differ
troubleshooting.fix: Compare resolved configurations, artifact revisions and trainable-parameter summaries

questions.prompt: What does lower training loss establish by itself?
choices: Safe hardware deployment
Improved fit to the training objective
A correct action mapping on the physical target
Successful generalization
questions.explanation: Generalization and behavior require held-out evaluation; training loss is a narrower measure.

questions.prompt: Why capture resolved configuration?
choices: It proves the exact same training outcome will recur
It establishes that the held-out split has no duplicates
Environment variables and overrides can change effective settings
Source files are never useful
questions.explanation: The executed settings may differ from defaults visible in a source file.

questions.prompt: What is a tiny-overfit test for?
choices: Replacing held-out evaluation
Claiming broad task success
Checking that the training pipeline can learn a small known subset
Measuring all-world reliability
questions.explanation: Overfitting a tiny subset is a diagnostic of pipeline function, not evidence of generalization.

lessons.title: Evaluate policy behavior beyond open-loop error
lessons.summary: Separate numerical action agreement from closed-loop task success. Build a repeatable evaluation with failures, uncertainty and inference latency.
objectives: Compare open-loop and closed-loop measures
Define task success before trials
Interpret timing and sample size honestly
prerequisites: Authorized checkpoint and official simulation environment for optional execution

sections.heading: Open-loop evaluation asks a limited question
sections.body: Given a recorded observation, a policy predicts actions that can be compared with a demonstration. This is useful for finding gross scaling, mapping and modeling errors. It does not show how the policy behaves after its own previous action changes the world. A small initial error can move the robot into observations absent from the demonstration, causing later errors to compound. Conversely, two different actions can both complete a task, so exact action agreement is not the only meaningful objective. Preserve open-loop metrics as diagnostics and label them correctly rather than presenting them as physical success rates.

sections.heading: Closed-loop trials need a fixed protocol
sections.body: A closed-loop trial feeds policy actions into an environment, observes the resulting state and continues until success, timeout or failure. Specify task set, initial-state distribution, random seeds, reset procedure, horizon and success rule before evaluating. Include a baseline under the same protocol. The official repository provides a LIBERO evaluation route, which is a concrete place to learn this workflow without implying direct compatibility with X2 or G1 hardware. A local environment that visually resembles a benchmark is not necessarily the same benchmark if reward logic, object placement or action scaling changed. Record all deviations. Keep environment resets reproducible and preserve the exact initial-state identifiers with each reported trial.

sections.heading: Count attempts and inspect failures
sections.body: Report total attempts, successes, timeouts and invalid runs with exclusion reasons. Do not remove difficult starts after seeing the outcome. A small sample has wide uncertainty even when the observed percentage looks impressive. Compare results at the same task and seed granularity where possible, and inspect failure categories such as missed grasp, wrong object, collision, stale observation or timeout. A single aggregate number can hide that one task improved while another became unusable. Save representative unsuccessful traces alongside successes. They are often more informative for the next development decision than another polished successful clip.

sections.heading: Latency changes closed-loop behavior
sections.body: An inference server adds capture, encoding, transport, queueing, model computation and return delay. The policy code's measured model time is not the complete observation-to-action latency. Action chunks can reduce how often inference is requested, but they also commit more future intent before a fresh observation. Measure the age of the observation when each command would be consumed. In simulation, inject additional delay and dropped responses to evaluate the supervisor's behavior. The final report must distinguish benchmark task performance from deployment readiness. A simulated success rate cannot establish real actuator limits, communication robustness or the appropriateness of the same policy on a different embodiment.

lab.title: Write and run a bounded policy evaluation
lab.environment: Official LIBERO setup with authorized artifacts, or offline trial-log fixture
lab.safety: Do not connect the policy server to a physical robot in this lab.
steps: Freeze the task set, seeds, horizon, baseline and success criteria.
Run a small closed-loop simulator trial set if compute is available; otherwise audit a clearly labeled synthetic trial log.
Record every attempt, result, timeout and exclusion.
Compare open-loop diagnostics with task outcomes and categorize failures.
Inject response delay or dropout and measure whether stale actions are rejected.
lab.expected: The report presents reproducible observations and their limits without hiding failed attempts.
acceptance: All attempts appear in the denominator
Open-loop error is not called task success
Injected latency cannot silently execute stale intent

troubleshooting.symptom: Open-loop error improves but task success falls
troubleshooting.cause: Compounding errors, distribution shift or timing may dominate
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect closed-loop traces and compare the same initial states and latency conditions

questions.prompt: Why can low open-loop error coexist with poor task success?
choices: Every alternative action is necessarily incorrect
The metric is always wrong
The measured state must always equal the commanded action
The policy changes its own future observations and errors can compound
questions.explanation: Recorded-observation prediction does not test the feedback consequences of prior actions.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a trial ledger?
choices: Only trials where the environment reported a successful reset
An aggregate percentage without attempt-level outcomes
All attempts and explicit exclusion reasons
Only successful clips
questions.explanation: Complete accounting prevents selective reporting and makes the denominator interpretable.

questions.prompt: What does model compute time omit?
choices: Only the camera image dimensions
Only the numerical precision chosen for inference
A completed state transition without observing the robot
Capture, transport, queueing and command-consumption delay
questions.explanation: End-to-end latency spans the entire observation-to-action path.

lessons.title: Capstone: prove an embodiment adapter before deployment
lessons.summary: Build an evidence-based transfer dossier for one specific robot configuration. Stop unsupported action mappings from reaching a controller.
objectives: Audit an embodiment transfer contract
Define shadow-mode and supervised gates
Produce a defensible deployment decision

sections.heading: Transfer is a mapping problem before a learning problem
sections.body: A policy output must acquire an exact physical meaning on the target robot. List each action component, unit, reference frame, target or delta interpretation, controller interface, rate and limit source. Then compare the source embodiment with the target: arm kinematics, gripper behavior, camera placement, state availability, mounting and firmware. Equal vector lengths do not establish compatibility. The official project includes embodiment-specific examples such as AgileX, demonstrating that deployment requires a particular integration. This course does not infer a turnkey GO-1 driver for X2, D1 or a purchased G1 configuration from the existence of a generalist checkpoint.

sections.heading: Build the adapter as a reject-by-default boundary
sections.body: The adapter should accept only a recognized artifact and configuration combination. Validate model identity, observation freshness, required cameras, state ordering, output dimensions and finite values before considering any command. Unknown action dimensions or missing camera roles should produce an explicit rejection, not silent truncation, padding or duplication. Limits must come from the target's approved model and procedure, and constraints may be coupled across joints. Clipping each scalar independently is not enough to prove that the resulting whole-body motion is feasible. Preserve the raw output and rejection reason for investigation without forwarding it to the hardware controller.

sections.heading: Progress through evidence gates
sections.body: Begin with offline contract tests, then recorded-data inference and shadow mode where actions are logged but not executed. Continue to an appropriate simulator and only then an operator-reviewed physical procedure. Shadow mode reveals timing and mapping faults while retaining human control, but it cannot establish the outcome of actions that were never applied. Hardware evaluation needs an independent stop mechanism, clear command ownership, bounded task and a trained operator using the device procedure. Keep the learned policy out of the role of deciding whether its own actions satisfy the entire safety contract. A separate supervisor can enforce tested conditions and reject stale or unsupported intent.

sections.heading: Make the final decision reviewable
sections.body: The capstone dossier contains source and target manifests, mapping table, rights/access record, artifact revisions, tests, timing measurements, failure traces and unresolved questions. Every compatibility claim points to evidence. If no official SDK or deployment contract is available for part of the target platform, mark that stage access-limited and complete the offline work instead of inventing an API. The best outcome can be a qualified not-ready decision that names exactly what would change it. The learner earns completion by demonstrating technical reasoning and reproducible evidence, not by asserting that a robot moved. This is a meaningful expert-level skill: managing the boundary between a promising research model and an accountable physical system.

lab.title: Deliver a policy-transfer readiness dossier
lab.environment: Offline target configuration and authorized research artifacts
lab.safety: No policy output is connected to physical actuation. Hardware gates require the real target procedure.
steps: Choose one exact target configuration and write the source-to-target action/observation map.
Implement a reject-by-default schema validator using synthetic valid and invalid outputs.
Specify recorded-data, shadow, simulation and supervised physical gates with measurable acceptance.
Inject missing cameras, wrong dimensions, stale state, nonfinite output and controller ownership loss.
Write a ready-for-next-stage or not-ready decision citing evidence and outstanding dependencies.
lab.expected: Unsupported output is rejected and the next permitted evidence stage is explicit.
acceptance: Equal dimension is not treated as compatibility
Every injected invalid output is rejected
Unverified hardware/API stages remain visibly pending

troubleshooting.symptom: The team wants to truncate an action array to fit the robot
troubleshooting.cause: Output dimensions lack a validated physical mapping
troubleshooting.fix: Stop at the adapter boundary and obtain the correct embodiment contract or train a compatible policy

questions.prompt: Can an action vector be truncated to match fewer target joints?
choices: Only if the remaining values are within scalar limits
No, without a validated semantic mapping it changes the policy meaning
Yes if the values are small
Only if the source and target share a manufacturer
questions.explanation: Matching length by deletion does not establish which physical variables the policy intended.

questions.prompt: What does shadow mode establish?
choices: Physical grasp quality
Safe contact force
Timing and interface behavior while outputs remain unexecuted
The unexecuted policy would succeed
questions.explanation: Shadow mode tests observation and software paths, not the physical consequences of actions.

questions.prompt: What makes a not-ready capstone valuable?
choices: It identifies concrete missing evidence and the conditions for proceeding
It allows a successful compile to replace missing timing evidence
It permits skipping the remaining hardware gates
It establishes compatibility with future firmware
questions.explanation: A precise evidence gap is an actionable engineering result; invented readiness is not.

lessons.title: State estimation, uncertainty, and calibration
lessons.summary: Compute a scalar Kalman-style update and investigate why repeated biased measurements do not become accurate. Design a calibration test that keeps fitting data separate from validation data.
objectives: Distinguish measurement noise, bias, and state uncertainty
Calculate a one-dimensional weighted estimation update
Design calibration and held-out validation evidence

sections.heading: An estimate is a value plus assumptions
sections.body:
A sensor measures something related to state; an estimator combines measurements and a model to infer the state of interest. Noise describes variation, while bias describes a systematic offset. Averaging can reduce independent zero-mean noise, but it does not remove an unknown fixed bias. A precise-looking number can therefore be consistently wrong.

Uncertainty belongs to the quantity, frame, and time represented by the estimate. Covariance describes how uncertain components vary together under a model; it is not a decorative field to fill with zeros. An unrealistically small measurement covariance can cause a filter to overtrust a flawed sensor. Conversely, a large covariance can make a valid measurement have little influence. Choose values from characterization and revisit them when operating conditions change, rather than tuning solely until a plot looks smooth.

sections.heading: Work a scalar measurement update
sections.body:
For a one-dimensional prior estimate x with variance P and an independent measurement z with variance R, the simple linear update uses K = P/(P + R), x_new = x + K(z − x), and P_new = (1 − K)P. With x = 1.0 m, P = 0.04 m², z = 1.1 m, and R = 0.01 m², K is 0.8 and the updated estimate is 1.08 m. The more trusted measurement contributes more strongly.

This example omits the prediction step, multidimensional covariance, nonlinear motion, correlations, and timing. It is not an EKF implementation. Its purpose is to reveal the meaning of the weighting. If the measurement has an unmodeled positive bias, the update can become more confident in a wrong value. If two inputs share the same underlying data, treating them as independent can double-count information.
sections.code:
import math

def scalar_update(x, prior_variance, measurement, measurement_variance):
    if prior_variance < 0 or measurement_variance <= 0:
        raise ValueError("invalid variance")
    if not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in
               (x, prior_variance, measurement, measurement_variance)):
        raise ValueError("finite inputs required")
    gain = prior_variance / (prior_variance + measurement_variance)
    updated = x + gain * (measurement - x)
    variance = (1.0 - gain) * prior_variance
    return updated, variance, gain

estimate, variance, gain = scalar_update(1.0, 0.04, 1.1, 0.01)
assert math.isclose(estimate, 1.08)
assert math.isclose(variance, 0.008)
assert math.isclose(gain, 0.8)
print(estimate, variance, gain)

sections.heading: Calibration requires an independent reference
sections.body:
Calibration identifies parameters that connect raw measurements to the quantity you want: offsets, scales, sensor extrinsics, or time alignment. Define the reference instrument or known geometry, its uncertainty, and the range of conditions used. Fitting one stationary pose does not validate all joint angles, speeds, temperatures, or payloads. Preserve a held-out set of observations to test the fitted parameters.

For a hypothetical position sensor with a fixed offset, collect repeated readings at several known positions. Fit the offset on one subset and report residual error on another. Plot residual against position and time; a trend suggests the offset-only model is incomplete. When integrating robot_localization or another estimator, document the input frames, covariances, time sources, and which state components each sensor actually observes. A filter should not be used to disguise a calibration or frame error that belongs upstream.

lab.title: Quantify weighting and a calibration bias
lab.environment: Python 3 offline; invented one-dimensional measurements
lab.safety: No real sensor calibration is written. All units and noise assumptions belong to the teaching dataset.
steps: Run and manually verify the scalar update.
Repeat with measurement variance 0.1 and compare the gain and estimate.
Generate ten invented readings with a +0.05 m offset at each of three known positions.
Fit an offset on two positions and evaluate residuals at the held-out third position.
Add a scale error to a second dataset and show why an offset-only calibration fails.
lab.expected: The update weights change predictably with variance; held-out residuals expose an incomplete calibration model.
acceptance: Variance units are squared measurement units
Calibration and validation observations are separated
Systematic bias is distinguished from random noise

troubleshooting.symptom: The estimate is smooth but consistently displaced
troubleshooting.cause: A bias or frame error may be unmodeled
troubleshooting.fix: Compare against an independent reference and inspect residual trends before retuning covariance.

troubleshooting.symptom: The filter becomes overconfident
troubleshooting.cause: Correlated inputs or unrealistic covariance may be double-counted
troubleshooting.fix: Trace each input to its originating measurement and revise the independence assumption.

questions.prompt: Does averaging many readings remove a fixed +5 cm bias?
choices: No, the fixed offset remains unless modeled or calibrated
Only if the topic is reliable
Only in C++
Yes, all errors average away
questions.explanation: Averaging independent zero-mean noise reduces variation; a systematic offset remains.

questions.prompt: In the worked update, why is the gain 0.8?
choices: ROS chooses it randomly
The measurement variance is smaller than prior variance
The measurement is always correct
The distance is 0.8 m
questions.explanation: K = 0.04/(0.04+0.01) = 0.8. This weights the stated uncertainty model, not a guarantee of sensor truth.

questions.prompt: Why hold out calibration observations?
choices: Because calibration cannot use numbers
To hide failures
To test whether fitted parameters generalize beyond the fitting data
To reduce evidence quality
questions.explanation: Independent validation can reveal overfitting or an incomplete model that fitting residuals alone miss.

lessons.title: Demonstrations, behavior cloning, and data leakage
lessons.summary: Train a tiny imitation model from synthetic demonstrations and audit the dataset contract. Separate low prediction error from successful closed-loop behavior.
objectives: Define observation, action, timestamp, and episode contracts
Fit a simple behavior-cloning model and evaluate held-out episodes
Identify leakage, covariate shift, and deployment mismatches

sections.heading: Demonstrations are synchronized decisions
sections.body:
An imitation-learning dataset pairs observations with actions selected by a demonstrator. The pairing must reflect the information actually available when the action was chosen. If a camera frame is delayed or an action timestamp is shifted, a model can learn a relationship that never existed causally. Record episode boundaries, time sources, observation preprocessing, action units, controller mode, and whether actions are requested or realized.

A dataset also needs task labels, failure labels, intervention events, and a provenance record. Successful demonstrations alone may omit the states encountered after small mistakes. Do not silently discard failed attempts if your evaluation claim concerns realistic operation. Keep private imagery and collection permissions in the dataset governance plan. A public dataset or library being available does not establish that it contains the exact robot variant, sensor configuration, or end-effector contract you intend to use.

sections.heading: Behavior cloning is a prediction problem first
sections.body:
For a deliberately simple example, imagine demonstrations that choose a scalar action proportional to observed position error. Fitting action = gain × error by least squares gives gain = sum(error × action)/sum(error²). The complete code below learns a gain from invented training pairs and evaluates different pairs. It contains no neural network, vendor policy, or robot driver.

The training labels are constructed to make the mechanism inspectable. In a real dataset, action normalization, clipping, latency, and controller interpretation all affect the learned relationship. A low held-out prediction error supports only the stated supervised prediction task. Once the policy acts in a loop, its own errors change future observations, which can move the system outside the demonstration distribution. That distribution shift is a central reason closed-loop task evaluation is necessary.
sections.code:
train = [(-0.4, -0.8), (-0.2, -0.4), (0.1, 0.2), (0.3, 0.6)]
test = [(-0.3, -0.6), (0.2, 0.4)]
denominator = sum(error*error for error, action in train)
if denominator == 0:
    raise ValueError("training errors contain no information")
gain = sum(error*action for error, action in train) / denominator
mse = sum((gain*error-action)**2 for error, action in test) / len(test)
print({"learned_gain": gain, "held_out_mse": mse})
assert abs(gain-2.0) < 1e-12
assert mse < 1e-24

sections.heading: Split by the source of correlation
sections.body:
Adjacent video frames from one episode are highly related. Randomly splitting individual frames can place nearly identical scenes in training and test sets, creating an optimistic score. Split by episode, collection session, object instance, or environment according to the generalization claim. Keep preprocessing statistics fitted on training data only. Preserve a final test set that is not repeatedly used to choose hyperparameters.

Build a deployment contract for the exact observation order, image transformations, joint order, action units, normalization, history length, and inference rate. A policy file is incomplete without that contract. Then evaluate closed-loop success, intervention rate, constraint violations, and performance under held-out conditions. Approaches such as dataset aggregation address policy-induced distribution shift, but they still require a valid collection and supervision process. A course exercise that fits a scalar gain demonstrates learning mechanics, not dexterous manipulation competence.

lab.title: Fit a transparent imitation baseline
lab.environment: Python 3 offline; synthetic pairs only
lab.safety: Do not load or deploy a robot policy. The learned scalar gain is not a physical controller parameter.
steps: Run the complete behavior-cloning example and derive the fitted gain.
Add noise to training actions and measure the change on the unchanged test set.
Create a small episode manifest with session, object, and split fields; ensure no episode appears in multiple splits.
Describe one plausible timestamp-alignment error and how you would detect it.
Write a closed-loop evaluation plan with task success, interventions, and constraint violations.
lab.expected: The synthetic gain is recovered, and the dataset plan prevents obvious episode leakage.
acceptance: Training and evaluation examples are distinct
Correlated episodes are not split by individual frame
Low supervised error is not presented as robot task success

troubleshooting.symptom: Validation accuracy is unexpectedly perfect
troubleshooting.cause: Train and test may share near-duplicate frames or preprocessing leakage
troubleshooting.fix: Audit split membership by episode and fit transformations on training data only.

troubleshooting.symptom: A policy output has the right shape but causes the wrong behavior in a mock
troubleshooting.cause: Action order, units, normalization, or mode may differ
troubleshooting.fix: Compare the deployment contract field by field before further evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why can random frame-level splitting overstate generalization?
choices: All test sets are invalid
Behavior cloning never works
Frames cannot be numbered
Adjacent frames from the same episode can appear in both sets
questions.explanation: Strong correlation lets the test resemble training too closely. Split according to the intended generalization boundary.

questions.prompt: A model predicts held-out demonstration actions accurately. What remains untested?
choices: Closed-loop task behavior under its own induced observations
Whether the file has bytes
Whether arithmetic was performed
The reported supervised metric
questions.explanation: Actions change future observations. Prediction accuracy alone does not evaluate that feedback loop.

questions.prompt: Which item must accompany a robot policy checkpoint?
choices: Only a marketing video
Observation/action ordering, units, preprocessing, rate, and version contract
Only the file extension
A claim of universal compatibility
questions.explanation: The checkpoint depends on an exact deployment interface. Matching tensor shape alone is insufficient.

lessons.title: Reinforcement learning without reward self-deception
lessons.summary: Train a tiny tabular policy and evaluate it with fixed task criteria. Learn why return, task success, and hardware readiness are separate measurements.
objectives: Explain state, observation, action, reward, return, and termination
Run a seeded tabular Q-learning experiment
Compare a policy against a baseline on held-out conditions
prerequisites: Python 3; basic probability and discounted sums

sections.heading: The learning objective is a mathematical choice
sections.body:
In reinforcement learning, a policy selects actions from observations, and an environment produces subsequent observations and rewards. Return aggregates reward over time, often with discounting. The reward is a designer's numerical proxy for desired behavior, not the task itself. An agent can improve return by exploiting a loophole that violates the intended outcome. Define success and constraint violations independently so this discrepancy can be detected.

A state describes the information needed to predict the environment under the model; an observation may reveal only part of it. A policy trained with simulator-only quantities can fail when those quantities are unavailable on hardware. Likewise, action scaling, control decimation, and termination rules are part of the training environment. Exporting weights without these settings does not reproduce the trained system.

sections.heading: Use a small problem where every update is visible
sections.body:
The toy environment below has five positions on a line. The policy starts at zero, chooses left or right, and receives a terminal reward at position four. Each nonterminal step has a small cost. Q-learning updates an estimate of action value using reward plus discounted best next value. A seeded random generator makes this particular training run repeatable.

This is a tabular learning exercise, not a locomotion policy. The training environment is deterministic and completely observed, so its apparent competence says little about contact-rich dynamics. Inspect the learned action choices and evaluate without exploratory actions. Keep evaluation code separate from training updates; otherwise evaluation changes the policy being measured. Record episode count, seed, learning rate, discount, exploration policy, and the exact environment transition rule.
sections.code:
import random

rng = random.Random(7)
q = [[0.0, 0.0] for _ in range(5)]
alpha, gamma, epsilon = 0.3, 0.95, 0.2
for episode in range(300):
    state = 0
    for step in range(40):
        action = rng.randrange(2) if rng.random() < epsilon else max(range(2), key=lambda a: q[state][a])
        next_state = max(0, min(4, state + (-1 if action == 0 else 1)))
        done = next_state == 4
        reward = 1.0 if done else -0.01
        target = reward if done else reward + gamma * max(q[next_state])
        q[state][action] += alpha * (target - q[state][action])
        state = next_state
        if done:
            break

state, path = 0, [0]
for _ in range(10):
    action = max(range(2), key=lambda a: q[state][a])
    state = max(0, min(4, state + (-1 if action == 0 else 1)))
    path.append(state)
    if state == 4:
        break
print({"evaluation_path": path, "success": state == 4})
assert path == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

sections.heading: Evaluate generalization and failure, not only return
sections.body:
Compare against a simple baseline, such as always moving right in this environment. If the learned policy does not outperform a suitable baseline on the target metric, its added complexity needs justification. Repeat training across seeds and evaluate on conditions not used to select the policy. Report the full scenario set, sample counts, failures, and uncertainty rather than a single best rollout.

For robotics, simulation evaluation should include parameter uncertainty, observation delay, disturbances, and recovery behavior within a justified operating envelope. Randomization is useful only when its ranges represent plausible deployment variation. A high-return policy can still violate joint, contact, thermal, or task constraints. Physical deployment additionally requires the exact platform's supported control interface and supervised commissioning evidence. Neither a checkpoint nor a course completion badge substitutes for those requirements.

A useful evaluation table includes a row for every attempted condition, including crashes and timeouts. Excluding failed runs changes the denominator and can turn an unreliable method into an apparently successful one.

lab.title: Train, freeze, and compare a tabular policy
lab.environment: Python 3 offline; deterministic five-state teaching environment
lab.safety: No trained output is connected to ROS commands or robot hardware.

Implement an always-right baseline and compare steps-to-goal under the same conditions.

Report task success, episode length, and failures separately from reward.

acceptance: Evaluation does not update the policy
All tested seeds and conditions are reported
Return and task success are separate fields

troubleshooting.symptom: Evaluation results change because learning continues
troubleshooting.cause: Training updates were left enabled during evaluation
troubleshooting.fix: Freeze Q values and use a separate evaluation function.

troubleshooting.symptom: Return rises while the intended task becomes worse
troubleshooting.cause: The reward proxy allows an unintended strategy
troubleshooting.fix: Inspect trajectories and independent task metrics; revise the objective with held-out reevaluation.

questions.prompt: A policy gets higher reward by avoiding task completion indefinitely. What is the likely issue?
choices: The evaluation should hide the episode
The source code must be encrypted
The reward proxy or termination design does not match the task
The robot is necessarily expert
questions.explanation: The policy is optimizing the provided objective. Independent task criteria reveal reward loopholes.

questions.prompt: Why freeze the policy during evaluation?
choices: To remove all randomness from the world
To avoid recording failures
Learning is always harmful
To measure a defined policy rather than one changing during the test
questions.explanation: A stable policy version makes results attributable and comparable. Environmental randomness can still be evaluated.

questions.prompt: The always-right baseline matches the learned policy in the toy task. What is the defensible conclusion?
choices: Learning has not shown a task-performance advantage in that comparison
The baseline result should be removed
The robot is ready for deployment
The learned policy proves general intelligence
questions.explanation: A baseline tests whether added complexity buys useful performance. This simple task may not need learning.

lessons.title: Capstone: a reproducible inspection application
lessons.summary: Build an end-to-end simulated inspection task and defend its behavior under faults. Submit a reviewable evidence package scored against an explicit rubric.
objectives: Integrate interfaces, configuration, timing, and task logic
Demonstrate bounded failure handling and reproducible results
Separate simulation qualification from supervised hardware competence
prerequisites: A local Jazzy simulator or clearly labeled mock application; version-controlled workspace

sections.heading: The assignment has an observable outcome
sections.body:
Build a simulated inspection application that visits three documented locations, acquires a synthetic measurement at each, and produces a final report. A measurement counts only when its unit, frame or location association, and freshness satisfy the contract. Represent the inspection as an action with feedback and a terminal result. Define cancellation and partial completion explicitly. Reuse the generic Nav2 simulator if available; a mock state machine is acceptable only when its narrower scope is clearly labeled.

Before implementation, write a one-page contract covering inputs, outputs, topic and action types, clock assumptions, command ownership, goal criteria, and failure outcomes. Specify task success before running trials. The application should not count a visited location merely because a navigation goal was sent, nor accept a measurement because some number arrived. Completion must follow the verified state transition and its associated evidence.

sections.heading: Faults are required evidence
sections.body:
Run at least three nominal trials from documented initial conditions and preserve every result. Then exercise four faults: missing measurement source, stale measurement, unreachable navigation goal or mock equivalent, and cancellation during execution. For each fault, measure detection time, final task state, whether partial results are retained, and what permits a retry. The retry procedure must avoid duplicating results or assuming an uncertain prior task did nothing.

Save the environment manifest, source commit, launch configuration, model version, selected bag channels, test results, and an acceptance table. Include enough data to reproduce a failed run. A short screen recording can supplement evidence, but logs and machine-readable results should identify the conditions and outcomes. A reviewer should be able to trace each report entry back to the observation and code version that produced it.

sections.heading: The rubric rewards evidence over confidence
sections.body:
Score the project out of 100: interface and state-machine correctness, 20; reproducibility and configuration, 20; task and fault handling, 20; timing and data validity, 15; tests and diagnostic quality, 15; technical explanation and limits, 10. A score of 80 or more is a course assessment threshold only. Missing provenance, undisclosed mock behavior, or an unresolved command-ownership conflict prevents acceptance regardless of points.

The oral or written defense should explain one failure from first observation to root cause, justify a QoS and timeout choice, transform one reported position between frames, and identify the weakest remaining assumption. The reviewer should rerun one nominal scenario and one fault. Passing this simulation capstone establishes the documented software competencies. An expert hardware assessment is a separate supervised activity on the exact robot, firmware, SDK, hand, and approved operating procedure; it requires commissioning, recovery, and repeated physical task evidence.

sections.heading: Make the handoff usable by another engineer
sections.body: Package the project with a short start guide, a dependency manifest, a data dictionary, and a known-limitations file. Provide one command or clearly ordered procedure for the nominal run and one for a fault scenario. Label estimated durations and unexecuted tests. If a simulator or hardware resource was unavailable, leave that criterion incomplete rather than substituting an unrelated passing test. A useful handoff lets another engineer disagree with your conclusion by inspecting the same evidence.

lab.environment: Ubuntu 24.04/Jazzy with the documented Nav2 simulator; or an explicitly labeled offline mock with reduced assessment scope
lab.safety: The capstone runs only in simulation or a mock. Physical commissioning is outside this assessment and requires the matching vendor track and supervision.
